statement: Excellent scientific presentations do not share a single style; delivery ranging from humble and soft-spoken to charismatic can each succeed.
Stylistic diversity among successful presenters does not make every presentation style acceptable; most technical talks are weak rather than excellent.
A common failing of scientific presentations is stating too many unnecessary details about the work, which leaves the audience without the main takeaways.
Slides that follow PowerPoint's program defaults commonly fail to help the audience understand or remember the content.

Topic-phrase slide headlines such as a bare 'Background' leave a slide unfocused: they convey little to the audience during the talk and do not force the speaker to work out the slide's main assertion beforehand.
Bulleted subtopic lists are inherently weak at showing connections between ideas.
Bulleted-list slides invite a mind-numbing delivery in which the speaker repeatedly turns back to the screen to read off each listed item.
Because audiences, occasions, and topics vary so widely, fixed rules for giving a strong scientific presentation are hard to establish and the rules that exist carry exceptions.
The tell-them-three-times strategy (preview, tell, summarize) is not universally applicable and works poorly with audience members strongly biased against the results.
exception: when audience members hold a strong bias against the results being presented

statement: The frequently cited 6-by-6 slide rule has no research basis and conflicts with established findings about how people learn.
Presentation advice should be grounded in the observed traits of excellent presenters rather than stated as simplistic universal rules.
Presenting skill is learnable: presenters whose early talks were weak, such as Hertz, Oppenheimer, and Wu, became strong presenters later in their careers.
Slides that convey technical information should be built from succinct sentence assertions supported by visual evidence, in place of phrase headlines over bulleted subtopics.
condition: for slides carrying technical content

statement: The assertion-evidence slide structure leads to presentations that are more informative, more memorable, and more persuasive, a result the author attributes to test evidence.

Thirteen recurring critical errors account for much of the failure of scientific presentations at conferences, lectures, and technical meetings; some, such as losing composure, are widely recognized while others, such as trying to cover too much, are subtle.
Scientific presentations are expensive in aggregate hours because both the audience's attendance time and the speaker's preparation and delivery time are consumed, and travel raises the cost sharply.
Presentations carry far fresher results than journals — often days or hours old against months for a publication — so in fast-moving fields they are the primary channel for new technical advances.
condition: in fields where advances outpace the publication cycle

statement: The person who speaks about a scientific result tends to receive the public credit for it even when they explicitly acknowledge the collaborators who did the work, as in the Chu and Hermann superconductor announcements.
Work that is not presented effectively to specialists inside and outside the field is unlikely to be built upon by other researchers.
Managers who do not receive an intelligible presentation of technical work are unlikely to make sound institutional decisions about it.
Policymakers are a consequential audience for technical work because they legislate on scientifically grounded problems while very few of them hold science or engineering backgrounds.
Excellent scientific presentations are marked by three traits: content worth the audience's time, visible passion for that content, and a keen sense of the audience.
Content must never be sacrificed in a scientific presentation: the audience has to understand, believe, and remember it for the talk to excel.
Scientific presenters routinely sacrifice content by burying key findings among extraneous details or on busy, heavily decorated slides.
Strong content can carry a talk even when the speaker cannot follow standard advice on voice, stance, and movement, as with Stephen Hawking.
Speakers should show genuine enthusiasm for their subject rather than imitate another presenter's exuberance, because a manufactured display reads as disingenuous.
A speaker who does not show that they care about the subject cannot expect the audience to care, especially once the content becomes hard to follow.
When presenting an idea that runs against what the audience believes, even charismatic presenters soften the voice and adopt a quiet but earnest delivery while keeping the passion evident.
condition: when the idea cuts against the audience's existing beliefs

statement: A keen sense of the audience means knowing who they are, what they already know about the work, why they are listening, and what preconceptions they hold.
Without a keen sense of the audience, even a dynamic speaker with valuable content is likely to miss the mark.
Before designing a presentation, ask whether a document or web page would deliver the information better for this situation.

A presentation has five advantages over a document: fielding audience questions, reading audience expressions, using delivery for emphasis, using a wider range of visual aids, and assuring that the audience witnessed the content.

Speakers should deliberately allot time for questions; short presentations usually serve the audience better by holding questions to the end, while other talks are better served by taking them throughout.
condition: question timing depends on presentation length and format

statement: Audiences continually emit non-verbal cues of agreement, understanding, confusion, boredom, or disagreement, and the speaker must be watching for them and flexible enough to adjust mid-talk to exploit them.

When blank looks reveal that a term the work depends on has not landed, improvising a concrete on-the-spot demonstration of that term can rescue the talk, as when a researcher used a lighter's smoke to show laminar versus turbulent flow.
condition: when audience cues show a load-bearing concept has not been understood

statement: Delivery gives a presentation emphasis tools a document lacks: pausing before an important point, raising the voice or dropping to a whisper, gesturing, and moving closer to the audience.
A presentation supports visual aids a printed page cannot: moving image sequences, inexpensive color, and demonstrations or models that let the audience hear, touch, smell, or even taste the work.
When it matters legally that the audience received the information, such as building evacuation procedures, a presentation with a sign-in sheet gives assurance that a document left unopened cannot.
condition: when there is a legal or compliance need to evidence that the audience received the information

statement: A presentation has five disadvantages against a document: one chance to speak and one to hear, no time for the audience to look up background, the audience held to the speaker's pace, success hostage to delivery, and the difficulty of assembling everyone.

Because a presentation is heard once, dropping a single load-bearing word such as a negation can mislead the audience, and a listener who pauses to think about one idea loses everything said meanwhile.
An unfamiliar technical term left undefined strands the audience, and the damage compounds when the format defers questions to the end.
The speaker controls the pace of a presentation, and the audience is lost if that pace is too fast and bored if it is too slow.
Delivery distorts perceived quality in both directions: a poor delivery makes a presentation look weaker than it is, and an exceptional one can make it look stronger than it is.

Teleconferencing solves the problem of assembling an audience but does not match the energy of being in the same room, and video recording is weaker still because it loses the audience interaction that makes a presentation valuable.
Many listeners tire and grow restless after roughly twenty minutes, which makes a presentation alone a difficult vehicle for complex, deep technical subjects.
exception: some listeners can attend for long periods

statement: Presenting benefits the speaker as well: questions from audiences of other disciplines yield new perspectives on the work, and preparing the talk solidifies the speaker's own ideas and can produce new insights.

In the assertion-evidence approach the speaker first specifies the assertions, insights, and results the audience should take away, then matches each to the evidence available, instead of listing topics and subtopics.
The assertion-evidence approach costs more preparation time than topic-subtopic listing but yields talks that are more persuasive and more focused.

Critiquing a presentation, whether a colleague's or one's own, becomes far more useful when the talk is analyzed from four separate stylistic perspectives: speech, structure, visual aids, and delivery.

Speech is what is said; structure covers the organization, transitions, depth, and emphasis of those words; visual aids are the projected slides, models, boards, films, and demonstrations; delivery is the interaction with the audience and the room.
Projected slides deserve disproportionate attention because they shape not only the audience's comprehension but also the speaker's own preparation and delivery.

Perspective-by-perspective critique can misrepresent a talk's overall effect, because strength in one perspective can offset weakness in another; the test that matters is whether a weak area distracts the audience from the content.

Judgments about who is an excellent presenter are inherently imprecise: no one presents excellently every day, some are strong with colleagues yet stiff with strangers, and informed opinions about the same speaker vary widely.
If a speaker is going to impress an audience with only one thing, it should be the content — the ideas, insights, findings, and conclusions — rather than the style of presenting it.
Style is the vehicle that carries content, so a strong presentation requires both: content presented without attention to style goes unnoticed, and style without content has no meaning.
A speaker's sense of their own pace is unreliable: Oppenheimer judged his early lectures too slow while the students who dropped the course found them far too fast.

Obscure allusions outside the audience's shared background, combined with an excessive pace, drive listeners away; slowing down, clarifying ideas, and making the connections between points explicit reverses this.
Giving the wrong speech means failing to match what is said to the audience, the purpose, and the occasion.
A scientific presenter must be both precise and engaging, because a technically correct talk that loses the audience's attention communicates nothing.

A technically sound safety argument can fail to persuade when the presenters do not anticipate the decision-makers' strong prior bias, as in the Morton Thiokol teleconference before the Challenger launch.
Few scientific presentations exist only to inform: most also aim to persuade, and some, such as a conference keynote or a closing course lecture, also aim to inspire.
The occasion sets the audience's expectations, so the same audience expects something different from a morning plenary at a conference than from an after-dinner talk later the same day.

A slide fails its audience when its main assertion is left implicit, its supporting evidence is buried in irrelevant detail, and the one variable the assertion depends on is missing, as in the Morton Thiokol O-ring damage slide that omitted launch temperatures.
A title slide that gives no presenter name or organizational identity forfeits an easy chance to establish the speaker's authority.
The less technical the audience, the harder targeting becomes, because the speaker must anticipate more terms and more background that the audience needs in order to follow the work.
A speaker's assumption about who will be in the room can be wrong, so the audience should be confirmed rather than assumed when preparing depth and terminology.
A common failing of technical speakers is tossing out field abbreviations and jargon without checking whether the audience knows them.
An abbreviation is not automatically less familiar than the full term it stands for; some abbreviations are the better-known form for a lay audience.

Pursuing precision at the cost of clarity harms a talk: an occasional long qualified sentence is survivable, but sustained wandering sentence structure makes it hard for an audience to stay with the speaker.
exception: a single long sentence is tolerable

statement: When preparing for an audience the speaker knows well, each detail should be tested against two questions: will they understand it, and will they be interested in it.
condition: when the audience is known to the speaker

statement: When the audience is unknown, mingling before the talk and asking what work people do, why they came, and what they know about the topic both sharpens targeting and reduces the speaker's nervousness.
condition: when the speaker does not know the audience well

statement: When mingling beforehand is impossible, trying the presentation out on someone with the same background as the intended audience substitutes for direct audience analysis.
condition: when pre-talk contact with the audience is not possible

statement: The same material can be retargeted for successive audiences by varying the examples, the depth, and the background information supplied, while watching expressions to check whether it is registering.
Mentally rehearsing the talk while imagining the audience's reaction to each assertion and each piece of evidence is a useful preparation technique.
When the audience looks tired, a speaker can recover engagement by stepping closer, raising the pace and volume, and drawing explicit connections between the content and the listeners' own work.
condition: when audience cues indicate fatigue or disengagement

statement: Reflection after a talk is part of the work: audience questions often mark points that the body of the presentation explained badly, and what the audience failed to notice is as informative as what they responded to.
A subject presented once will usually be presented again, so post-talk reflection is an investment in later versions rather than wasted effort.

Reaching a mixed audience is harder than reaching a single one, and presenting the intricacies of one's work too densely can cause listeners outside the discipline to dismiss genuinely important results, as happened to Barbara McClintock's 1951 transposon talk.
In a mixed research audience, specialists in the speaker's field expect depth in the specialty to be demonstrated at some point in the talk.
condition: when specialists from the speaker's own field are present

statement: Researchers from other fields may follow the general theory behind a work yet miss its significance unless the speaker explicitly shows that significance, and they are listening for insights that connect to their own research.

Officials and managers with little technical background often understand neither the significance of the work nor the theory behind it, yet may have the largest say in funding it, so the talk must find a way to connect with them.
condition: when non-technical decision-makers are in the audience

statement: There is no way to satisfy an entire mixed audience throughout an entire presentation; the achievable goal is that everyone is satisfied by the end, reached by addressing the different audiences at different moments of the talk.
condition: for audiences mixing technical levels

statement: A depth strategy for a mixed audience opens shallow enough to orient everyone and to show rather than merely state the subject's importance, begins each middle division in the shallows before diving deep, and returns to the shallows at the end so all listeners leave with the main points.
condition: for audiences mixing technical levels

statement: Presenting material an audience already understands does not necessarily bore them, provided the explanation is done well; experts attended Feynman's freshman lectures for exactly that reason.
condition: provided the explanation is well done

statement: When a recognized expert on the topic is in the room, naming them, conceding they could explain it better, and then presenting as well as possible tends to recruit the expert as an ally and makes any correction they offer a kind one.
condition: when someone in the audience knows more about a topic than the speaker

statement: Scientists and engineers routinely overlook the general public, which matters because it contains the officials who decide energy, health, security, and environmental policy and the next generation of scientists and engineers.
Communicating science well to a general audience can transform the presenter's own reach, as an eighteen-minute public talk did for Jill Bolte Taylor.

Because the general public spans too wide a range of education and interest to address as a whole, a workable proxy is to prepare for one specific non-scientist the speaker knows well and imagine that person saying 'I don't get it' or 'So what?', which sharpens wording and strengthens arguments.
condition: when the audience is the general public

statement: Most presentations carry a mixture of purposes rather than a single one, and the purpose mix determines how the speech is crafted.

When the purpose is primarily to inform and the speaker's credentials are accepted, the audience applies far less critical scrutiny than to new research results, so the objective is to deliver the information as logically and directly as possible with emphasis on warnings and key steps.
condition: when the primary purpose is to inform and the speaker has accepted credentials

statement: The preview-tell-summarize adage does serve an informative occasion: the introduction prepares comprehension, the middle delivers the steps in order, and the ending reinforces them by repetition.
condition: when the presentation's purpose is primarily instructional

statement: An audience that needs to act under pressure wants the how rather than the why, as the exhausted Apollo 13 crew did when NASA transmitted improvised recovery procedures.
condition: when the audience must execute instructions under time pressure

statement: Effective persuasive scientific speakers combine logical evidence with appeals to emotion and to their own character rather than relying on logic alone.
condition: when the primary purpose is to persuade

statement: Assertions differ sharply in how much evidence they demand: asserting that a design is effective requires showing it meets every criterion, whereas asserting that a design is not effective requires showing only that it fails one.
condition: assuming the audience is initially neutral toward the assertion

statement: Not every persuasive presentation aims to move the audience to the speaker's position; some aim to negotiate a compromise, which can turn a competitive situation into a productive collaboration.
When the purpose is primarily to inspire, the speaker may be right to abandon projected slides entirely.
condition: when the primary purpose of the talk is to inspire

statement: A theatrical inspirational opener can far outperform a conventional slide talk, but its power comes from the audience not knowing what will happen, so it cannot be repeated to the same audience, and it works only when the chosen persona and material genuinely fit that audience.
condition: when the persona and material fit the specific audience and the audience has not seen it before
exception: cannot be reused with the same audience

statement: In teaching, where the aims are learning the material and inspiring continued study, simply telling students the main points is not always most effective, because students who discover material themselves are more likely to own it.
condition: in a teaching context

statement: For any given subject and audience several teaching methods work and at least as many fail, and unusual methods that would be out of place in a business or conference talk can succeed with the right teacher and audience.
condition: in a teaching context with a suitable teacher and audience

statement: The occasion of a presentation is defined by several concrete variables: formality, time limit, time of day, logistics, location, and number of attendees.
Where time limits are fixed because other speakers are waiting, overrunning them risks upsetting or angering the audience.
condition: when the slot has a hard limit and others follow

statement: The time of day should temper how ambitious the talk is, since a mid-morning audience has more energy than a late-afternoon one and can absorb more main points.
In a teleconference the speaker cannot read expressions and adjust, so the slides themselves must carry the main assertions and the evidence for them.
condition: when presenting remotely without a view of the audience

statement: Room occupancy changes whether humor lands: in a packed room laughter is amplified and reads as success, while in a half-empty room it dissipates quickly.

A formal or very short slot argues for a speech that stays tight to the targeted subject, while an informal occasion or a generous time budget allows weaving in examples, stories, humor, and personal connections.

Projecting one bulleted list after another bores audiences because the sheer number of listed details overwhelms them while the list format hides the connections and the relative importance among those details.
Without an anchor for understanding and a mnemonic for recall, an audience retains little even when the speaker has said a great deal.
Four strategies make technical content connect and stick: stories, examples and analogies, a personal connection with the audience, and humor.
Humor is effective only when it arises naturally from the content and offends no one in the audience.
condition: humor must emerge from the content

statement: Stories create anticipation that makes an audience lean in and listen more intently, letting them feel the excitement the researchers felt while awaiting results.
Stories aid retention by giving the listener a frame for recalling the sequence of details, a claim the author reports is supported by psychology research on memory.

A presentation sits between a document and a story, so a strong presentation blends the descriptions that inform and persuade with narrative elements that hold interest and ease recall, rather than becoming a story outright.

A scientific story can be structured by stating the hypothesis up front, ordering details so tension builds, breaking from the narrative to explain the science, and releasing the tension at the answer.

A talk can sustain more than one peak by foreshadowing the next question during the build-up to the first resolution, so the middle becomes a chain of stories in which each discovery leads to the next.
Stories serve two distinct roles in a scientific talk: engaging listeners so they attend in the moment, and supplying a memorable sequence so they can recall the content hours later.
When describing a concept the audience does not know, anchoring the description in examples or explaining it by analogy is a powerful strategy.
condition: when the concept is unfamiliar to the audience

statement: Presentations often fail because the speaker keeps the discussion purely abstract or mathematical, while most listeners need an image or a physical perspective to follow at all.
exception: some listeners can learn from a purely abstract treatment

statement: Attaching a physical example to a derivation gives listeners something to anchor the mathematics to, and can even expose errors that listeners tracking only the algebra would miss.
Analogies do a different job from examples: they are the tool of choice for conveying the scale of something unfamiliar or the likelihood of an unfamiliar event.
condition: when conveying unfamiliar magnitude or probability

statement: Vivid comparisons that genuinely support the content become the keepers an audience carries out of the room, whereas a typical conference talk leaves nothing recallable two days later.
condition: the comparison must support the presentation's content

statement: A good test of a presentation's success is what the audience still remembers two days later.

Numbers become meaningful and memorable when restated in terms the audience already experiences — capacity as a count of familiar items, size as fitting in a pocket — rather than in raw technical units.
A warm personal atmosphere — eye contact, humility, and evident concern that everyone understands — connects with an audience in a way that speaking to impress them with one's knowledge does not.
Explaining what personally motivated the speaker to take up the work is one way to make a scientific talk personal.

Uninhibited enthusiasm and openly personal remarks — including about the difficulty and opposition the speaker met — carry listeners along and can be a source of lasting influence, as with Boltzmann's lectures.
Naming audience members whose work connects to the speaker's — particularly experts who know a sub-topic better — signals respect and recruits them to the speaker's side.
condition: when the relevant experts are present in the audience

statement: Learning listeners' names and referring to their own experience turns what an audience expected to be an anonymous session into a personal one, which both raises their concentration and increases the speaker's credibility with them.
Humor can relax an audience, give them a way to respond, engage them, and provide a needed rest during a technical talk.

Not every speaker can make a crowd laugh: landing a humorous line depends on pausing, timing, and emphasis, and attempts before an unfamiliar professional audience often draw groans instead of laughter.
Opening a talk with a joke is the hardest moment to succeed, because humor depends on an unexpected grain of truth and an audience that does not yet know the speaker has no expectation to violate.
condition: especially when the audience does not know the speaker

statement: A failed opening joke compounds: the speaker is most nervous at the start, the audience is sizing the speaker up at exactly that moment, and the failure makes both parties uneasy — so humor is far more effective in the middle of a talk, once credibility exists.
Experienced speakers advise never planning humor, letting it emerge from the material and the audience's mood instead.

Humor carries professional risk: a remark that works over an informal lunch can read as crass in a formal meeting where listeners sit beside their managers, and humor touching a controversial subject irritates rather than relaxes.

No line can be drawn that makes everyone laugh, because in any large professional audience someone is sensitive to race, gender, religion, or death; sexual remarks are out of bounds in a professional setting.
Self-effacing humor about the speaker's own failings is typically the safest kind in a professional talk.
If a first attempt at humor draws no laughter, the speaker should back off and play the rest of the talk straight.
condition: when an initial humorous remark does not land

statement: A speaker known for constant humor pays a cost: listeners start reading jokes into statements meant seriously.

Strong content and strong delivery cannot rescue a talk whose structure and visual aids fail; an interesting topic delivered by an energetic speaker still emptied the room when it ran to 62 mostly-bulleted slides.
Animating bullet points onto the screen one by one produces a hypnotic cadence that deadens an audience, and slides that repeat nearly every spoken detail add nothing.

Trying to cover every aspect of a subject instead of two or three forces a depth so shallow that every point becomes generic, leaving no room for the stories, examples, and personal connections that hold attention.
Announcing a long enumerated list late in a talk and then spending multiple slides on each item drives listeners out of the room, even at the social cost of insulting the host.
A bad scientific presentation can be worse than no presentation at all, when the same hour spent in direct discussion among the attendees would have communicated more.

The presenter is a guide leading the audience up the mountain of the work to reach the view the speaker has already attained, so organization is the choice of entry point, direction and steepness of the trail, and ending point.
Structure has four levers that can each fail a talk: organization, the number of changes in direction, the signalling of those changes, and the emphasis of key details.
The four major structural pitfalls of a scientific talk are trying to do too much, leaving the audience behind at the beginning, losing them in the middle, and not being persuasive enough.

The standard organization opens with the big picture and narrows to the topic, treats the topic logically in the middle, and returns in the ending to how the work bears on the big picture raised at the start.

The logical ordering of the middle follows from the kind of topic: a process suggests chronological order, an object suggests spatial order, a system suggests following the flow through it, and a classifiable topic suggests grouping into parallel parts.
Audience expectations can dictate the organization: a research audience expects hypotheses or research questions, then how they were tested, then the results and their discussion.
condition: in a research presentation

statement: An ending analyses the work from an overall perspective, summarises its most important details, and provides closure through recommendations, unresolved questions, or the work's effect on the big picture.
Failing to organise a presentation logically costs a speaker future audiences: Pauling cited exactly that lack of organisation as his reason for skipping Millikan's lectures.

The number of divisions in a talk's middle should be limited to two, three, or four, because listeners can process lists of that size and larger lists tax them; announcing six, seven, or eight main points is a structural failure.
A transition can be signalled through three channels: the wording of the speech, a change in the visual aids, and the delivery, such as a deliberate pause.
Major transitions occur between the introduction and the middle, between each pair of sections in the middle, and between the middle and the conclusion.
The transition into the conclusion is the one the audience most needs to recognise, because listeners who know only a minute or two of concentration remains will sit up and attend more closely.

A change of speaker makes a transition harder because the audience must adjust to a new voice, stage presence, and set of movements; occasional handovers give a long talk variety, but too many in a short talk cause confusion.
condition: in a group presentation

statement: Emphasis matters as much as organisation: since listeners remember only a fraction of what they hear, a well-organised talk without emphasis can leave the audience carrying away its least important details.
Repetition, illustration, and placement are the emphasis mechanisms a presentation shares with a written article or report.

The beginning is a prime emphasis slot because the audience is least tired and listening most sharply, so it should carry something important: the scope of the talk, the importance of the work, or the single most important result.
Opening with the most important result works only when that result strikes the audience as positive or neutral and when they understand and appreciate it.
condition: when the result is received positively or neutrally and is understood and appreciated by the audience

statement: Retention through the middle of a talk holds up when the audience can identify and recall the logical strategy of the path the speaker chose, whatever that strategy is.
The ending is the single best opportunity for emphasis, but only if the audience has been told the ending has arrived.
condition: the audience must be signalled that the ending is at hand

statement: The slide left projected during the question period is on screen for minutes and should therefore carry the conclusions — the presentation's most important results — rather than a wasted question mark or the word Questions.

Junior researchers commonly allocate talk time in proportion to the effort each activity consumed rather than to the significance of its results, so the most interesting findings get the least airtime.
Research presentations are judged by the quality of the new insights communicated, not by the quantity of work performed, so many tasks actually done must be excluded from the talk.

The right depth is whatever the audience needs or wants, which requires assessing what they already know, starting the discussion there, and accounting for how much more they need to learn; determining it becomes markedly harder with multiple audiences.

Scope is sometimes fixed by the occasion, as in a progress review, and sometimes chosen by the speaker, as in a research seminar; the wider the scope, the harder it is to satisfy the audience on depth.

For a fixed talk length, scope and depth trade off like the dimensions of a fixed-volume vessel: a wide scope raises the chance that something connects but lowers achievable depth, and a narrow scope deepens the treatment but risks failing to connect at all, so a balance must be struck.
condition: for a presentation with a fixed time limit

statement: Slides pitched deeper than the depth the speaker can actually deliver frustrate an audience, because each slide flashed past for seconds leaves unanswered questions while the speech stays shallow.
The best presenters set explicit limits on the talk and state out loud what they are excluding, anticipating the omission the audience would otherwise puzzle over.
An insecure presenter covers as much as possible to impress the audience or to intimidate them out of asking questions; a few listeners may be impressed but most are not.

Broad-scope talks should not be avoided outright, since keynotes and large-audience talks often call for a big picture; what they require is that the speaker still find a way to deliver satisfying depth.
condition: when the occasion calls for a big-picture perspective

statement: Depth inside a broad talk can be supplied by memorable stories and examples spread across the scope, whose details should above all be concrete and simple, and sometimes unexpected or emotionally charged.
condition: when the talk must cover a broad scope

statement: When scope has grown large through sheer number of topics, grouping them into two or three memorable categories and going deep on one example per category keeps the coverage at category level while still satisfying on depth.
condition: when the scope is large because of the number of topics

statement: Presenting work effectively means selecting only the details that let the audience understand it, sorting them so no on-the-spot cataloguing is required, and giving them a hierarchy so listeners know which to hold onto if overwhelmed.
A drive for completeness harms clarity when each mentioned detail drags in another the audience was not prepared for, especially after the speaker has promised to mention only one.
A strong technical opening moves the audience quickly from the general to the specific without detouring onto side paths, as Nüsslein-Volhard's Nobel address did.
Lists of six to nine items overwhelm most listeners, who give up and drift; the repair is to break the long list into two or three categories the audience can hold.
Because listeners differ in how many details they can absorb, the speaker must give the details a hierarchy so the audience knows which to hold onto and which to let go.

Stating the essentials up front — as Feynman did by writing a summary of them at the start of each lecture — lets a speaker offer tangential material that stretches the strongest listeners without losing those struggling with the main points.

Three concrete emphasis strategies are available: repeating a detail at the beginning, middle, and end; placing key results and images on the slides while leaving lesser details to speech alone; and using delivery — a pause, a change in volume, or stepping closer to the audience.
Lowering the voice before an important point is often more effective for emphasis than raising it.

Two hallmarks of losing the audience at the start are flashing the title slide away before anyone can grasp the subject and projecting an outline list of topics that no one can recall a minute after it leaves the screen.

Losing the thread at the beginning wastes the audience's entire investment when the format defers questions to the end or the room is large enough to inhibit asking for clarification, so making the beginning as clear as possible is a goal in itself.

Attendees do not expect to understand everything, but they do expect to understand something for the time invested, and many presenters instead open as though the audience had spent the week reading all the speaker's papers.

The author suspects that presenters skip orientation out of fear of seeming simplistic, since orienting the audience takes courage: once they understand what was done, they are in a position to critique it.

An audience arrives with four questions — what exactly the subject is, why it is important, what is needed to understand or believe it, and in what order it will be presented — and a strong beginning ensures they are answered.

Not every one of the audience's four opening questions must be addressed explicitly, since some audiences already know one or two answers; the requirement is that none remains open once the introduction ends.
condition: some questions may already be answered for a given audience

statement: More than any other part of the talk, the beginning should target the widest possible audience, so that even listeners lost in the middle can tell a colleague afterwards in general terms what was done and why it mattered.
condition: when the audience varies in level

statement: Introduction length should scale with the slot: an audience will accept up to ten minutes of introduction in a fifty-minute talk, but no more than five in a fifteen-minute conference presentation.
An overlong introduction makes an audience impatient, and a long introductory story at a conference leads many listeners to assume the speaker has little to report.
condition: at a conference presentation

statement: Restless presenters wrongly assume the audience knows the subject as well as they do and rush into details, whereas a calm speaker patiently prepares the audience for the problems to be discussed.

Assuming the posted title and abstract have already told the audience what the talk is about is dangerous: they were read hours or days earlier, people retain only a small fraction of what they read, and the spoken review adds emphasis through loudness and cadence that text cannot.

Spending only twenty or thirty seconds on the title slide is too short, because the audience is still adjusting to the speaker's voice, movements, and facial expressions and must not be overloaded during that adjustment.
Reading off a conventional title slide of title, name, affiliation, date, and logos and then switching leaves every one of the audience's four opening questions unanswered and the listener unsettled.

At least one of the audience's opening questions should be answered before the first slide change, which a key image on the title slide makes possible by giving the speaker an entry point into the subject.
Naming the presenters and sponsors is worth doing because it answers what the audience needs in order to believe the subject, not merely to understand it.

Patience at the opening matters most for young speakers who carry no credibility yet, because the audience is actively judging whether the talk will waste their time and must be shown up front that it will not.
condition: when the speaker is junior or unknown to the audience

statement: Listening is difficult work and audiences stop concentrating without sufficient reason, so a speaker should not move into the middle of a talk until confident the audience understands why the subject matters.
Importance usually connects to money, safety, health, or the environment, and thirty or forty seconds spent making that connection pays for itself later when the material turns steep.
When the work has no direct practical payoff, curiosity replaces importance as the motivator, and the speaker's job is to instil in the audience the same curiosity they feel about the question.
condition: when the work offers no direct benefit in cost, energy, environment, health, or security

statement: Grounding the problem in a specific physical example, rather than discussing the technique in the abstract, carries much of the audience through the mathematical stretches of a talk.
Audiences carry an unspoken fear of not understanding, and many will not ask for clarification even when permitted, for fear of appearing ignorant or of distracting the rest of the room.

When the time limit prevents supplying all the background, stating up front what knowledge is being assumed lets listeners who lack it set realistic expectations and relax, which can leave them understanding more than if they had tried to follow every step.
condition: when the time limit precludes covering all needed background

statement: Background does not all belong in the introduction — it can be delivered as needed — but the introduction is the place to tell the audience what background is coming, and details such as the work's major assumptions are better placed up front.

A background block long enough to feel like its own section may be moved from the introduction into the middle, provided the middle does not thereby gain too many sections and the audience can see how that section relates to the rest.
condition: provided the middle does not become over-sectioned and the relationship stays visible

statement: Background splits into what the audience needs to understand the subject and what they need to believe it; the second kind is credibility material — institution, colleagues, and a review of the literature the work builds on.
Showing that the speaker knows the key players in a research area establishes credibility with an audience that does not know the speaker.
condition: when the audience does not already know the speaker

statement: Mapping the talk matters more in a presentation than in a document, because a reader can glance ahead at headings while a listener has no idea where the talk is going unless told.

A clear, memorable map lets the audience judge at any moment how much has been covered and how much remains, which they need in order to pace themselves; listening without any sense of how long the talk will run tires people quickly.
A strong mapping slide uses images that are repeated in the corresponding divisions later, and omits generic entries such as Introduction and Conclusion that every presentation has.

Dividing a talk into sections, knowing roughly how long each runs, and rehearsing the entries and exits while leaving the interiors unrehearsed produces delivery that is genuinely spontaneous inside a structure that prevents wandering.

Well-prepared written organisation does not survive undisciplined delivery: Maxwell's lectures were organised well enough to print, yet he digressed into long tangents beyond his audience's comprehension until the time ran out and the planned structure was never delivered.
Audiences become lost in three specific ways: gaps in the logic they cannot bridge, an unsignalled major change of direction, and exhaustion from too many details.
Even with sound structure a listener will drift — often while pursuing a connection to their own work — and return to find the talk has moved on, so the structure must make recovery possible.

A speaker who cannot clearly see the destination cannot lead an audience there, which is why presenting topics one understands reads as lucid and confident while presenting topics one is still grappling with reads as groping.

Presenting strong suspicions rather than settled facts is a genuine gamble: a wrong bold claim invites public embarrassment, while a right one earns credit for the bold step that a more cautious colleague forgoes.
Whatever the speaker chooses to present, they must make explicit to the audience which claims are solidly grounded in theory and experiment and which are the speaker's own suspicions.

How much speculative material to present depends on audience, purpose, and occasion: a funder or any audience before whom the speaker cannot afford to stumble argues for facts only, while colleagues with whom credibility is established make a calculated risk cheaper.
condition: depends on the audience's tolerance and the speaker's standing with them

statement: Presenting a deliberately provisional straw-man solution can turn the audience into a source of the answer, which makes a presentation usable as a test of an idea rather than only a report of a finished one.
condition: when the speaker is stuck on a problem and the audience is a suitable one

statement: Downplaying a result the speaker does not yet understand risks both its exclusion from the audience's decisions and its exposure as an uncertainty during questions, because questioners gravitate to exactly the parts they did not understand.
The alternative to downplaying an unexplained result is to feature it: state up front that it is not understood and make the search for its explanation an emphasis of the presentation.
condition: when a result the speaker cannot yet explain must be presented

statement: A listener who has lost their place spends effort hunting for clues about where the talk is, and that extra effort tires them further, so keeping the audience oriented is most critical exactly where the presentation changes direction.
Transitions operate on two levels: the major ones between beginning and middle and between middle and ending, and the secondary ones between each division of the middle.
The transition from beginning to middle matters because it lets listeners file each subsequent detail under the right major division of the talk.

Inexperienced speakers end abruptly with a bare request for questions, denying the unprepared audience the chance to view the work from a big-picture perspective and to judge which parts mattered — which lowers the odds they will catalogue and remember the important details.
Listeners need to know which division of the middle they are in so they can pace themselves, which is why each division boundary must be marked explicitly.
The most straightforward transition is a spoken one that closes the finished division and names the next, with phrases such as 'in summary' or 'to conclude' reserved for the shift into the ending.

Putting a key image for each division on the mapping slide and then repeating that image as a small corner icon on every slide of its division gives the audience a continuous, wordless signal of where they are in the middle.

A pause is not read by an audience as the speaker being lost but as the speaker collecting their thoughts, and it gives the audience the same room to sort, synthesize, and analyse the details just delivered.

Delivery offers several transition signals beyond the pause: counting the division on the fingers, changing vocal level at a new section, moving closer to the audience at each main division, taking a fixed stage position at the start of a division, and repeating a consistent ritual motion between segments.
Announcing a decision to a hostile audience and only afterwards addressing their concerns fails: the reassurance arrives too late, listeners stop listening, and the meeting is lost.
condition: when the audience holds a strong prior objection

statement: Understanding the audience's bias determines both the strategy and the energy an argument will require, because consolidating a sympathetic or neutral audience is far less demanding than winning over an antagonistic one.
The same argument can succeed with one audience and fail with another purely because of the strength of their prior bias, as the Morton Thiokol delay case showed within a single day.

An audience's initial bias is sometimes the overriding determinant of a presentation's outcome, independent of the speaker's stature, as the contrast between Bohr's failed meeting with Churchill and Teller's successful one with Reagan illustrates.
An audience is much more likely to believe an argument when they know and appreciate its assertions — in a scientific talk, the speaker's claims, insights, features, and results.
The first step toward an argument the audience will accept is for the speaker to recognise exactly what they are asserting.

Preparation should start from the main assertion the data supports, because only once that assertion is fixed can the speaker decide how best to graph the data and present it, so that every detail spoken and shown drives toward it.
Some assertions sit too far up the mountain for a single graph or dataset to reach, so the speaker must build a chain of sub-assertions that carries the audience high enough to accept the main one.
condition: when the audience is not yet positioned to accept the main assertion

statement: Each sub-assertion in the chain needs its own evidence, and the evidence type should fit the sub-assertion — a concrete incident plus statistics for a threat claim, theory for a claim that a current method is inadequate.
An audience also needs the key background pieces — what lawyers call warrants — without which they cannot appreciate an assertion even when they follow every word of it.

Technical speakers must overcome the Curse of Knowledge — the expert's inability to recall what it was like not to know — by stepping away from the work and viewing each assertion as the audience will.
Evidence falls into appeals to logic, to the audience's emotion, and to the speaker's own character; scientists and engineers name logic as decisive but systematically underrate the other two.

Because many political decisions about science and engineering are made by non-technical people who are swayed by character and emotion, a persuasive technical argument should account for all three appeals rather than logic alone.
Logical evidence ranks by descending strength as deductive reasoning, inductive reasoning, referenced facts, statistics, examples, and finally analogies.

A deductive argument can be made visual and decisive by establishing referenced cut-off criteria, applying each as a shading overlay on a map, and letting the single unshaded region stand as the conclusion.

Statistics range widely in persuasive force: experimental data showing a definite trend sit at the strong end, while a comparison of quantities that are not actually comparable — ignoring variables that differ between them — sits at the weak end.

The force of an example depends on the assertion it supports: one instance of harm is powerful evidence that something is dangerous, while one instance without side effects is weak evidence that it is safe.

Analogies explain how something works or how large it is but are generally ineffective as support in an argument, because they tie two dissimilar things from one narrow perspective and a skeptical audience can attack the differences visible from any other.

Appeals to emotion can outweigh sound logical evidence in policy outcomes, particularly when the deciding audience is non-technical, as fear-based campaigning did against the nuclear power industry's statistical counter-arguments.
condition: especially when the decision-making audience is non-technical

statement: The identical claim carries far more weight from a recognised authority in the field than from an unknown speaker.

A speaker without eminent credentials can still appeal to character by taking a position that runs counter to their own background and stated history, making the reluctance itself part of the evidence.
condition: when the speaker's prior record points the other way

statement: Reputation is part of character and is earned only through sustained work and testing; a researcher whose result conflicts with another's strengthens it by also showing why the other result is wrong, not merely that their own is right.
condition: when the speaker's result conflicts with a published one

statement: Character also covers the speaker's connection to the audience: an effective speaker must be liked and trusted, and the way to earn that respect is to show respect for the audience first, never displaying superiority and leaving listeners free to question and criticise.

Expectations should be kept low when addressing an audience antagonistic to the position, because an important scientific innovation rarely wins over and converts its opponents; the realistic aims are reducing the opposition's vehemence and winning those who are neutral.
condition: when the audience is antagonistic to the speaker's position

statement: With an antagonistic audience, defining the question up front while withholding the results keeps the speaker's position unknown, which preserves credibility and makes opponents far more likely to actually listen to the arguments.
condition: when the audience is antagonistic to the speaker's results

statement: The Rogerian strategy — demonstrating genuine understanding of the opposition's main arguments and acknowledging their strengths before mounting any defence — lowers the audience's initial antagonism and builds the speaker's credibility, and it fits best when the goal is a compromise rather than a victory.
condition: when the goal is to reach a compromise with an opposed audience

statement: The two standing criticisms of presentation slides are the overwhelming number of details they carry and the tiresome drumbeat delivery that bulleted lists produce.

When a stretch of the talk gains nothing from a slide, the speaker should blank the screen — via a black slide, the remote's blank button, or the B key — which moves the focus from the screen's light to the speaker; personal stories and acknowledgements are natural occasions.
condition: when slides do not contribute to understanding or retention for that portion of the talk

statement: Projected slides should carry far less detail than a handout, because a viewer reads a slide while a speaker talks at 120 to 140 words a minute, whereas a handout is read afterwards at the reader's own pace in a quiet place.
Forcing the projected deck to match the documenting handout exactly is what locks many presenters into projecting far too many words; the two artefacts should be allowed to differ.
Slides are for the audience, not the speaker; projecting one's own speaking notes produces the robotic cycle of turning to the screen for each bullet and back to the room for a sentence.

Analysis of thousands of conference, meeting, and classroom slides found the overwhelming majority strongly shaped by PowerPoint's defaults, which is unsurprising given the program's roughly 95 percent share of presentation slideware.

PowerPoint's defaults were never founded on research and originated when embedding graphics was difficult, yet they produce slide designs that stand in direct contrast with what research says helps audiences understand and remember.

The alternative slide masters the program offers sit two navigation levels deep and repeat the same two weakest defaults — the headline setting and the large body text block — so switching master does not fix the problem.
A 44-point headline centred on a single line pushes presenters toward headlines only a few words long, and in scientific presentations headlines are phrases more than 85 percent of the time.

The right test of a headline type is not whether it is short but which type leads the speaker to prepare a more focused talk with fewer words overall and which better orients a listener who missed the transition onto the slide.
A phrase headline such as 'Computational Results' gives a lost listener no help, whereas a sentence headline stating what the computational results show re-orients them immediately.
The default body text box that auto-fills as a bulleted list leaves about two-thirds of science and engineering slides carrying bulleted lists.
Bulleted lists damage a slide twice over: their word count makes reading and listening simultaneously difficult, and their position on the slide greatly reduces the space left for graphics.

No research shows bulleted lists help audiences comprehend or remember details in a scientific presentation, while critics charge that they fail to show connections between details — and making those connections is essential to communicating science and engineering.

The defaults produce a topic-subtopic slide structure in which the phrase headline names the topic and the bullets name subordinate ideas; two-thirds of examined scientific slides used it, over 40 percent as bullets alone and over 26 percent as bullets plus a graphic.
Even a slide that obeys the 6-by-6 rule carries too many words, because scientific slides are typically projected for about a minute while the speaker delivers 120 to 140 words in that same minute.
When an audience tries to process too many written words and spoken words at once, cognitive overload sets in and the comprehension rate drops below what it would have been with no slides at all.

Spoken words and written words are processed by the same part of the brain, so an over-worded slide leaves the listener only three bad options — ignore the screen, tune out the speaker, or toggle between them — and all three make the key message hard to identify.

Images are processed in a different part of the brain from text, and by this dual-coding route the multimedia principle holds that people learn more effectively from words plus relevant pictures than from words alone.
Applying the multimedia principle to slide design means every projected slide should include relevant visual evidence — a photograph, drawing, diagram, graph, or film.

The coherence principle holds that audiences understand and remember more when extraneous information is removed, so a slide should be stripped of any phrase or decorative image that does not connect directly to the spoken content, maximising its signal-to-noise ratio.

Five measured practices characterise scientific slides: over 85 percent open with phrase headlines, over two-thirds carry bulleted lists, only about half include a relevant image, about half use stock decorative backgrounds, and audiences typically face 35 or more words a minute to read.
Stock decorative backgrounds are a double cost: they can waste as much as a quarter of the slide's area and they add visual noise.

Default-following slides are cheap to make in an hour or two the night before, and presenters underrate the cost of that shortcut because slide design shapes three distinct things: how the speaker prepares, how the speaker delivers, and how much the audience understands and remembers.

The assertion-evidence structure replaces the phrase headline with a succinct sentence stating the slide's main assertion — a hypothesis, assumption, insight, or result — and replaces the bulleted list with visual evidence: photographs, drawings, diagrams, graphs, equations, short tables, or films.
Bulleted lists do not occur at all in the assertion-evidence structure.

An assertion-evidence slide conveys the same information as its topic-subtopic equivalent with far fewer words and a much clearer main point, and its images are recalled first with the headline's meaning following.

The assertion-evidence structure is recommended on two grounds: it follows the psychology principles of how people learn, and it is designed specifically for communicating technical assertions; other alternative structures exist for less technical assertions.
condition: for communicating technical assertions in science and engineering
exception: less technical content may be better served by other slide structures

statement: In a controlled comparison holding the narrated speech constant across two audiences of over 50 undergraduates with equivalent low prior knowledge, the audience shown assertion-evidence slides scored significantly higher on every test of comprehending and retaining the MRI process, with the essay test reaching p < .01.

The comparison was run against a conservative baseline: the topic-subtopic slides were made slightly better than common practice in words and lines, followed medical-school convention on including an image, and used a widely distributed format from a nationally known engineering course.

The assertion-evidence advantage is attributed to better emphasis of the most important details — carried by the sentence headline or the visual evidence — whereas in topic-subtopic slides audiences struggled to separate primary from secondary details in the bullets and the visual evidence had to share space with the list.

Slide design measurably changes how much an audience understands and remembers, and the assertion-evidence structure, though more time-consuming to create, is superior for comprehension and retention of complex concepts.
Slide design shapes the speaker as well as the audience, changing both how the talk is prepared and how it is delivered.

Slides that hold the speaker's bulleted speaking notes drive the speaker to keep turning back to refer to or read the next point, and the resulting alternation between audience and screen becomes hypnotically repetitive.
Animating bullets in one by one worsens the effect: much of the audience stops watching the animations altogether and either watches the speaker read or disengages from the talk.

Because assertion-evidence slides put most of their words in the sentence headline, speakers preparing them absorb each slide's main assertion into their natural speech and can therefore hold far more eye contact with the audience.

When a speaker turns to the slide to explain part of an image or the shape of a curve, the audience naturally follows and looks at the slide too — unlike the reading-aloud pattern, which pushes them away.

Adopting the assertion-evidence structure visibly improves delivery in three ways: more engagement through eye contact, more natural speech because words are fashioned on the spot to explain images rather than read from a scripted list, and an appearance of greater confidence because the information plainly comes from the speaker rather than from notes on the screen.

The structure's effect on preparation is stronger than its effect on delivery, because the sentence-assertion headline forces the speaker to identify each slide's most important takeaway and only then select the evidence needed for it.
A sentence-assertion headline causes the speaker to converge on more effective evidence, whereas starting from a phrase headline commonly has the opposite effect.

Although the sentence headline costs more words than a phrase headline would, it filters unneeded words out of the slide's body, so assertion-evidence slides end up with fewer words per slide and — the metric that matters more — fewer words projected per minute.
Surveys measured assertion-evidence presentations at fewer than 20 projected words per minute against 35 to 40 for typical scientific presentations using topic-subtopic slides.

Laboratories that made the assertion-evidence structure their norm report that presentations are more effective, audiences understand and remember more, and the questions asked afterwards operate on a higher plane.
The measured gain in comprehension of complex concepts from assertion-evidence slides corresponds to one and sometimes two letter grades.
Professionals who adopt the assertion-evidence structure do so over a significant period and through four distinct stages: interest, doubt, experimentation, and conversion.

Adoption is slowed by entrenchment: the topic-subtopic structure is not only the dominant model projected in scientific presentations but is mandated by many institutional and university slide templates.

Adoption is also slowed because the structure is genuinely harder: it requires overcoming the software's weak defaults, doing the intellectual work of defining the key assertions, and spending the extra time to create the visual evidence.

The structure originated when one national laboratory treated proposal slides as decisive for proposal success and defined two requirements: a short sentence headline, left justified and no more than two lines, stating the slide's main purpose, and a body carrying a supporting image such as a photograph, drawing, or graph.

An assertion-evidence slide is not meant to hold everything the speaker has to say about its takeaway: the headline carries the main message, the body carries the evidence for it, and the secondary details such as how the experiment was run are carried in the spoken words.

The assertion-evidence guidelines rest on three stated assumptions: that slides are appropriate for this talk at all, that they serve as a visual aid during the talk rather than a handout after it, and that they are designed foremost to help the audience understand rather than to hold the speaker's notes.

The headline rules are: keep it to no more than two lines, left justify it for easier reading, capitalise it as a sentence with the period optional, and when it runs to a second line break the first line so that phrases stay together.

The body rules are: support the headline with visual evidence — photographs, drawings, diagrams, graphs, films, equations, or short tables — use words only where necessary, and design so that no more than 20 words per minute are projected.
Bulleted lists should be avoided because they do not show connections; where a list is unavoidable it should be kept short and presented instead as a sequence of images or a short table.
exception: if a list is unavoidable, keep it short and consider images or a short table

statement: Bullets fail on three counts at once: they do not show connections, they do not reveal hierarchy, and they leave the critical assertions unspecified.

Typography for slides should be readable at a glance: a sans serif face such as Calibri, boldfaced for larger rooms, at 28 point for the headline, 18 to 24 point for body text, and 12 to 14 point for reference listings.
Italics, underlining, and text set in all capital letters should be avoided on slides.

Colour should serve the audience and the room: use either dark type on a light background or light type on a dark one, avoid hot background colours such as red, orange, or yellow, avoid decorated backgrounds, and do not let logos detract from the content.

Layout rules for a slide are: keep text blocks and especially headlines to no more than two lines, hold any list or set of call-outs to two, three, or four items, use animations only when they serve the audience and never gimmicky ones such as flying in, and leave enough blank space that the slide breathes.

Crafting the sentence-assertion headline is the hardest part of the structure, because it demands that the speaker identify each slide's single most important message — usually an insight, a feature, or a result — rather than merely naming a topic.
Properly crafted sentence headlines read in sequence give the bare-bones story of the work, leaving the speaker to flesh that skeleton out in spoken words.

A strong slide presentation keeps a balance between what is shown and what is said: on each slide the speaker supplies the secondary background details that deepen understanding rather than projecting them.

Supplying the surrounding background aloud builds the speaker's credibility by demonstrating ownership of the material, and a scientific presentation succeeds only if the audience believes in the speaker.

The opening slide's assertion should serve as an entry point that both motivates the audience to care about the work and arouses curiosity, which the speaker can then use to transition into the actual focus of the study.
A workable slide sequence establishes the key insights from what is already known first, and only then presents the result of the experiment that tested the effect of those insights.
If the speaker genuinely knows the work, the visual evidence alone should be a sufficient trigger for stepping through the story, with no scripted text needed on the slide.
condition: when the speaker knows the work

statement: Animation has a legitimate use in withholding: a second visual element can be animated in only after the speaker has finished explaining the first, controlling the order in which the audience takes the slide in.
condition: when the sequence of explanation matters

statement: Because the detail lives in the speech rather than the slide, the same slide sequence flexes to the audience and the time available — the speaker can add or drop method details without redesigning anything.
Using visual evidence rather than bulleted words as the trigger for what to say requires the speaker to practise with the slides, and that practice is what produces the more natural delivery.

With assertion-evidence slides there are only two legitimate reasons to look at the screen: a quick glance to confirm the slide advanced, and pointing out a detail of an image or graph — which the audience is looking at anyway.

A sentence headline orients the audience to the slide's purpose far better than a phrase headline, which matters most for the listener who was distracted and missed the spoken transition onto the slide.

Writing each slide's assertion as its headline makes the talk more focused because it puts the speaker in a position to see exactly what evidence is needed to support that headline; one experienced practitioner judged this speaker-side effect the more important of the two.

In the Challenger launch-delay slides the presenters neither made their assertions clear on the slides nor supplied enough evidence for the assertions they attempted in speech, and the slide body never showed the relationship their whole argument rested on.

Had the Challenger engineers written their assertion as the headline — that lower launch temperature went with more O-ring erosion — they would have been driven to reconsider their evidence and to plot erosion against launch temperature across all prior launches.

Any text block on a slide should be formatted to be read quickly so that attention returns to the speaker, which makes both the type size and the number of lines design decisions rather than aesthetics.

Focus groups in which audiences reported what slide text they actually read found that nearly everyone reads a block of one or two lines, but more than half will not read a block of three lines or longer.
A headline should be set at 28 points — large enough to stand out from the other text on the slide, yet small enough to let a meaningful sentence assertion fit in two lines.
PowerPoint's 44-point default headline size is simply too large to carry a meaningful sentence assertion within one or two lines.
Even at 28 points, holding an assertion to two lines while keeping it precise takes real work, so every word in the headline must contribute.
The headline should start in the slide's upper-left corner, because eye-tracking studies show Western audiences first look there when a new slide or page appears.
condition: for Western reading audiences

statement: Headlines should be left justified as graphic artists do in newspapers and journals; the centred default is slow to read once a headline runs past one line and moves the starting point from slide to slide.

A sentence headline should be capitalised like a sentence — first word and proper nouns only — because title-style initial capitals slow reading and consume space, a capital letter taking about 35 percent more horizontal room than a lowercase one.
A period at the end of a headline is optional because a standalone sentence has no neighbouring sentence to separate itself from, so the period contributes only a small amount of noise.
exception: a presenter who prefers the period may keep it

statement: Where a two-line headline breaks affects how fast the audience reads and comprehends it: avoid leaving a single word orphaned on the second line, and keep noun, verb, and prepositional phrases intact across the break.
A headline that fills both lines completely leaves no choice about where to break, and a second line substantially longer than the first is widely considered unattractive.

Properly chosen and well designed visual evidence — photographs, drawings, diagrams, films, equations, or small tables — is the most effective way to support an assertion headline, because unlike a bulleted list it lets the audience grasp the connections between the supporting details at a glance.

The type of visual evidence to use follows from the headline assertion: a background fact may need only a map and photographs, a trend claim a combination of photographs, timeline, and graph, a process a diagram, and a quantitative relationship a line or bar graph.
Speaking the supporting details from images rather than reading them from a list shows the audience that the speaker owns the information, which raises credibility.
If everything the speaker says is already written on the slides, many listeners tune the speaker out and concentrate on reading instead.

Blank space between the elements of a slide is more valuable than blank space around its edges, which is why the headline is often worth moving up from its default position to open a gap above the visual evidence.
Images should be sized large enough to view yet small enough that the slide body does not feel crowded.
Images should be arranged so the order to view them is unmistakable, following the natural viewing order of the audience's reading direction; animation or layering can enforce the same order.
condition: arrangement should follow the audience's reading direction

statement: Image sources must be credited and copyright law observed when selecting visual evidence for slides.

A diagram carrying equations or code should be designed so the audience only has to recognise those blocks as equations or code, not decipher them, and such a diagram can be assembled with simple copying, pasting, and arrangement rather than professional artwork.
A graph should be presented methodically — what the y-axis is, what the x-axis is, what each curve represents — and only then should the marking that highlights the slide's assertion be animated in.

The outer box that graphing programs draw around a plot by default should be removed, because it adds only noise: just as every word in the headline must contribute, so must every line in the visual evidence.

A border does serve a photograph or rectangular drawing by separating the image edge from the background, but adds nothing to a line drawing that already reads as distinct, so borders should be applied by purpose rather than uniformly.
condition: when the image edge would otherwise blend into the background

statement: Presenters commonly rush a graph and skip defining its axes or curves, leaving the audience understanding little and believing even less; the speaker has lived with the graph for months while the audience is seeing it for the first time and needs soak time.
condition: when presenting graphs or other complicated visual evidence

statement: An equation counts as visual evidence because it is a visual arrangement of symbols showing the connections between the variables they represent.

Revealing every connection of a complicated visual at once overwhelms an audience; animation lets complicated visual evidence be delivered piecemeal so the audience can follow one connection at a time.
condition: when the visual evidence carries many simultaneous connections

statement: Animating a slide from an empty body is too much animation: some visual evidence should be present for the whole time the slide is projected, so the audience can process a relevant image while listening and is not left facing bright blank light.

Decorative animation schemes such as Fly In, Bounce, Swivel, Pulse, Teeter, and Spin distract and annoy audiences and undercut the professionalism of a technical talk; the plain Appear transition is the right default, and the others belong only where actual physical movement in the science is being shown.
exception: when the animation depicts real physical movement in the science

statement: A table qualifies as visual evidence because, unlike the one-dimensional bulleted list, its two-dimensional arrangement of words and numbers can express multiple connections at once.

Most tables in scientific talks fail because too many rows and columns shrink the text below readability and leave the audience unsure where to look, an effect a laser pointer cannot repair; the two-to-four rule of thumb should govern both rows and columns.

Table sections can be brought in by animation one group at a time, or emphasised with colour — black type in the cells under discussion against light grey elsewhere, or a yellow background behind those cells.
Anchoring tabular information to a map makes the locations more memorable, and revealing the information sequentially keeps the audience focused on the part under discussion.
condition: when the tabular data is geographically indexed

statement: The core defect of a bulleted list is that it presents details without showing how they connect, and since the real relation may be chronological, spatial, hierarchical, causal, or a mixture, the audience is left to work it out.

Each kind of relationship has a visual replacement for the bulleted list: chronological details become a timeline, spatial details become call-outs arranged around an image, relative sizes become a pie graph, and a flow of blood, current, oxygen, or information becomes a diagram.
A timeline conveys more information than the equivalent list and conveys it faster, because the audience can read the separation in time between events directly off the visual.
condition: when the details are connected chronologically

statement: Call-outs placed around an image beat a separate bulleted list because the audience sees each detail both in relation to the whole and in relation to the other details.
condition: when the details are connected spatially

statement: A flow diagram can express a straight chain, a cycle, or a chain with feedback loops, and an audience given the same feedback relationship as a bulleted list would be hard pressed to identify those connections at all.
The second defect of bulleted lists is that they put too much text on the slide, destroying the balance between what the speaker says and what the speaker shows.

When most of a speaker's sentences come from sentences or phrases the audience can already read on the slide, many listeners stop listening — a senior official once cut a rehearsed talk short by telling the presenter to say nothing further and simply advance the slides.
