A deck in which more than two-thirds of slides carry no images serves little purpose beyond supplying the speaker with sentences to read for the next 45 seconds.

Bulleted lists are easy to create precisely because they let the speaker skip the work of deciding how the details relate — only parallel grammar is required — so a list is really brainstorming dressed up as a finished presentation, with a few good ideas surrounded by weeds.
Bulleted lists represent surface thinking rather than deep thinking and should be a presenter's last choice, not their first.
The choice of typeface for a slide should be governed by reading speed rather than tradition, because the audience is reading the type and listening to the speaker at the same time.

In the short text blocks of a billboard or a slide, sans serif typefaces are read more quickly than serif ones, and their straighter, less noisy strokes matter especially for audience members viewing the screen from a sharp side angle.
condition: for short text blocks viewed at a distance or an angle

statement: Calibri is a particularly good sans serif choice because it is present on most computers — an advantage when loading a deck onto a meeting room machine — and because it is narrower than Arial, leaving more blank space at the edges of a text block.

The reading-speed penalty of a serif typeface becomes decisive when projection quality or room lighting is poor: a degraded projector bulb rendered serif slides unreadable through a ninety-minute meeting while sans serif slides on the same projector the next day read fine.
condition: especially when projection or lighting conditions are suboptimal

statement: Slide type should be boldfaced, especially for a larger room, because boldfacing makes the letters readable from a greater distance.
condition: particularly in larger rooms

statement: Italic type, useful for emphasis in a printed instructional document, is too slow to read on a projected slide especially from side angles, and underlining is worse still because the underscore adds noise that impairs letter recognition.

The governing criterion for type size is that everyone in the room can read the headline and the body; 10 and 12 point type is legible only in the first few rows, and failing to spend the time to make a slide readable is inconsiderate to the audience.

The 28-point assertion headline is not a novel recommendation: it has been the standard for assertion headlines at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory for more than three decades and is endorsed by other slide designers.

The recommended type sizes for an assertion-evidence slide are a 28-point boldfaced headline, 18 to 24 point boldfaced body text, and 14-point non-bold reference listings, dropping to 12 points for a small room.
Boldfaced body text between 18 and 24 points is readable at the back of most rooms, and where a block falls in that range should follow from its importance and the space available.
A reference listing on a slide is much shorter than the full citation that belongs in the handout or notes page — often just an author surname and a year.
Everyone in the room need not be able to read a reference listing, but everyone must be able to see that one exists for any photograph, drawing, or graph taken from someone else's work.

Failing to acknowledge another group's contribution during a presentation is at minimum an insult to its owners and is more typically regarded as theft, and an unattributed figure can be challenged from the floor in front of the funding agency.

Text set in all capitals is read dramatically more slowly because readers identify words partly by their shape — the ascenders and descenders — and capitals erase that shape, forcing every letter to be read.
All capitals also consume about 35 percent more space than mixed case, and space not needed for type and images should be left blank to make the slide more inviting to read.

A colour combination that shows adequate contrast on the author's computer screen can be entirely unreadable when projected, so the combination must be tried out on a projected screen before the talk.

Colour combinations differ in reading speed: black on yellow is fastest, which is why caution signs use it, black on white is next, black on red is among the slowest and red on black slower still, while dark blue or dark green on white is fast enough to serve a scientific talk.

Mid-tone colours are unusable as a slide's main text or background colour because they are neither dark enough to contrast with white type nor light enough to contrast with black type; from a colour palette, take dark colours from the edge and light colours from the centre.

A white background suits shorter talks because equations and graphs imported from other programs already come on white, while a darker background is softer for the audience over a longer talk — but an aged projector bulb or a bright room makes white the safer bet.
condition: choice depends on talk length, projector condition, and room lighting

statement: Colour blindness affects a significant number of people at rates that vary by gender and ancestry, and the troublesome combinations involve red, green, and brown — which should be avoided both for type against background and as more than one of the curve colours on a single graph.

Colour carries an emotional effect independent of contrast: blue and green read as soothing to Western audiences while orange, red, and even yellow backgrounds agitate them, an effect the author observed when switching a course from black-on-yellow to white-on-blue calmed the class noticeably.
condition: for Western audiences

statement: An institution's identifying colours are a secondary consideration behind contrast and emotional effect; where the institutional palette fails on those grounds, the main type and background colours should be something else.

Stock decorated backgrounds — fireballs, starry nights, clouded skies, rippled oceans, wave borders — are pure noise in a scientific presentation and consume valuable area, one popular background wasting 23 percent of the slide.
When a distinctive background is wanted without compromising content, an airbrushed blend of two related dark colours gives high contrast against light type.
Whether the audience will print the slides is itself a background-colour consideration: a white background saves the printer toner of students and others who print a deck to annotate.
condition: when the audience is likely to print the slides

statement: Showing the institution's logo at some point in a talk is appropriate, and so is putting it on any distributed slide, but the common error is making it prominent — the logo must stay secondary to the content.

Logos are needed only on the first and last projected slides, since the speaker's affiliation will not change mid-talk, and any logo that crowds the visual evidence should be removed without hesitation.
exception: a handout may carry the logo on every slide

statement: A logo belongs in one of the bottom corners, never in the upper-left corner, which is the most valuable real estate on the slide because Western audiences look there first — the very reason the assertion headline begins there.
condition: for Western reading audiences

statement: Groupings on a slide should hold no more than four items, because audiences remember groupings of two, three, and four but forget larger ones — and many will not even attempt a large grouping displayed for a minute.

Faced with a photograph carrying seven call-outs an audience notices the count, reads perhaps the first one, and turns away; the fix is to place only the three or four most important call-outs on the slide and fold the rest into the speech.

When the items of a long list are of equal importance, they should be folded into two or three memorable categories on the slide with the individual members named in the speech, because the audience recalls three categories far better than seven items.
condition: when the listed items carry the same relative importance

statement: A long list is legitimate in the one case where the presenter does not expect it to be read but only wants the audience to see that many instances exist, and grading the type contrast from dark for the most serious items to light for the least turns the list into an image rather than text to be worked through.
exception: only when the list functions as overwhelming visual evidence rather than as text to read

statement: Animation is one way to work more than four call-outs or diagram blocks onto a slide, but the number of animation stages per slide should be limited to four unless the aim is deliberately to overwhelm.
exception: unless the intent is to overwhelm the audience with the sheer number of items

statement: Sounds attached to slide builds — clicks, whooshes, screeching brakes — grate on an audience and have no place in a professional presentation.

Too little blank space between a slide's text blocks and graphics does three separate kinds of damage: the slide feels crowded, the viewing order becomes ambiguous, and the audience reads it inefficiently, bouncing between elements and back again.

The default slide master causes the crowding by reserving large gutters at the top and sides that bunch content into the middle — a margin needed in the 1980s because slides were printed as transparencies that projectors could crop, and obsolete now.

The default master compounds the problem by setting headline and body text larger than they need to be, further reducing the blank space; correcting the sizes, raising the headline, and resizing the images produces a slide the audience can navigate easily.

The argument is not that presentation software should be avoided but that each of its defaults must be assessed against the actual audience, purpose, and occasion, and changed proactively where it does not serve them.

Weak practices spawned by the defaults have been baked into company and laboratory slide templates, making it hard for individuals to break the mould and leaving younger engineers and scientists unaware that alternatives exist.
Bulleted lists are seductive because they are simple to create and give the appearance of significant thought, even though they reveal little hierarchy or connection to the audience.

Change requires individual scientists, engineers, and technical managers to step back and critically assess common slide practice — which includes analysing when the assertion-evidence approach itself is effective and when it too should be challenged.

The assertion-evidence approach is the right choice for the large majority of scientific slides, but special audiences, purposes, or occasions call for other structures that are equally grounded in principles of how people learn.
condition: for the majority of scientific presentation slides
exception: special audiences, purposes, or occasions may warrant another grounded structure

statement: Two effective slide structures exist — assertion-evidence and TED, the latter suited to communicating with the general public — alongside four variations for sequencing such slides: an evidence-assertion order, pecha kucha, the Lessig approach, and Prezi.
Title, outline, and conclusion slides carry organisation rather than only content, and the shorter the presentation the less each of them is needed.
Opening on a blank black slide with the focus squarely on the speaker is often effective, particularly when the audience already holds a concrete image of the topic.
condition: when the audience already has a concrete image of the talk's topic

statement: A research-conference talk usually needs no outline slide, because the audience already expects hypothesis, then methods for testing it, then results.
condition: when the audience already expects the talk's sequence

statement: The default title master, which yields only a title, names, and institutions, turns the opening into a hurried obligation instead of an engaging entry point, and leaves the audience disoriented the moment the slide changes.

Relevant images on a title slide give the speaker several possible entry points into the same talk — scope, importance, or history — so one title slide can be adapted to different audiences in ways a words-only slide cannot.
Letting an image bleed off the edges of a title slide can be powerful, provided the photograph's background gives enough contrast for the title and presenter information laid over it.
condition: provided the image gives sufficient contrast for the overlaid text

statement: Where presenting the main result up front is appropriate, the title itself can be a sentence assertion stating that result, in which case the title slide ends up resembling the conclusion slide.
condition: when leading with the main result suits the audience and the result

statement: A mapping slide earns its place only when the talk's divisions are not what the audience expects or the talk runs long enough that they could get lost; short talks can map in speech alone.
condition: when the divisions are unexpected or the talk is long

statement: Most scientific talks map themselves with a bulleted list, which is close to the least memorable form a list could take.

A mapping list can usually be cut down: Introduction and Conclusion appear in every talk, the occasion already fixes when acknowledgements and questions come, background can often be covered before the map appears, and specific sub-methods are not needed at that point — the audience needs only the order of the divisions.

The strongest mapping slide integrates the talk's divisions into a single image that also supplies the background, producing a map memorable enough to be recalled weeks later and reconstructed years later.
condition: when the content allows the divisions to be integrated into one image

statement: When the topics cannot be integrated into one image they should each be anchored with a representative image, because a large body of experiments found an audience twice as likely to recall a topic anchored that way, the word and the image being coded by the brain in two separate ways.

Each image used to anchor a division on the mapping slide should reappear on the first slide of that division, and such an image counts as evidence rather than decoration when the section genuinely discusses what it depicts.

Templates that list all the talk's topics down the side or top of every slide are well intentioned but inefficient, spending 10 to 20 percent or more of the slide's most valuable space on a job an effective mapping slide plus thoughtful spoken transitions already does.

In a long talk the cheaper navigation cue is a small icon from the mapping slide repeated in a bottom corner of each slide of its division — under 5 percent of the slide, in low-value space, and able to replace the logo many presenters put on every slide.
condition: in a long talk whose sections each span several slides

statement: Clip art, acceptable on slides in the 1980s, is out of place today because it reads as unprofessional and undercuts the seriousness of the topic; a real photograph — even of the blackboard on which a model was derived — carries a far more professional tone.
Because questions follow it, the final projected slide is displayed the longest, which makes an empty one worse than nothing — a blank screen would at least be less distracting.
A Thank You slide wastes the screen, since words on a slide are far weaker than voice and facial expression at conveying a presenter's emotion; thank the audience by looking them in the eyes instead.
A slide devoted to the word Questions is equally wasted, because once the speaker calls for questions the audience already knows the question period has begun.
The final slide should summarise the talk's most important takeaway, which both emphasises what matters and gives the audience content from which to fashion questions.

A concluding slide may legitimately carry more words than a typical assertion-evidence slide, because it stays projected through the question period and because its image and assertions were already stated earlier in the talk.
condition: provided the material was already presented and the slide remains up through questions

statement: An abrupt ending followed by a bare call for questions produces an uncomfortable silence while the audience scrambles for something to ask, and no raised hands reads as though nobody understood or cared about the talk.

A closing sequence that reliably produces questions is: a headline beginning 'In closing' or 'In summary' so listeners start composing questions as soon as the slide appears, a strong final sentence followed by a pause for applause (thanking the audience if none comes, which cues clapping), and then animating in the word Questions as the applause subsides.
The TED slide style — few words if any, with powerful images that often fill the screen — is the effective structure for communicating science to the general public.
condition: when the audience is the general public

statement: The TED design method begins away from the computer: write each message or takeaway on its own sticky note, arrange the notes into an effective order, and build a slide only where a message warrants a scene.

In the TED style a message may or may not appear on the slide — when it does the slide is effectively assertion-evidence, when it does not the speaker carries the message while the slide carries the evidence — but the message for every slide is identified before the talk, and that act itself focuses the presentation.

TED-style slides can make either a logical appeal through a graph or an emotional appeal through a photograph, with cropping and placement used deliberately — aligning a subject's eyes with a statistic, or positioning that statistic about a third from the top and left for emphasis.

When the message is left off the slide the whole burden of communicating it falls on the speaker, who must both settle on the assertion beforehand and practise enough to state and support it while looking at the audience.
condition: when the slide carries only an image and no stated message

statement: TED-style slides cost more preparation time than assertion-evidence slides — a graphic artist logged over 20 hours for a talk under 13 minutes — and demand artistic ability for choosing, cropping, and positioning images and for sizing and arranging text; their apparent simplicity is engineered.

The simplicity behind that style comes from concrete moves — raising the signal-to-noise ratio, eliminating unneeded text and lines, and using empty space deliberately — captured in the injunctions to practise design rather than decoration and to build scenes rather than slides.

A presenter lacking the time or artistic skill for the full TED approach can still borrow individual strategies from it, such as letting a photograph bleed off the page, into otherwise conventional assertion-evidence slides.

Slides are typically sequenced linearly with each scene projected for one to two minutes, but four variations on that sequencing exist: an evidence-assertion order, pecha kucha, the Lessig method, and Prezi.
Presenting the evidence before the assertion suits three situations in particular: teaching, conveying a complex assertion, and swaying skeptics.
condition: when teaching, when the assertion is complex, or when the audience is skeptical

statement: In teaching, a principle a student pieces together from the supporting evidence sticks better than one they are told, so the slide can show the evidence under a question headline, the class can discuss it, and only then is the answer animated in.
condition: in a teaching context

statement: For an assertion too complex to state at the top of a scene, delaying it buys time to orient the audience to the visual evidence first, and the slide should be left projected after the assertion animates in so it receives proper soak time.
condition: when the assertion is too complex to show at the start of the scene

statement: Withholding a controversial assertion until the evidence has been explained does not guarantee winning over an opposed audience, but it does let the speaker deliver the evidence before the naysayers start composing their rebuttal.
condition: when the assertion is controversial for this audience

statement: The evidence-assertion order is not symmetric: showing evidence before the assertion is legitimate, but a slide should never appear with the assertion alone, since at least some visual evidence must be present to exploit the audience's ability to process an image while listening — and on a white background a headline-only slide leaves over 80 percent of the screen glaring back at them.

Pecha kucha fixes 20 slides at 20 seconds each on automatic advance, and because a slide lasts only about two sentences of speech presenters quickly discover that bullet-ridden slides cannot work and switch to a visual structure.

Pecha kucha is not ideal for scientific presentations but raises an organisation's presentations well above default practice on a single guideline with minimal training, which is why some managers and professors now require it.
condition: when there is no time to teach a more sophisticated structure

statement: Pecha kucha's drawbacks are that it demands substantial preparation just to compress each scene's speech into 20 seconds against automatically advancing slides, and that some scenes such as a graph do not fit a 20-second window — partially remedied by animating a detail to extend soak time.

A flexible time window per scene would be the ideal, but the rigid one is what forces the change: given flexibility many presenters revert to bullet-ridden slides, whereas the fixed window makes adapting to image-based slides the only way not to fall short of the group.

The Lessig style flashes short phrases and images for about a second each in synch with the speech, with the phrases sized, coloured, and positioned to reflect their meaning — in effect simple TED-style scenes sequenced very fast.

The Lessig style is extremely expensive to produce and deliver: one 15-minute talk ran to more than 300 slides, and the speaker must know almost exactly what they will say and keep it synchronised with the sequence, requiring continual practice to hold the timing.
Because of that time cost, the Lessig style should be reserved for talks or portions of talks that will be delivered on multiple occasions.
condition: when the same material will be presented repeatedly

statement: Audiences perceive the Lessig style as light-hearted, so it works best for keynotes and after-dinner talks where wit is welcome rather than for a standard technical presentation.
condition: for occasions open to a witty tone

statement: The Lessig style projects more words per minute than even common practice yet does not appear to cause cognitive overload, plausibly because very few words are on screen at once in pre-made groupings, because visual and auditory attention are almost perfectly synchronised, and because the upbeat style raises attention.

Prezi replaces the deck of frames with one large map the presenter zooms into and out of, which makes it particularly effective for explaining a whole system divided into parts, such as a timeline, a diagram, or a map.
condition: when the content is a whole divided into parts

statement: Prezi costs more learning time than other visual-aid software and does not allow details to be animated into a scene once focused — the whole canvas is what is shown — though enlarging the view can simulate an animation.

Prezi's twisting and rotating transitions physically unsettle audiences, who describe the experience as a roller coaster, so a presenter should stay with zooming in and out unless the motion genuinely captures the subject's physical movement.
exception: unless the rotation depicts real physical movement in the subject

statement: Each sequencing strategy has its own fit: evidence-assertion for teaching technical content or introducing complex and controversial assertions, pecha kucha where there is no time to teach a sophisticated structure, Lessig for keynotes and after-dinner talks, and Prezi for zooming through a large system or timeline.
In the assertion-evidence structure the sentence assertion doubles as a safety net for any listener who missed the spoken transition into the slide.
Projected assertion-evidence slides can be turned into an effective handout by putting the secondary details on the notes pages rather than on the slides themselves.

Both effective structures require the presenter to define each scene's main assertion, and that act works as a filter ensuring every slide contributes to the talk while sharpening what the presenter will say.

Setting title slides aside, a topic-phrase headline does not convey enough information to justify the valuable space it consumes; either a succinct assertion headline or no headline at all is superior.
Omitting the headline entirely frees space to enlarge the graphic, at the cost that the speaker's spoken words alone must then carry the slide's message.
The claim that bulleted slides are useful for generating ideas in a discussion is better served by a writing board than by projected slides.

The topic-subtopic structure persists mainly through inertia: the software filled a void and was adopted fast, its defaults are easy to apply, examples saturate government, industry, and education, and templates at respected colleges, conferences, laboratories, and companies compel students and professionals to follow it.

Because common practice is so weak, a presenter who rises above it stands apart, and students and professionals who did so have won proposal competitions, secured job positions, and earned best-presentation awards — a return that justifies the extra effort when the content is strong.
condition: when the underlying content is strong

statement: The form of Murphy's Law that fits presentations is that whatever can go wrong will go wrong, and at the worst possible time.
A live demonstration attempted without rehearsal can injure the presenter and hijack the lesson entirely, as when an unpractised pendulum demonstration knocked its own presenter unconscious.

Demonstration failure carries real stakes: a software vendor's own presentation program crashed during a public demonstration, and an architectural firm whose stadium-roof model failed to open at the culminating moment of its bid did not win the contract.

Projection failures come in a predictable set — no image, no sound, no internet access for a film, a software mismatch with the room's computer, or a resolution mismatch — and across dozens of institutions on five continents the author found it roughly even odds that something is amiss at the start.

A presentation in an unfamiliar room must not depend on internet access, since many companies and laboratories restrict the web for security or proprietary reasons; every image and film should be embedded in a local file, with a backup copy on separate media.
condition: when speaking in a room new to the presenter

statement: A presentation transmitted by teleconference should be kept simple, because films that run fine in the room can lock up in transmission and sound clips that work locally can produce feedback across sites.
condition: when the presentation is transmitted to remote sites

statement: Slides using unusual typefaces, settings, image formats, or films argue for bringing one's own laptop, though that choice introduces its own set of problems.
condition: when the deck depends on non-standard fonts, settings, or media

statement: Whether to include a visual aid should be decided on three factors — the complexity of the demonstration or equipment, the gain if it succeeds, and the loss if it fails — proceeding only when the benefit outweighs the risk and always planning a response to failure.

Rehearsal is invaluable because it exposes the pitfalls that would otherwise startle the presenter during the performance — including the presenter's own reactions, which is exactly what the unpractised pendulum demonstration failed to surface.
Rehearsal guarantees nothing — both the architectural firm and the software vendor had practised their failed demonstrations — but it greatly increases the odds of success.

Rehearsing with the actual equipment surfaces device-specific traps that would otherwise strike at the start of a talk, such as a slide remote that must have its antenna inserted before the program enters slideshow mode.

Arriving early is what makes a failure recoverable: ten minutes of margin let a presenter discover that the room's computer had lost the deck's typeface, substitute an available one, and refit the text boxes before the audience saw anything.

Presenters who arrive as the session starts routinely tax a large audience with missing typefaces, dead media, or laptop connections that do not fit the projector, producing one of the most painful scenes in scientific presentation — a quiet crowd watching a speaker work frantically on a computer.
Once the structure and slides are set, the presenter should deliberately imagine the worst and devise a plan for equipment failure — an act of preparation rather than of dwelling on failure.

Where the projection equipment is unproven, designing the talk so it can be delivered from handouts alone lets the presenter start on time and lose neither the minutes nor the audience's patience when the system is late.
condition: when the presenter cannot rely on the room's equipment

statement: Presenting in an unfamiliar room warrants a troubleshooting kit — a video cable, an audio cable, and a small speaker that runs off the computer — plus knowing how to change the laptop's screen resolution to match the projector.
condition: when presenting in a room new to the speaker

statement: Disasters usually arise from a chain of causes rather than a single one, which is why imagining the worst compound case is more useful preparation than anticipating individual problems separately.

Even a presenter who rehearses, arrives early, and anticipates the worst will meet at least one occasion where everything fails; the response is to keep one's cool, retain control of the proceedings, and where possible turn the apparent failure to advantage.

Delivery is the speaker's interaction with the audience and the room — voice, gestures, eye contact, stance, and movement — and it determines not only how intently the audience listens but whether they trust the speaker.
Whatever the subject, an audience engages only if the speaker delivers it engagingly — a course as narrow as beekeeping drew crowds because the faculty were passionate about it and knew it deeply.

There is no single correct delivery: a poised, well-prepared professional style and an unpolished, self-absorbed but passionate style can both hold an audience, and not every speaker is suited to a charismatic model.
A caustic question is best met with a calm but resolute voice, because keeping cool demonstrates that the speaker rather than the questioner controls the presentation.
condition: when handling a hostile question

statement: Methodically working through several perspectives on the concern a hostile questioner raises refuses the either-or trap such questioners typically lay.
condition: when a question is framed as a forced binary

statement: A speaker can violate every prescribed rule of dress, eye contact, and stance and still distinguish themselves through sincere passion for the subject, deep knowledge of it, and enough sensitivity to the audience to make sense of a poorly phrased question.

Developing a personal delivery style begins with reflecting on what kind of delivery the speaker is actually comfortable giving, such as whether they prefer to move in front of the audience or to stand behind a podium.

The audience shapes delivery style: a familiar, smiling audience invites walking around, storytelling, humour, and vocal variation, while an unfamiliar or antagonistic one naturally produces a more serious, businesslike delivery with less variation.
Criticising a speaker's lack of warmth without accounting for the hostility of the audience they faced is unfair, as in the criticism levelled at Rosalind Franklin's 1951 DNA talk.

The room is the aspect of occasion that most affects delivery: a lecture hall with vaulted ceilings and tiered seats imposes a formal barrier between speaker and audience that moving toward the front rows or aisles only partly bridges.
How full the room is matters as much as how large it is: a filled room amplifies a laugh while in a half-filled room the same laughter dissipates, making engagement much harder.
When the goal is discussion among the audience, a U-shaped seating arrangement works far better than rows, because listeners can make eye contact with one another.
condition: when discussion among audience members is desired

statement: Anxiety about a time limit makes a speaker talk faster, which compounds the problem — Hertz's evaluation panel unanimously judged that he had raced, and unanimity on that point is itself a signal, since at least one listener in most audiences is too polite to criticise.

Delivery improves with deliberate effort over time through continual reflection and revision — cutting the notes, slowing the tempo, and then actively querying the audience about the result, the querying itself being the mark of a speaker intent on improving.
As a speaker improves their self-criticism grows harsher rather than softer, and praise from an audience may reflect modest expectations rather than a successful talk.

Two ways to shorten the improvement cycle are having colleagues critique the presentation — naming what was strong as well as what was weak — and videotaping oneself and reviewing the recording critically.

Trying to orchestrate every element of delivery at once — posture, stance, hand and body movement, expression, eye contact, volume, variation, filler words — risks neglecting bigger things such as genuine enthusiasm and leaves the speaker stiff and self-conscious.
The most captivating speakers in science and engineering are those who love their subjects and know them well, since a speaker who does not convey interest cannot expect the audience to feel any.

Conveying enthusiasm does not mean singing and shouting, and a pretence will be seen through; genuine enthusiasm shows in a sincere voice, sustained eye contact, animated facial expressions, and natural gestures that aid understanding.
Scientific audiences are suspicious of a delivery with too much dazzle, especially at the opening, tending to assume the talk is more style than substance.
condition: particularly at the beginning of a talk

statement: Studying other speakers' delivery with a critical eye — deliberately observing a respected instructor before a first teaching assignment, for instance — accelerates improvement.

Imagining a model speaker delivering one's own presentation — their vocal rhythm and their movement on stage — shortly before going on stage borrows the whole-motion learning method used in sport, and having such models does not diminish the speaker's individuality but draws out the traits they value.

Preparing a strong presentation takes time on three fronts: understanding the content well enough to organise it comprehensibly, gathering images and graphing results into well-designed slides, and rehearsing to find the right words for difficult concepts and to smooth the transitions.

Young researchers underestimate how much time good lectures take: preparing a celebrated freshman physics series consumed 8 to 16 hours a day for two lectures a week and displaced the lecturer's own research.

Opening the slide software and listing phrases one intends to say is the wrong first move, because it produces talks full of unneeded information; the story — the main message and the assertions the audience must accept first — should be settled before the computer is opened.

The story is best developed by writing the main message and each supporting assertion on separate sticky notes on a wall and rearranging them into the order that tells the best story; in a research talk those assertions include the hypothesis, the reason for testing it, what distinguishes the method, and each individual result.

The story is the argument: the supporting assertions are the steps that carry the audience up the mountain to the main message, and once they are fixed any detail that supports none of them is excluded.
The main reason so many scientific talks are awash with extraneous details is that the presenter never spent the time and energy to define the main message and its supporting assertions.

Visual aids should be built only after the story is settled, and building them takes time of its own: tightening each drafted assertion into a headline the audience can comfortably read during the talk, and creating the graphics that support it.
Reusing a paper's graphics in a talk is a mistake, because a graph or table that works in a document usually carries too much detail or lettering too small to be effective when projected.

A collaborative presentation needs still more preparation time because every speaker should comment on a draft; ideally one person owns slide creation for a consistent format and a deck that reveals the organisation, while everyone meets early to shape the story and can help build the visual evidence.
condition: for a collaborative or group presentation

statement: Effort spent far beyond the communication requirement and tinkering with slides up to the last hour, at the cost of rehearsal, produces a failed talk in which the speaker cannot find a rhythm or the transitions between scenes.

Practice does three things even for a speaker with an excellent deck: it smooths the transitions from one assertion to the next, it works out the explanations of difficult concepts so the words are ready, and above all it reassures the speaker that the talk can be delivered.

The greatest source of a speaker's nervousness is the fear of standing before an audience with nothing to say, which is dispelled by having walked through the whole presentation beforehand, even in a mumble.

Accomplished speakers reserve time alone immediately before a talk — at least thirty minutes even on a tenth delivery, an hour of thinking about nothing else, or an entire afternoon — and skipping it is treated as disrespectful to the audience.

Presenting in a second language calls for extra preparation: enriching the field's vocabulary, practising the pronunciation of its common words, using assertion-evidence slides that hand the audience each takeaway with visual support, and preparing podium notes to fall back on when a word or phrasing goes missing.
condition: when presenting in a non-native language

statement: Memorising and practising a talk in a second language is not enough, because questions must be understood and answered on the spot; where listening comprehension is weak, a colleague in the audience can help decode difficult questions and supply a forgotten word.
condition: when presenting in a non-native language with limited listening comprehension

statement: A speaker working in a second language must accept that mistakes will happen, since embarrassment leads to avoiding speech and improvement is impossible without speaking; one eminent physicist who never felt at ease in English compensated by writing out entire presentations and rehearsing them repeatedly, and her persistence served her career.
condition: when presenting in a non-native language

statement: A presenter's words can come from four sources — extemporaneous speech, impromptu speech, memorisation, or reading — and occasions exist in which each of the four is the appropriate choice.

Extemporaneous speech buys earned credibility, easy adjustment, eye contact, and a natural pace at the cost of inexact wording and much preparation, while reading buys precision and smooth delivery at the cost of an unnatural pace, lost eye contact, no ability to adjust, and lost credibility.

Each source of speech has its occasions: extemporaneous for conference talks, business meetings, seminars, and lectures; impromptu for answering and asking questions and for roundtable discussion; memorisation for the first or last sentences, a short quotation, or a brief introduction of another speaker; and reading for a press conference, a quotation, a scrutinised management talk, or an emotional speech such as a eulogy.

For most scientific presentations a practised extemporaneous talk is the best overall strategy: a rehearsed talk following an established organisation that may be held in memory, written as notes, or conveyed through the visual aids.
condition: for most scientific presentation occasions

statement: A meticulously memorised speech collapses when the audience opens on the offensive, as Bohr's carefully prepared and memorised case to Churchill did within twenty minutes once he was forced to improvise.

Projecting a large share of the spoken sentences splits the audience three ways — reading and tuning the speaker out, listening while ignoring the text, or attempting both at mismatched paces — and none of the three serves comprehension.
In an extemporaneous strategy only a small fraction of the spoken sentences belongs on the slides — the assertion-evidence ratio being roughly one projected sentence for every ten spoken.

Holding note cards in the hand throughout a talk, as many speech classes teach, distracts the audience and undermines the speaker's authority, because science and engineering audiences expect the speaker to look them in the eye and speak from what they know; notes should stay out of view and be glanced at silently.
condition: particularly in science and engineering settings

statement: The one legitimate exception to keeping the eyes on the audience while speaking is explaining a graphic, equation, or film on the screen, since the audience is looking there too.
condition: when explaining a projected graphic, equation, or film

statement: The most important advantage of speaking extemporaneously is the regard it earns: because the speaker is fashioning the words, the audience perceives that the speaker owns the information.

The target is to practise until the talk can be given with no notes at all by memorising its organisation, and a good test of that state is knowing what the next slide is before advancing to it, which is what makes the transition possible.
Speaking the next slide's assertion aloud just before advancing lets listeners who grasp it turn straight to the visual evidence, while the projected headline still catches those who did not.

Speaking without notes scales to sustained teaching, not just one-off talks: Boltzmann delivered four years of university lectures across classical mechanics, hydrodynamics, elasticity, electrodynamics, and kinetic theory without them.

One workable method for note-free public speaking is to build a repertoire of four-to-five-minute segments given many times, select which segments a given talk will use, and then spend the preparation on the transitions into and out of each.

Speaking extemporaneously automatically aligns the speaker's pace with the audience's comprehension, because the words come less easily on a difficult idea — exactly where the audience needs more time — and more easily on an easy one.
Because the wording comes from within, the extemporaneous speaker can keep their eyes on the audience, read them, and adjust the presentation when listeners look confused or bored.

The main disadvantage of extemporaneous speech is groping for the exact word, a risk heightened for a non-native speaker, and the remedy is repeated practice until the speaker is sure the words will come.
condition: especially when presenting in a non-native language

statement: A scientific audience does not expect an actor's fluency and does not judge a pause for the right word harshly; properly spaced, such pauses actually emphasise key points.

Where exact wording genuinely matters — a difficult concept, or the text of a law or statute — that wording can be placed on the slides or in discreetly positioned notes without abandoning extemporaneous delivery.
condition: when precise wording is required for part of the talk

statement: Speaking impromptu for an entire scheduled presentation is unsound given the cost of assembling a professional audience: the odds of arriving at an efficient structure with proper emphasis and smooth transitions are low, the potential for the speaker to become lost is high, and there is little scope for visual aids beyond a writing board.
The prospect of becoming lost is itself a deep source of a speaker's nervousness, and the best countermeasure against nervousness is preparation.

Practising short impromptu talks is nonetheless time well spent, because question periods force off-the-cuff speaking on both the presenter answering and the audience member asking, and practice builds the confidence those moments demand.

A question should be met with a deliberate pause, which both buys time to consider the answer and lends emphasis to its first sentence; audiences are far more patient with visible silent thought than with empty chatter or filler words.

Eliminating filler phrases takes several days and begins with learning which ones you actually use, typically from a colleague's critique; once identified, catching yourself saying one means the habit is already breaking.
Filler phrases surface far more when a speaker is tired, which is reason enough to get a full night's sleep before an important presentation.

Silence carries tension and power: a speaker should pause at least a couple of times long enough to hear the room's ventilation hum, which gives the speaker emphasis and the audience reflection, and a speaker who values silence stops wasting it on fillers.
Memorising a talk offers dramatic delivery, constant eye contact, and control of the exact wording — as long as the speaker's memory does not fail.
condition: so long as the speaker's memory holds

statement: Memorisation is prohibitively expensive at presentation length: a speaker delivers roughly 130 to 140 words a minute, so a 15-minute talk means memorising over 2,000 words — more than most scientists and engineers, who present often, can afford.

A memorised talk cannot be changed mid-stream, which forfeits one of the main reasons for presenting rather than merely documenting the work, and it recalls words faster than an audience can absorb them.

Memorisation still has a place for a few words — introducing a colleague, or the first couple of sentences of a difficult talk — which secures a good first impression and gets the words flowing before the speaker transitions to extemporaneous delivery.
condition: for short, high-stakes fragments of a talk

statement: For many speakers the opening is the hardest part because of pre-talk nervousness, and memorised opening lines carry them to the point where concentration shifts to the science and the nervousness disappears.

A read speech typically runs too fast for comprehension, rattling off complex ideas that needed slowing, and it puts the speaker's eyes on the page so that neither can the speaker read the audience's reactions nor the audience read the speaker's eyes for emphasis and intent.
The gravest cost of reading a speech, or even carrying note cards, is that the audience begins to wonder whether the speaker knows the subject or is merely repeating what others gathered.

The credibility penalty for reading is discipline-specific: in fields with a tradition of reading papers aloud at conferences it does not shadow the speaker's credibility the way it does in science and engineering.
condition: depends on the norms of the speaker's discipline

statement: Reading becomes the right choice where every word will be examined — a press conference, a welcome address to a large conference, or a management talk on a controversial issue — because there the precision outweighs the disadvantages and a misspoken phrase can follow the speaker for years.
condition: when the audience will scrutinise the exact wording

statement: A read speech works when three conditions hold: every idea in the text counts and the sentences are engaging and often surprising, the wording is precise with pleasing sentence rhythms, and the speaker has practised enough to look up at the audience, keep a natural pace, and use pauses for emphasis — so that it does not come across as read at all.
condition: when reading is the chosen mode

statement: Reading full text or large portions of it off a projected slide is a disaster: the audience reads ahead or guesses the gist, so surprise is destroyed, and speaker and audience both end up looking at the screen instead of each other.

The rare exception to projecting spoken text is the Lessig style, where rehearsal is deep enough that one-to-four-word phrases appear simultaneously with or just after being said, so the audience cannot read ahead and surprise survives, while images rather than words accompany much of the speech.
condition: only when rehearsal makes the phrases appear at or after the moment they are spoken

statement: Many presenters carry themselves as though disconnected from everything around them — the room, themselves, the audience, and the time — which Darwin described as feeling that only his head remained.

Audiences arrive at a scientific presentation fearing the worst because so many have been empty experiences, so a speaker facing a new audience should show early that they mean business and will deliver.
The lights, the arrangement of the front of the room, and sometimes the audience seating are the speaker's domain, and exhibiting control of them is part of the delivery.

Presenters who stay passive about the room end up on the wrong side of the screen or boxed in by furniture, and those who never check the lighting options project washed-out slides or stand in a room too dark for eye contact.

Taking charge of the room is concrete: bring a remote advancer if you intend to walk, move a table that blocks your walking space, and lower the front lights or adjust the shades if the projection is washed out — because the speaker is the one credited or blamed for the result.

A speaker in a shared conference session has less freedom to rearrange the room but should still arrive early, learn the setup, and decide how to work with it — arriving at the last minute and demanding different equipment can wreck the following speaker's talk as well as one's own.
condition: when presenting within a multi-speaker session

statement: Control of the room continues during the talk: shut a door that is letting in distracting noise, mitigate someone's early departure by looking to the opposite side of the room, and stop speaking entirely when an outside noise is loud enough that no one can hear.

A speaker cannot control the disturbance but can control their reaction to it, and a well-practised speaker can carry on from memory through a total failure of the stage lights and even turn the incident into a closing joke.
A speaker significantly influences the perceived formality of an occasion through attire, and a professional appearance gives a new audience a good first impression.
Appropriate attire is not always formal: a deliberately casual look can be exactly right when it positions the speaker or their organisation as the outsider.
condition: when the informal look serves the speaker's intended positioning

statement: A speaker can do little about the pitch or accent of their voice but can control its inflection and loudness, and a voice with no variation in loudness or speed tires an audience quickly.

Varying speed and loudness both engages an audience and emphasises key details, but the variation must be the speaker's natural conversational inflection — an audience senses when a speaker is acting.
condition: the variation must arise naturally rather than be performed

statement: A stance should convey confidence while remaining comfortable: hands relaxed at the side reads as confident though many find it unnatural, hands rested lightly on a podium works, and clenching the podium reads as defensive.
A hand in a pocket conveys ease but not at the opening of a talk, and once there the hand must stay still; keys and change should be emptied beforehand so they are not absent-mindedly rattled.
condition: not at the beginning of a talk

statement: Lists of forbidden postures are well intended but should not inhibit a speaker's energy: an accomplished lecturer may adopt several of them, provided it is after the audience is already engaged and only briefly.
condition: provided the audience is already engaged and the posture is held only briefly

statement: The best presenters move, but with purpose so that the movement contributes: walking toward the audience emphasises a point, and using the hands to illustrate lets the audience see as well as hear what is being said.

Repetitive movements — fidgeting with a tie, necklace, or belt, shifting weight from foot to foot, or pacing like a caged animal — hypnotise the audience and contribute nothing, so they must be watched for.
Blanking the projector when it is not needed does double duty: it removes the bright white glare and frees the speaker to occupy the part of the room that would otherwise be in the projected light.
A long metal or wooden pointer keeps the speaker out of the blinding projector beam and can be grounded against the screen for steadiness.

A laser pointer amplifies a nervous hand into a wild vibration on the screen, so a speaker with an unsteady hand should anchor it against their side, watch where it is aimed, and use it sparingly — highlighting nearly everything provides no emphasis at all.

An audience follows the speaker's eyes: look at the floor and they look at the floor, look out the window and they do the same, engage them and they return the look and concentrate harder — partly from the sense of being watched and partly from feeling part of the presentation.

Rather than counting seconds per person, the workable rule is to have made eye contact with everyone before the end in a small room, and in a large one to have looked several times at every section and met individual eyes within each.

The advice to look above the heads of the audience at the back wall is a myth, because eye contact exists both to engage people and to read how they are responding, and a wall tells the speaker nothing.
An audience communicates continuously without speaking: intent stares signal concentration, nodding signals agreement, and closed eyes or a gaze at the floor signal that concentration has stopped.

Most listeners reveal delight, confusion, anger, or boredom in their faces, and a good speaker adjusts accordingly — slowing when the audience looks confused, speeding up when it looks bored, and cutting tangential points when it looks tired.
exception: some audience members hold a poker face throughout

statement: A speaker should read the mood of the whole audience but never overreact to one individual: an angry face may have nothing to do with the talk and is best not looked at directly, and a listener determined to sleep should be left to sleep while the speaker attends to everyone else.
When a question is asked the speaker's most important task is to listen, because the relief of finishing the last slide makes it easy to miss the first question entirely and have to ask for a repeat.

Question periods are opportunities rather than threats: they deliver feedback from colleagues seeing the work with fresh eyes, and Feynman regretted for years having failed to listen to an objection at his first presentation that might have let him correct the theory.

Speakers who stay passive while a questioner rambles at length lose the room: the audience's irritation transfers from the questioner to the panel, and the failure to seize control undermines an otherwise worthwhile presentation.

A strong scientific presentation is two-way communication: the speaker holds the primary role of preparing, organising, and presenting, but also carries the responsibility to learn from the audience and adjust for them.

Overrunning the allotted time carries real professional cost: a speaker who ignored the session chair's signals and spoke through the scheduled break left a memorial session remembered for anger at him and embarrassment for the bereaved family rather than for the work being honoured.
Who controls the clock depends on the format: without interruptions the speaker owns the time, while in a format where the audience can interject, control of time is shared with them.
Meeting a deadline in an uninterrupted talk is mostly a preparation problem: define a scope that can be covered adequately in the time allotted, and plan to show no more slides than that time allows.
condition: when the presentation runs without audience interruption

statement: Slide counts must respect soak time: planning 20 slides for a 15-minute talk makes no sense outside a Lessig sequence, even a title slide deserves about 60 seconds so the audience can orient and adjust to the speaker's delivery, and a complex graphic needs more still.
exception: a Lessig-style sequence is the deliberate exception

statement: Practising the whole presentation with the slides builds confidence both that the words will come for each idea and that the talk will fit the time limit.

Rehearsal timing does not transfer directly to the live talk: nervousness makes most speakers faster in front of an audience than alone, though a few become slower, and a speaker must know which they are and correct for it.

The other timing variable is digression — adding a story or dwelling on an interesting point, especially when the audience is responding well — for which the remedy is in-talk benchmarks such as finishing the introduction or reaching the second main point by a set time, checked with a glance at a watch or room clock while changing slides.
Building an optional point into the talk makes benchmarks actionable: cover it if the benchmark is met and skip it if running behind.

Slides can be skipped invisibly by typing the target slide number and pressing Enter, so a presenter should plan one or two possible jumps and keep the relevant slide numbers — including any wanted for the question period — on a sticky note beside the laptop.

When the audience can interrupt, the speaker remains the leader and should keep things moving by postponing premature questions that the talk will reach later and by declining out-of-scope questions with an offer to discuss them afterwards, which most questioners accept if the refusal is diplomatic.
condition: when the format allows questions during the presentation

statement: Whether to yield to a persistent questioner is a judgment call: a manager or a funder usually has to be given their time, and a tangent several listeners want may be worth deferring to, but when one person alone is holding up everyone else the speaker must move on, because the audience's irritation at that questioner turns into anger at the speaker who let the talk derail.
condition: depends on the questioner's standing and whether others share the interest

statement: Severe stage fright can cost a talk before it starts: a presenter who reads the paper rather than speaking to the audience, and reads it fast enough to finish two papers inside one slot, draws no questions at all because nobody understood enough to ask one.

Losing composure during questions follows a recognisable spiral: a question trips the speaker, confidence drops, the audience senses a flaw and presses the same point, confidence falls further, and the questions turn more biting.
Feeling nervous before a presentation is entirely normal and was shared by great scientists; what matters is only that the nervousness does not pull the presentation down.
Nervousness commonly drives a speaker into a zombie state in which the face loses expression and the voice loses energy.

Nervousness that keeps a scientist from presenting has cost real credit, since the collaborator who does present receives the recognition — a pattern visible in the fission, protein-structure, and developmental-genetics cases where the reticent partner was overlooked.
Merely overcoming nervousness enough to present is not the goal; what distinguishes the best speakers is channelling that nervous energy into positive energy that serves the talk.
Unchannelled nervous energy escapes as distracting movement — jingling coins, fiddling with a pointer, swaying in place — and scrunching the toes gives it an outlet the audience cannot see.

Nervousness reaches the voice in several distinct ways: it can leave the voice shaking for minutes, strip the nerve to speak so the presenter reads dully and incomprehensibly, or accelerate delivery so far that a 50-minute talk is over in 30.
A bad case of nervousness usually signals insufficient preparation, and the remedy is two or three full practice runs with the visual aids before an important talk.
A colleague's critique must come early enough that valid criticisms can be worked in, because making major changes just before a presentation can do more harm than good.
With preparation done, only the room's small things remain — confirming the slides project, checking the advancer, and adjusting the lights.

Nervousness eases when the speaker shifts focus off themselves and onto the listeners — meeting them beforehand and asking them questions — because the speaker is working for the audience and residual nervous energy then works for the presentation.

Presentation nerves resemble athletic nerves, and the same positive-visualisation strategy applies: imagine delivering a successful talk, imagine stating each main assertion, and imagine the audience focused and nodding in agreement.
Nervousness has a predictable cycle that subsides as soon as the presentation begins and the speaker concentrates on the subject, and knowing that cycle is itself a comfort in the days beforehand.

Deep, quiet breathing before being called on lets the body counteract the chemistry of nervousness, and too little oxygen lets the nervousness escalate; progressive tightening and releasing of muscles from the feet upward serves the same purpose.
A useful reframe for nerves is that the audience does not expect much: most are resigned to yet another boring presentation, which turns the talk into a challenge in the positive sense.

An alarming event mid-talk may have nothing to do with the talk — half an audience once walked out of a well-received presentation to attend a required meeting — so the operative rule is that however bleak things look, the speaker must not lose their cool.
Audiences do not hold a speaker responsible for failed bulbs, fire alarms, or other listeners' behaviour — only for how the speaker reacts to them.
Even devastating criticism from an admired figure immediately before speaking leaves the presenter one correct move: go up and do the best they can with the cards dealt.

Handling a question runs through an ordered sequence: listen to it, ask for clarification if it is unclear, repeat or rephrase it when the room is too large for others to have heard, pause to think, and only then answer.
Asking a questioner to clarify is legitimate rather than embarrassing, because the question was almost certainly fashioned on the spot.
An answer must balance two competing demands: satisfying the questioner and staying concise enough that others still get a chance to ask.

The fear of an unanswerable question is largely unfounded, because the audience does not expect the speaker to know everything about the topic and many questions fall outside the presentation's scope in the first place.
A question outside the talk's scope should be identified as such, with the speaker still trying to connect it to something they do know.
condition: when the question lies outside the presentation's scope

statement: A speaker must never bluff an in-scope answer they do not have: exposure is likely, credibility collapses when it happens, and the sharks in the audience begin to circle.
condition: when the question is in scope and the answer is unknown

statement: The honest replies to an unanswered question are to admit the answer is incomplete and then state what is known, to say that nobody yet knows if that is true — which can win respect and shows command of the literature — or to promise to look it up afterwards and then actually do so.

A challenge from the floor is usually not a personal attack: eminent scientists rigorously challenged work they believed inaccurate, and such challenges often strengthen the science even though they overwhelm many presenters.
One workable response to a challenge is to stand very straight and answer loudly enough for the whole room, restating even the same point made in the formal talk with volume and confidence.
condition: when the speaker's work is challenged during questions

statement: A second response is to distinguish sincere questions from attacks — answering the first politely and meeting the second by rebutting directly and quoting the pertinent literature.
condition: when the questioner is attacking rather than asking

statement: Calmly enumerating the published papers that support a challenged assumption, one after another, settles the exchange by making clear to the room that the speaker has read the literature and the sarcastic questioner has not.
condition: when the speaker's assumptions are challenged and the literature supports them

statement: A challenge to the assumptions of a work demands a strong response, because an audience that comes to regard the assumptions as flawed discounts the entire result.
Holding one's ground under challenge need not create animosity — in one case the challenging researcher invited the presenter to lunch immediately afterwards to hear the work in depth.
Lowering the voice rather than raising it is an alternative response to a harsh question that can guide the audience's sympathy toward the speaker, and it works as long as the speaker stays resolute.
condition: only while the speaker remains resolute

statement: Whatever the response to a hostile question, stumbling into filler phrases makes the speaker appear weak and confused.

A third response to an attacking question is to pause, fix the eyes on the questioner, answer decisively, and immediately call on someone in a different part of the room, denying the original questioner a follow-up.

When a challenger turns out to be right, the correct move is to consider the point publicly and then state plainly that the questioner is correct and that the work beyond that step is wrong — a response that marks the speaker's aim as truth rather than personal glory.
condition: when the challenge to the work is correct

statement: The willingness to admit being wrong is perhaps the clearest sign of a speaker's security, and it earned Bohr much admiration.
Asking how to handle nervousness is the wrong question; the better question is how to achieve confidence.
One route to confidence is deliberate denial of the audience — not thinking about them once on stage but focusing on the science and the passion for the ideas and letting that carry the talk.
Passion alone is only a source of confidence; it is passion combined with preparation that produces the strongest form of it.

The preparation levels behind confident public talks are far above what most presenters assume: rehearsing the opening 10 to 15 times, or practising an 18-minute talk two or three times a day for the two months before it.

A useful two-phase pattern before a major talk is to spend the earlier time meeting the audience to learn who they are, what motivates them, and what they know about the work, and then to withdraw alone in the final hours to rehearse the route through the talk calmly, much as a skier memorises a slalom course.

A quiet block for final rehearsal is essential even for a talk already given several times, and where scheduling forbids it just before the session it should be taken the night before or early that morning, to solidify the structure and the use of the visual aids prepared over the preceding weeks.

Even among speakers who prepare heavily, memorising the actual words is the exception rather than the norm — one did so only because she had far too much to say for an 18-minute slot — while the standard remains a practised but extemporaneous talk.
condition: memorisation reserved for unusually compressed slots

statement: The confidence worth aiming for rests on knowing the subject, loving it, genuinely enjoying explaining it, and having prepared with that passion fuelling the preparation.

Three errors account for most underperforming scientific talks: choosing a scope too broad to reach a satisfying depth, projecting slides that bury the main message in the noise of bulleted lists, and delivering the message without the passion or confidence it deserves.

A strong presentation requires three things of the speaker: understanding the subject well enough that what is imparted is worth the audience's time, showing genuine enthusiasm for it, and holding a keen awareness of what the audience knows, what will engage them, and what biases they carry.
A speaker is not expected to know everything about the subject, and need not present with exceptional charisma — but every speaker should instil in the audience a respect for the subject.
A great presentation is remembered for decades — Meitner could still recall every detail of a first lecture she heard from Einstein many years later.
The default structure of a phrase headline supported by a bulleted list is ineffective for communicating science and engineering, and the assertion-evidence structure is the effective replacement.
Assertion-evidence slides take much more time to create, and the benefits outweigh that cost when the message is important.
condition: when the message being presented is important

statement: The comprehension gain from assertion-evidence slides grows with the technical difficulty of the message: the more technical the content, the larger the increase in what the audience understands.

The three benefits of the assertion-evidence structure are better audience comprehension, a better connection between speaker and audience because the speaker no longer turns to read points off the slides, and — most important — a more focused talk.
The focus gain comes from a specific mechanism: the speaker identifies the talk's main takeaways and then uses those takeaways as a filter for selecting the supporting evidence.

The single closing instruction to scientists and engineers is to aim higher — not to settle for the staid presentation style most resign themselves to, but to craft, for the given audience, purpose, and occasion, a talk genuinely worth the audience's time.

Effectively critiquing a scientific presentation means examining it from multiple perspectives and naming both what was strong and what could be stronger, recognising that not every criterion applies to every talk and that team presentations need additional ones.
The content-and-speech criteria for a critique are whether the audience was targeted, whether the purpose was achieved, and whether the occasion was met.
The beginning of a talk is critiqued on four points: whether the scope was given, the importance shown, the background and credibility established, and the mapping made memorable.

The middle of a talk is critiqued on whether the assertions were emphasised and supported, whether the needed information was conveyed with terms defined and background given, and whether the emphasis was appropriate.
Scope and depth are critiqued as three separate questions: whether the scope engages, whether the key limitations were stated, and whether the depth satisfies.

Transitions are critiqued at three junctures — beginning to middle, between the main points of the middle, and middle to ending — and the ending is critiqued on whether the main assertions were summarised and closure achieved, with repetition and placement used effectively for emphasis and sources acknowledged.
Slide headlines are critiqued on whether each slide conveys a message and serves the audience, whether each headline states the key assertion, and whether each is succinct at one or two lines.

Visual evidence is critiqued on whether it supports the assertion and was explained, whether the level of detail is appropriate and extraneous details excluded, whether bullet lists were avoided and text blocks held to one or two lines, whether reference listings of author and year were given, and whether fewer than 20 words per minute were projected.

Slide format is critiqued on whether the type is easy to read, blank space used effectively, weak software defaults avoided, the slide left room to breathe, and any animation purposeful and professional.

Delivery is critiqued on whether the speaker showed passion, made effective eye contact, controlled nervousness, moved in ways that contribute, exuded confidence, handled the equipment properly, kept the voice clear and engaging at an appropriate speed, avoided filler phrases, handled questions convincingly and succinctly, and kept to time.
Every presentation carries a persuasive component, because even a nominally informative talk aims to move the audience from uninformed to informed or from inaction to action.
The presenter must tune the message to the audience's existing frequency; the audience is not obliged to tune itself to the presenter.

Resonance is achieved by understanding the audience's existing beliefs and desires and constructing a message that matches what is already there, rather than by introducing content the audience has no attachment to.

A presentation should be shaped as a deliberate contour with multiple peaks rather than a dramatic story's single climax, because a presentation carries disparate pieces of information and more layers than a lone protagonist's arc.

The proposed presentation shape was validated by overlaying it onto two structurally different game-changing talks — Steve Jobs's 2007 iPhone launch and Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' — and both mapped to the form.
Improving slide visuals cannot rescue a presentation whose content is meaningless; the message must be fixed before the visual layer.

In an executive survey conducted by Distinction, 86.1 percent reported that communicating with clarity directly impacts their career and income, while only 25.2 percent spent more than two hours preparing for a high-stakes presentation.

Preparation time for a high-stakes presentation should be budgeted deliberately, because a high-quality in-person presentation requires planning and discipline that ordinary time pressure will otherwise crowd out.
Use the question 'how badly do I want this idea to live?' as the decision test for whether a given presentation justifies a full investment of preparation time and discipline.
condition: when deciding how much effort to commit to a particular presentation

statement: Obscurity, not opposition, is the primary obstacle to persuasion: an idea that blends into its environment loses both clarity and its chance of adoption.
Nothing has intrinsic attention-grabbing power; attention comes from how far a thing stands out from its surrounding context, so contrast must be engineered relative to the audience's environment.
Show explicitly how the idea contrasts with the audience's existing expectations, beliefs, feelings, or attitudes in order to earn their close attention.
Contrast need not mean rebelling against the organization's existing messages and content; the requirement is to lift that content out of its drab traditional treatment.
A presentation's forward momentum comes from bursts of contrast across three dimensions — content, emotion, and delivery — and a presentation with no contrast loses audience interest.
Facts alone do not produce persuasion; a body of evidence can be logically agreed with yet still fail to move an audience to act.
Use plenty of facts but pair them with emotional appeal, rather than abandoning facts or replacing them with emotion.
Adding emotion does not mean splitting a presentation half fact and half emotion; it means introducing humanness that appeals to the audience's desires.

Piling on more proof does not convert a determined skeptic, because a listener who chooses not to believe will always find a reason to reject the evidence; over-reliance on proof displaces the emotional connection that does the persuading.
A persuader should be able to name the audience's emotions, describe their causes, and know how they are aroused — Aristotle's condition for commanding persuasion.
When two offerings carry the same features, the one that appeals to an emotional need is the one selected, so functional specification alone is an insufficient message.
condition: when competing options are functionally equivalent

statement: Stories are the practical mechanism for evoking a visceral audience reaction, because they bind information to experience and arouse the listener's emotions and energy.

Constructing a conventional list-and-argument case takes rationality but little creativity, whereas presenting an idea with enough emotional power to be memorable demands storytelling skill and vivid insight.

A personal story whose conflict or complication exposes the presenter's flaws carries the most inherent power to change others, even though telling it requires vulnerability toward people the presenter does not know well.
Jargon and emotionally neutral corporate phrasing are the easier default but block the human connection an audience attends a presentation to get.

In-person presentation is the one communication medium that is genuinely human, and the visceral connection it creates is often what makes an audience adopt an idea — which explains why average ideas gain traction and brilliant ones die.

Organizations pass through startup, growth, maturity, and decline unless they reinvent themselves, which makes persuasive internal communication of each strategic move a survival requirement rather than a courtesy.
A future direction often cannot be justified with statistics, facts, or proofs because the data does not yet exist, so leaders must communicate intuition-led moves into uncharted territory.
condition: when moving toward a future for which no statistics have yet been generated

statement: Information is static while stories are dynamic, so a story helps the audience visualize what the presenter does or believes in a way that raw information does not.
The presenter is not the hero of the presentation; the audience is the hero and the presenter occupies the mentor role.

Deference to the audience is a practical necessity rather than politeness, because the idea fails if the audience does not engage and believe — the presenter's success depends on them, not the reverse.

Opening a deck with company background — history, market cap, headcount, locations — is the selfish structure; that information belongs in a handout so the presentation itself can start at the audience's frequency.
exception: the audience does need to know something about the presenter and the company, so the information is relocated rather than dropped
