statement: Help each audience member see themselves as the hero of the story and feel the presentation is addressing them personally, whether the plot is beating an adversary or hitting a business objective.
The mentor's job in a presentation is to hand the audience guidance, confidence, insight, advice, training, or tools so they can overcome initial fear and enter the new journey.
A presentation is not an occasion to demonstrate the presenter's brilliance; the success test is whether the audience leaves holding insights and tools they did not have before.
Audience insight and resonance are only available to a presenter who adopts a stance of humility.

Writing falls on a spectrum between report and story: a report organizes facts by topic and informs, a story organizes scenes dramatically and entertains, and a presentation sits between them as an explanation containing both.
Reports should be distributed and presentations should be presented; projecting a document as a read-along produces a 'slideument' that is neither.
Layer fact and story alternately through the presentation — fact, then story, then fact — because the alternation creates a pulse and makes information more digestible.
The first move in building a presentation is a mindset shift from transferring information to creating an experience.
A dramatic experience is produced by creating desire in the audience and then showing how the presenter's idea fills that desire.
Something must be at stake such that the audience is convinced a great deal will be lost if the goal is not obtained; if nothing is at risk the material is not interesting.
All stories reduce to the pattern situation, complication, resolution.

In Syd Field's three-act paradigm the second act often runs twice the length of the first and third acts: act one establishes characters and the hero's unfulfilled desire, act two supplies confrontation and obstacles, act three resolves — meaning solution, not merely ending.
A plot point is any incident or event that spins the story in another direction and sets it up for a change.

A great presentation resembles a screenplay in four respects: a clear beginning, middle and end; an identifiable inherent structure; a first plot point (turning point) that captures audience intrigue; and a beginning and end much shorter than the middle.

These story models are forms rather than formulas: they fix structure and character transformation while leaving room for flexibility and creativity, and Field's screenplay model is only partially applicable to presentations.

The Hero's Journey, as simplified by Vogler from Campbell and Jung, runs twelve stages: Ordinary World, Call to Adventure, Refusal of the Call, Meeting the Mentor, Crossing the First Threshold, Tests/Allies/Enemies, Approach to the Inmost Cave, the Ordeal, the Reward, the Road Back, Resurrection, and Return with the Elixir.

Beyond the outer journey of physical events, the hero undergoes an inner transformation of heart and mind at each stage, and the circular representation draws a clear line between the ordinary world and the special world.
A presentation should carry the audience from their ordinary world into the presenter's special world, where they gain new insight and skills to take back.
The audience crosses the threshold by conscious choice and cannot be forced; the presentation's objective is to bring them to that decision point well enough that they cross voluntarily.

Plan for the audience to resist the proposed point of view and to raise obstacles and roadblocks; the requested change will not come without a struggle, and the presenter must acknowledge that struggle rather than deny it.
The audience must change internally — altering perception — before they will change how they act, so the presentation must target perception first.
As mentor, the presentation should prepare the audience for the later stages of the journey they will undertake after leaving the room, setting them up to succeed there.
condition: when the audience has decided to cross the threshold and adopt the perspective

statement: Unlike a film, a presentation is not bound to chronological sequence and may address the later journey stages out of order.
A good story requires some conflict or imbalance that the audience perceives and the presentation resolves; that sense of discord is what makes them care enough to engage.

Create imbalance by deliberately juxtaposing what is with what could be — contrasting who the audience is entering the room with who they could be leaving it — because drawing attention to that gap forces them to contend with it until a new balance is reached.
The presentation form has two turning points that separate its three parts: the call to adventure divides the beginning from the middle, and the call to action divides the middle from the end.
The form does not stop at the end of the talk: because presentations persuade, it includes a subsequent action the audience performs after leaving.
The beginning of the presentation sets the baseline of what is — a concise formulation of what everyone agrees is true, drawn from historical or current state including the present problem.

Accurately capturing the audience's current reality and sentiment demonstrates the presenter understands their perspective, context and values, creates a common bond, and makes them more open to a new perspective; audiences are grateful when their contribution and experience are acknowledged.
Without first establishing what is, the dramatic effect of the new idea is lost, so the what-could-be proposal must land against an explicitly stated baseline.
The beginning should not consume more than about 10 percent of total presentation time, because the audience is anxious to learn why they are there and what is being proposed.
exception: it may run longer than a short statement, but not long-winded

statement: The call to adventure is created by putting forward a memorable big idea that conveys what could be, at the moment the audience first sees the stark contrast with what is; this turning point must be explicit, not muddled or vague.

The call to adventure plays the role of a film's inciting incident, which first throws the protagonist's life out of balance and then arouses the desire to restore it — the imbalance is what makes the audience want a different reality.
After the call to adventure, the entire remainder of the presentation should be about filling the stated gap and drawing the audience toward the presenter's view of what could be.

The middle of a presentation is built from contrast and should visibly move up and down so the audience feels events continually unfolding; the communicator's job there is to create and resolve tension.

Three distinct kinds of contrast can be built into a presentation: content contrast between what is and what could be (and the presenter's views versus the audience's), emotional contrast between analytical and emotional material, and delivery contrast between traditional and nontraditional methods.

Oppositional content is stimulating and familiar content is comforting; both extremes are needed in a presentation because their polarity is what produces forward movement, so audience differences are a resource rather than a problem.

Know the audience well enough to state where the presenter's views are similar to and different from theirs, because listeners continuously catalogue what they hear against their own knowledge and biases.

The call to action must state exactly what the audience is being asked to do, as discrete tasks, because successful persuasion leads to action and the audience must decide at that line whether they are in.

Audiences contain four action temperaments — doers (instigate activities), suppliers (get resources), influencers (change perceptions) and innovators (generate ideas) — and the call to action should offer at least one action suited to each so members can pick the one they are comfortable performing.

Requested actions should be simple, straightforward and easily executed, the most critical ones emphasized, and each mentally connectable by the audience to a positive outcome for themselves or the greater good.
Do not end a presentation on the call to action, because closing on a to-do list is not inspirational; follow it with a vivid picture of the reward and the new bliss created when the idea is adopted.
The end of a presentation should sit on a higher plane than the beginning, leaving the audience with a heightened sense of what could be and a willingness to be transformed.
Audience transformation — understanding something new or doing something differently — is the goal of persuasion, so it is the criterion against which a presentation's ending is judged.
The ending should repeat the most important points and then deliver inspirational remarks describing what the world looks like once the idea is adopted.

By the principle of recency, audiences remember the last content they hear more vividly than points made in the beginning or middle, which is why the closing material must carry the inspirational payload.
Describe the possible future outcomes with wonder and awe — what the audience's lives, humanity, or the planet will look like — so the audience can see the reward is worth their effort.
The presentation should close by asserting not merely that the idea is possible but that it is the right and better choice.

A dramatic, rousing conclusion that gets the audience to cheer, rise and vocalize creates positive emotional contagion and a strong emotional takeaway, and the ending of a narrative is the first thing an audience remembers.

Adoption remains inconclusive when the presentation ends: the audience determines the outcome, which resolves as comedy — a rise in the fortune of a deserving hero — if they act, or as tragedy if they do not.

A sparkline visualizes a presentation's contour: the line moves up and down between what is and what could be and changes colour to signal contrasts in emotion and delivery, giving each presentation a unique diagnosable pattern.
The presentation form is a flexible form, not a formula; rigid adherence to it risks making presentations too predictable, so its versatility must be exercised.

In his 2008 TED talk Benjamin Zander deployed all three contrast types at once — structural (a stated gap between those who love classical music and those who do not), delivery (alternating speech and piano, making the audience sing, leaving the stage to move among them), and emotional (stories that alternate laughter and tears).

A mentor-presenter hands the audience a usable tool: Zander taught the audience to hear impulses and chord progressions so they could perceive the layers of beauty that had previously kept them from loving classical music.

A presentation can carry one engineered emotional peak — a S.T.A.R. moment — such as Zander asking the audience to remember a lost loved one while replaying Chopin after training their ears to hear an unresolved chord's longing.
Putting a presentation into story form gives it three properties at once: structure, an imbalance the audience wants resolved, and a clearly identified gap the audience can fill.
Designing a presentation without a specific audience in mind is like writing a love letter addressed 'to whom it may concern'.

Build empathy by answering concrete questions about the audience — what makes them laugh, cry, unites them, incites them, and what makes them deserve to win — rather than by cataloguing their attributes abstractly.
Do not treat the audience as a homogeneous blob; imagine them as a line of individuals waiting for a face-to-face conversation, which produces the conversational tone that keeps them interested.

An audience is a temporary assembly whose members hear the same message simultaneously yet filter it differently; finding common ground makes each individual's filter more readily accept the presenter's perspective.

Narrowly targeting the message at the highest-priority individuals in the room, so it reads as a personal conversation, is a legitimate option and is worthwhile even if only that one right person acts on it.
condition: when specific high-priority individuals in the audience hold the decision

statement: Segment a large audience into subsegments and target the one that will yield the most additional supporters — the group offering the greatest impact for the least effort.
Appealing to the broad audience while simultaneously connecting deeply with the key subset is difficult but worth the effort.

Demographic segmentation is the most common method but yields only assumptions: workplace, title, geography and company do not explain what moves an audience, because demographics are only part of the story.

Effective audience understanding requires active research — running a survey, reading industry blogs and icons, following their social conversation, reading their press releases, annual report and their own presentations — until the presenter feels they know the audience personally.
Audience research pays off even when only a portion of the insights appear in the delivered presentation, because the research is what produces the presenter's empathy and sense of connection.

Avoid clichéd or over-broad segmentation: defining the audience too broadly makes the presenter seem impersonal or unprepared and can make the audience feel like a statistic or a stereotype, which can be offensive.
The audience must be defined in a way that is accurate and appropriate for the specific kind of presentation being delivered, rather than by a default segmentation scheme.

Circumstances can dictate a situational segmentation that overrides conventional distinctions: after the Challenger disaster Reagan segmented by relationship to the event — bereaved families, the general public, schoolchildren, NASA staff — because addressing the nation by gender or party would have been inappropriate.
condition: when the occasion itself creates a natural situational segmentation

statement: Addressing each subaudience in turn while binding them back to the collective whole is what allowed a four-minute address to meet the differing emotional requirements of several audiences at once.
Credibly moving in and out of different speaker roles for different audience segments — eulogist and head of state in the same address — is a distinguishing skill of a great communicator.
Establish the audience-hero's likability to yourself before writing content — the screenwriting 'save the cat' device — because liking the audience is the precondition for being genuine with them.

Profile the audience along six dimensions — lifestyle, existing knowledge and biases, motivation and desire, values, influences and decision-making, and how they give and receive respect — rather than by role alone.
Keep answering audience questions until the picture shifts from what they do for a job to who they are as people; knowing their titles is not enough.
The objective of audience analysis is to determine what the audience cares about and link the presenter's idea to it.
Look specifically for how the proposed idea would relieve pressure on the audience's real, messy circumstances if they act on it.
A mentor carries two responsibilities — teaching and gift-giving — and appears at the critical juncture to move the hero past doubt and fear.

Plan explicitly what the presentation gives the audience under three headings: guidance (insight to navigate the journey), confidence (so they are not reluctant), and tools (skills or gifts they take with them).
The presenter should supply important, useful, previously unknown information, so the audience leaves every presentation knowing something new and able to apply it to succeed.

The presenter must not frame the audience as helping them on their journey; a mentor may occasionally gain knowledge from the exchange but that must not be the goal, because an audience can always spot selfish motives.
exception: the mentor legitimately gains something from the relationship on occasion, provided the greater benefit goes to the hero

statement: Common ground is built by identifying and articulating shared experiences and shared goals, which constructs enough trust for the audience to feel safe crossing to the presenter's side.
Qualifications must be revealed humbly and selflessly, framed as why the presenter is uniquely fit to guide this audience and what similar journey they have completed successfully.
Audiences validate a presenter against their own criteria and experience before adopting a new perspective, so emphasising commonalities is what bolsters credibility.
A presentation that creates common ground can unite an otherwise diverse group toward a common purpose, because people set aside differences when strongly connected to a shared goal.
When a presentation is misinterpreted the fault lies with the presenter, who chose the words and images, not with the audience; the presenter must own the misalignment with audience experience.

An urgency message pitched to an audience with no lived experience of the danger can read as manipulation: a 2007 downturn-warning delivered to staff who had known only prosperity stalled progress and took a year to reframe, because no shared symbols or experiences were used.

An audience chooses whether to connect and will usually respond only when it is in their interest; because personal values ultimately drive behaviour, the message should identify and align with values the audience already holds.
Mapping the overlap between presenter and audience simultaneously clarifies what lies outside the overlap — precisely the material the audience must be brought to embrace.
The presenter's objective is to find the most relevant and believable way to link their issue to the audience's top values and concerns.

A presentation must have a defined destination — where the audience should be when they leave — because without mapping it the audience will not get there, and every piece of content should propel them toward it.
Moving an audience away from their familiar world produces a felt sense of loss, because persuasion asks them to let go of old beliefs or habits before adopting new ones.

Audience resistance cannot be controlled but can be harnessed like a sailboat tacking against the wind: plan for it and adjust the message so the opposing force produces forward progress, which requires moving back and forth rather than straight ahead.
A big idea is the single key message — the screenwriter's controlling idea — that supplies the impetus for the audience to set a new course.
A big idea has exactly three components: it articulates the presenter's unique point of view, it conveys what is at stake, and it is written as a complete sentence.

A topic is not a big idea: 'the fate of the oceans' is a topic, whereas 'worldwide pollution is killing the ocean and us' carries a point of view; the view need not be unheard-of, only the presenter's own rather than a generalization.

Stating the big idea as a complete sentence forces it to carry a noun and a verb; answers like 'it's the third-quarter update' are not big ideas, and including the word 'you' is better still because it ensures the idea is written to someone.
Without a compelling statement of what is at stake a big idea falls flat, because the stakes are what let the audience recognize the need to participate.

Emotional appeal reduces to pleasure and pain: a persuasive presentation either raises the likelihood of pain and lowers pleasure for rejecting the big idea, or raises pleasure and lowers pain for accepting it.

Successful change efforts begin when individuals look hard at the organization's competitive situation, market position, technological trends and financial performance, and then communicate that broadly and dramatically with respect to timely crises, potential crises or opportunities.
The gravity of a presentation must match the severity of the actual situation and accurately reflect what is at stake — no more and no less — so urgency is neither inflated nor understated.
A story analyst can judge a screenplay's character arc from its first and last pages alone, and a hero who has not changed enough by the last page makes a boring film.

Plan the audience journey by specifying both the from and the to, and both the inward and the outward transformation; the outward change is the observable proof that the big idea was understood and believed.

If no audience transformation is required, the material should be written and distributed as a report rather than presented — but routine-looking meetings often do contain a persuasive situation demanding a defined journey.
condition: when the session genuinely requires no change in the audience's beliefs or actions

statement: An alternative way to define the journey is process segmentation: locate the phase the bulk of the audience occupies — in a project process, a sales cycle (awareness, interest, desire, evaluation, action, loyalty) or an adoption curve (innovators, early adopters, majority, laggards) — and build messages to move them to the next phase.
Adopting a new perspective always requires a sacrifice — at minimum abandoning what the audience previously held true — because change couples the addition of the new with the abandonment of the old.
Even an apparently trivial request such as the audience's time is a real sacrifice of an irretrievable slice of their lives, and the presenter should be conscious of it when asking.

Audience resistance is usually traceable to the sacrifice the audience knows will be required, so enumerating their sacrifice and perceived risk in advance is what prepares the presenter to manage and overcome apprehension.

Everyone affected by change experiences emotional turmoil, and even changes that appear positive or rational involve loss and uncertainty, with reactions ranging from passive resistance through active undermining to sincere embrace.
An audience can understand and even mentally accept a plea and still not be moved to action, so intellectual agreement must not be treated as evidence of adoption.

Audience members push back or hunt for errors because otherwise they must live with the contradiction between their old position and the new one, so resistance ranging from quiet skepticism to open revolt must be dealt with squarely rather than ignored.

Use the audience's anticipated objections as inoculants: state the opposing points inside the talk before the audience can raise them, which shows the presenter has thought everything through and lowers their anxiety.
Most people do not resist for the sake of resisting; they resist because the request requires a risk or a sacrifice of some degree.
exception: some people do resist purely for its own sake

statement: What the presenter reads as resistance the audience may experience as valor — protecting reputation, credibility or honour — so the presenter should acknowledge the resistance as legitimate while assuring the audience they are in good hands.

Analyse the refusal of the call along six axes: comfort zone and change tolerance, fears (separating valid from dispellable), vulnerabilities and recent errors, likely misunderstandings, mental and practical obstacles, and politics or shifts in the balance of power.
No matter how stimulating the plea, an audience will not act unless the presenter describes a reward that makes the action worthwhile and makes the payoff obvious.
Rewards should appeal to physical, relational or self-fulfilment needs and can be drawn from seven categories: basic needs, security, savings, prize, recognition, relationship, and destiny.
The reward offered to the audience should be proportional to the sacrifice being asked of them.
State the benefit at three widening scopes: what the audience gains personally, what it gives their sphere of influence such as peers and direct reports, and what it does for humanity or the planet.

A change message can be structured as a repeated matrix of move-from-being, move-to-doing, benefit or outcome, and a personalized story — the structure underlying Beth Comstock's 'Growth in a Downturn?' presentation to GE's sales and marketing team.
Contrasting words should be paired with contrasting images to amplify the message, and contrast can be carried in the presentation's title itself.
Sprinkling a talk with personal stories of risk, frailty and victory — including stories in which the presenter was corrected — makes the presenter credible and transparent.
Companies that relentlessly focus on the customer and invest more in the pipeline during a downturn can expect to stay ahead for up to five years after recovery.
condition: in a downturn, for firms that both sustain customer focus and increase pipeline investment

statement: Do not open presentation software during the idea-generation phase; content collection and creation precede any work in the tool.

The first and most obvious idea is rarely the best; the genuinely clever ideas usually appear in the third or fourth round of idea generation, so generation should continue along a theme until possibilities are exhausted.
The generation phase uses divergent thinking with judgment suspended and structure abandoned, because broadening the pool of possibilities is what produces unexpected outcomes.

Idea collection and idea creation are different processes: collection mines existing material wide and deep — industry studies, competitor insights, news, partner programs, surveys, tangential topics — while creation invents from instinct and intuition in an admittedly foggy view of the future.
Reusing a peer's slides is a poor way to connect with an audience; collected material is a starting point that must be supplemented by purposeful mining of other relevant sources.
Gather as much as possible about competitors' messages specifically so the presenter can position their own message differently.
Persuasion requires all three Aristotelian appeals — ethical (ethos), emotional (pathos) and logical (logos) — so facts must be complemented by credibility and by content that reaches the heart.

Reciting fact after fact never signals which facts matter and forces the audience to work out the decision themselves; emotion should be used deliberately as the tool that gives selected facts emphasis.
A flat factual register can be adequate for a written scientific report but fails for the oral delivery of persuasive content.
condition: when the content is persuasive and delivered orally rather than written for a scientific report

statement: Logical appeal — developing a structure that holds the presentation together, making a claim and supplying supporting evidence — is necessary in all presentations, not optional.
Ethical appeal is built by connecting through shared values and experiences and by striking the right balance of analytical and emotional appeal, which is what bolsters the presenter's credibility.

Olson's four organs of communication map a spectrum from analytical to emotional: the head (logic and analysis), the heart (passion and sincerity), the gut (humour and instinct, less rational and more impulsive) and the groin (pure passion with no logic but enormous power).
Institutions reward analytical work, so most people default to head-region content and avoid the emotional regions where hunches, hypotheses and passions — which big ideas also need — are generated.

The correction runs in both directions: a purely analytical communicator should move lower because many decisions are emotional, while a purely emotional communicator will lose an analytical audience for lack of proof and can ruin their own credibility.
Practise integrative thinking by generating ideas from the emotional regions first — bolder, riskier and more interesting — and then deliberately moving back to the head to analyse them.
Taking a strong and clear position is what opens the space for a compelling counter-position, and moving back and forth between the contradictory poles is what keeps the audience fully engaged.

The what-is versus what-could-be gap need not be today versus tomorrow: it can equally be the customer without the product versus with it, or the world from an alternate point of view versus from the presenter's — the gap is any contrast between where the audience is and where they could be.
An analysis of 476 British political speeches and over nineteen thousand sentences found that half of all bursts of applause followed a moment where a form of contrast was communicated.

Confronting the audience's alternate perspective earns credibility, so every brainstormed point should be paired with its intelligent counterargument during preparation even if the counterargument is never delivered.
Contrasting the commonplace with the lofty is what produces the up-and-down shapeliness of the presentation form.
Features and specifications are meaningless until a human is added: an attribute becomes valuable when it visibly impacts a person, which is where meaning resides.
Sharing an experience as a story creates a shared experience and a visceral connection, because the mind attaches meaning to information in order to categorize it, decide, and judge worth.

Where a specific emotion is wanted from the audience, recalling a time the presenter felt that same emotion connects the audience to them credibly and sincerely, so a personal catalogue of stories indexed by emotion is a working resource.
Chronological life-timeline recall is only one retrieval path; breaking the chronological pattern and recalling by people, places and things surfaces a deeper and possibly dormant set of stories.

Sketching a remembered space room by room, or sketching a valued object in its usual setting, triggers scenes, scents and sounds that a written list does not, because switching to drawing engages a different part of the brain and body.
exception: if sketching is uncomfortable, find images to serve as the visual trigger instead

statement: Record with each recalled story how the presenter felt as it unfolded, so the catalogue can later be drawn on to tell that anecdote with conviction.
Stories, analogies and metaphors add meaning and stimulate the senses, and may be as short as one sentence or run through an entire presentation as a theme.
Recasting information in anecdotal form charges it emotionally, makes it digestible, and makes it easy for the audience to repeat.
Technology is meaningless until the audience is shown how humans use and benefit from it; the standard failure is emphasizing the object and its features rather than the user's benefit.
A description can be accurate and succinct yet still fail because it answers what and how while ignoring why; the reason to care starts with a story that supplies a human element.
Hook the audience with the story first and only then reveal how the mechanism works — explaining how a magic trick works before performing it loses the audience.

Introduce the story's hero early and give the audience a reason to root for them, then set up the conflict clearly without revealing how it will be overcome, because that mystery is what holds attention.

Reveal a solution that is not easy: a secondary challenge that raises the stakes keeps the audience on edge, and the story should then be brought to a head with all stakes laid out for all characters.
Place the technical or data-heavy explanation at a story cliffhanger: the audience stays in suspense, they are privileged with information the characters lack, and the hard data still gets delivered.

Build to the resolution by showing incremental steps, and create a climax that resolves every thread except the original challenge — leaving that final resolution as the movement that lifts the hero from one state to another.

Animating a static two-variable chart over time can surface an insight the still figure hides — Rosling's fertility-versus-life-expectancy bubbles migrating from short-lives-large-families in 1962 to long-lives-small-families by 2003.

A presenter of quantitative information is responsible for more than sifting and passing on data: the message must be designed to lead the audience on a journey of discovery so what matters is clearly seen and understood.
Numbers rarely speak for themselves; leaving bumps, anomalies and trends to individual interpretation forfeits the meaning, which narrative must supply.

Three devices give numbers a narrative: scale — contrasting a very large or small figure with items of familiar size; compare — putting a figure beside a similar-value number from a different context; and context — explaining the environmental and strategic factors that drove the change.

Overlaying a revenue trend on the same time increments as past strategic decisions let an audience see why the next plan deserved support, meeting little resistance — telling the narrative implied in the numbers is what made the meaning visible.
Divergent thinking generates ideas and convergent thinking sorts and analyses them toward the best outcome; both are needed and must be run repeatedly, not once each.
The big idea is itself the best filtering device: eliminate every piece of collected material that does not distinctly support that one idea.
After filtering, re-check that enough interesting contrast survived; contrast must not be lost on the cutting-room floor during vetting.

An unfiltered presentation makes the audience work too hard to discern what matters and draws a negative response, which today can be broadcast publicly to a speaker's detriment through the audience's social networks.
Presentation quality depends as much on what is removed as on what is included; audiences ask for clarity, not for more content, and rarely wish a presentation had been longer.
Cluster the surviving content into roughly three to five major topics supporting the big idea, with three to five supporting ideas around each.

Apply the MECE test to the topic set: mutually exclusive so topics do not overlap and confuse the audience, and collectively exhaustive so nothing the audience expects — such as one of the competitors — is conspicuously missing.
Topics are neutral and messages are charged: each topic must be rewritten as a full, emotionally charged sentence before structuring, exactly as a big idea must be a sentence rather than a topic.

Each message should carry as much contrast as the point needs: announcing a new acquisition without acknowledging what was learned from a previous failed one leaves the audience expecting the new one to fail too.
Most presentations suffer from too many ideas rather than too few; exploring hundreds of ideas is right, but only the most potent may be conveyed.

Without structure ideas are easily forgotten; dumping unstructured information on an audience signals that the presenter does not know what to do with the material they gathered, and audiences expect structure.

Presentation applications are linear and push attention onto individual slide details, so structuring work should move out of the tool into a spatial layout — sticky notes, slides taped to a wall or laid on the floor — to expose holes and keep the whole in view.
Clustering content spatially shows how much weight each portion carries and how many supporting points each message needs, confirming that emphasis and time allocation land on the right content.

Structure must accommodate the audience's comprehension rather than the expert's mental map: subject-matter experts naturally link ideas that are adjacent in their own minds, and those relationships are not visible to the audience.
Most presentations that fail do so because of structural deficiencies; when the structure is sound the presentation is sound.

Reviewing a substantial outline rather than a slide show lets a reviewer absorb the whole structure at once and find their own concerns immediately, converting review time from interruption into contribution.
condition: when securing feedback or buy-in from an executive or review team

statement: Viewing structure holistically delivers four benefits: it keeps focus on the construct rather than the details, verifies one clear big idea with supporting topics, filters tangential subtopics that do not purely support it, and lets reviewers give faster and more thoughtful feedback.

Four organizational patterns have a natural storylike form — chronological, sequential, spatial and climactic — and four have contrast built in and suit persuasive presentations — problem-solution, compare-contrast, cause-effect and advantage-disadvantage; any of them can replace a topical structure or organize content inside a subtopic.
Whichever organizational structure is chosen, guide the audience through it with clear verbal or visual cues that state where the presenter is and where the audience is being taken.
Deliberately alternating approaches within a lecture catches different listeners on different hooks, so that no single segment of a mixed audience is bored the whole time.
condition: when the audience is mixed in background and interest

statement: Feynman's analytical devices were signalling — stating the structure at the outset and marking transitions with rhetorical questions and verbal cues — itemizing by announcing how many points would follow, and visualizing with slides, overheads and chalkboard used sparingly alongside gesture and sound effects.

Feynman's emotional devices were wonderment — marvelling at the subject rather than only explaining it — and self-deprecating, subject-related humour interjected at roughly even increments across a lecture, on the understanding that an entertaining story is often received more readily than a well-reasoned one.

Where and how one piece of information is placed next to another creates meaning and determines how it is received, so message order is a lever for the emotional impact the audience carries out of the room.
The same quarterly-update material reordered so each point builds on the previous one, with a small addition of emotional appeal, changes the presentation from demotivating to a motivating crescendo.

An audience's communal physical response — laughter, gasps, cries — is an integral part of the telling and a binding force the presenter must learn to orchestrate through appeals to the senses and emotions.

Presentation content divides into analytical types (diagram, feature, data, evidence, example, case study, system, process, facts, supporting documentation) and emotional types (stories, benefits, analogies and metaphors, props or dramatization, suspenseful reveals, shocking statements, evocative images, invitations to wonder, humour, surprises, offers), and existing decks are overwhelmingly analytical.

Analytical material carries no emotional charge but can be converted: a neutral diagram becomes charged once the struggle behind it is told, and data stays purely analytical until the presenter explains why the ups and downs occurred.
Inventory the existing slides and identify every piece of content that could be transformed from analytical to emotional, changing it wherever appropriate.

Screenwriters call alternating emotion beats — the smallest structural element, several to a scene — and check that each scene shifts emotion between pain and pleasure; alternating analytical and emotional content engages a presentation audience the same way.
Media-conditioned audiences expect rapid change and most begin to squirm within about ten minutes of an unvaried speaker, so delivery must change modes rather than run a single slide read-along.

Several delivery-mode changes can and should occur within an hour — alternate media, multiple presenters, interaction, physical movement, a dramatic gesture — but each mode change must be carefully planned rather than improvised.
The key to getting and holding attention is having something new happen continually, creating the sense that something is always going on.

Overusing slides diminishes the power of human connection; because an audience judges a presentation successful when they feel they interacted with the presenter, lowering slide dependency is what facilitates that connectedness.
Put one idea on each slide: slides are free, so give each idea its own moment, because the audience visually re-engages every time the presenter advances.

Sketch each slide small on paper or a sticky note before opening presentation software, because the constrained space forces simple, clear words and pictures; where no image exists, large type beats dense prose.

Convert a bullet slide into a picture by circling its verbs or nouns and identifying the relationship they form with each other, since that relationship usually falls into a known category of visual relationship.

The build sequence is fixed: collect and create ideas, filter to those supporting the big idea, cluster by topic, turn topics into charged sentences, order the messages for impact, attach supporting evidence slides, confirm the beginning-middle-end with strong turning points, validate content, emotional and delivery contrast, and only then turn words into pictures.

Structure is what lets an audience follow the presenter's thought process; without it the talk jumps around making connections the audience cannot see, while sound structure makes ideas flow logically and shows how points connect.

Plant one S.T.A.R. moment — Something They'll Always Remember — in every presentation, profound or dramatic enough to become watercooler conversation or a headline, so the message keeps travelling after the talk ends.
A S.T.A.R. moment matters most when the audience sees many presentations, because the decision is often made weeks later and the presenter needs to be the one remembered.
condition: when the audience is evaluating multiple presenters or vendors and will decide later

statement: The S.T.A.R. moment must be significant, sincere and enlightening, and must magnify the big idea rather than distract from it.
There are five types of S.T.A.R. moment: memorable dramatization, repeatable sound bites, evocative visuals, emotive storytelling, and shocking statistics.
A S.T.A.R. moment must not be kitschy or cliché and must fit the specific audience — an overly emotionally charged device is wrong for an audience of biochemists — or it reads as a bad camp skit.

A physical demonstration can settle a technical argument in seconds — Feynman clamping a Challenger O-ring in ice water and releasing it to show the rubber had no resilience at 32 degrees, when it should have expanded in a millisecond.

A prop can be introduced early and left unexplained to hold suspense, then paid off later at the moment of the argument — Pollan setting a fast-food bag on stage at the start and later filling twenty-six ounces of oil beside the cheeseburger it produced.
Plant a handful of succinct, clear, repeatable sound bites so the audience can recall, repeat and transfer the message beyond the room.
Coordinate key phrases in the talk with identical language in the press release, and prepare at least one fifteen- to thirty-second message salient enough that a reporter will obviously feature it.
condition: when press or camera crews will cover the presentation

statement: Treat each audience member as a broadcast node with their own following, so key concepts must be crisp enough to be repeated verbatim and forwarded far beyond the room.
Historically memorable phrases are mindfully planned rather than spontaneous — Armstrong used the six hours and forty minutes between landing and first step to craft his line.

Three techniques make a crafted phrase stick: repeat it more than once, punctuate it with a pause long enough for the audience to write it down, and project the words on a slide so it lands visually as well as orally.
Memorable sound bites can be built with named rhetorical devices: imitating a famous phrase, and repeating words at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of a series.

Recalling an image also recalls the emotion attached to it, so a photograph or illustration often leaves a more vivid imprint than descriptive words — particularly for abstract issues where images carry emotional force words cannot match.
Pairing two images can create conflicted emotion and jarring contrast — visually identical ink-stained fingers meaning defiant democratic participation in one case and coerced voting in another.
A talk can be woven like a loom: a master theme holds the latitudinal messages while one master story shuttles back and forth through the whole, with recurring references keeping it present.
Closing by returning to the premise of the opening story brings the audience back to where they started with new insight, making the story more meaningful and the whole more complete.

Seven years of neutrally presented reports failed to produce action on Long Island, while the identical information retold visually with emotional urgency moved citizens and elected officials — the format, not the data, was the difference.
Repeating one deliberate phrase several times in a keynote while using the identical wording in the press release drove the press to adopt it as the next day's headline.
A shocking statistic should not be stated raw but recast at a scale the audience can feel — five million songs a day restated as fifty-eight songs every second of every minute of every hour.

Sustaining a presentation whose bulk sits in what could be requires a tightly rehearsed demonstration that showcases the new capability in humorous and unexpected ways; few presenters can hold momentum there otherwise.
condition: when most of the presentation's time is spent in what-could-be rather than alternating with what-is

statement: The presentations that get repeated contain memorable moments, and those moments do not happen on their own — they are rehearsed and planned to carry the right amount of analytical and emotional appeal.

Communication has five parts — sender, transmission, reception, receiver and noise — and the message can be distorted at any step, so the presenter's top priority is keeping the signal free of interference.
Four types of noise interfere with a presentation's signal: credibility noise, semantic noise, experiential noise and bias noise, each occurring at a different point in the communication chain.
Every step of presentation development either strengthens the signal or adds noise that makes the audience tune out, and noise is reduced or eliminated through careful planning and rehearsing.

The first impression is set by more than words — room type, lighting, music, items on chairs, the image on screen, the presenter's clothing and their entrance all decide the mood the audience starts in.
Within the first few seconds an audience classifies the presenter and judges whether they can connect, so that impression should be deliberately shaped rather than left to chance.

Aristotle held that trust should be created by the speech itself rather than by a prior impression of the speaker, but today's audiences do judge in the first seconds, so the presenter must work with that rather than against it.

A first impression need not be dramatic or gimmicky: it is about revealing the presenter's character, motivations, abilities and vulnerabilities, because the audience must decide whether they like the presenter before they will walk in their shoes.

Part of the first impression is formed before the presenter enters the room, by the invitation, the agenda framing, the email wording and the speaker bio, so all pre-presentation communications must be framed appropriately.

Because audiences instinctively compare themselves to the presenter, making the similarities and differences clear early gets them through the sizing-up phase quickly and establishes a common identity.

How the presenter behaves in the room before starting sets the tone: arriving harried and cross-checking files signals distraction and yields a cold audience, whereas arriving early to greet and question attendees wins them before the first word.

An expert cannot assume the audience has kept up with their field; using specialized jargon with nonspecialists reduces the help and funding the idea receives purely because listeners do not understand it.
When an idea genuinely requires special terminology, the presenter must be prepared to translate it into lay language and must know how and when to switch between specialized and common registers.
condition: when the idea cannot be expressed without specialized terminology

statement: Do not choose words that fall outside the listener's vocabulary; tailor the language to what the audience actually uses.

Communication style can bury a genuine discovery: McClintock's 1940s finding that genes switch physical characteristics on and off went misunderstood until the 1970s because her rapid-fire leaps from observation to model to conclusion outpaced her audiences.

Jargon is not confined to specialized professions: departments inside one organization speak different languages and trade in acronyms, and many good ideas die failing to navigate the organization that produced them.
An audience will not adopt an idea it does not understand, and the idea's perceived value is judged less on the idea itself than on how well it is communicated.
Presentations fail from too much information rather than too little; share only the right information for that exact moment and that specific audience.
Lincoln's 278-word, two-minute Gettysburg Address outlasted Everett's two-hour eulogy on the same platform, and its brevity is what forced the central ideas to be clear.

Even a two-minute address can carry the full presentation form: the Gettysburg Address states what is, startles the audience with what could be, issues a call to action, and closes on the new bliss of a free nation.
Impose a self-constraint on speaking time — given an hour, target forty minutes — because restricting time forces clear structure and filters the content down to imperative messages.
The shorter the talk, the longer the preparation it requires — a ten-minute speech needing a week where an hour-long one could be given immediately.
Slides should serve as stage setting or backdrop and rarely as the sole focus, because the presenter, not the slides, delivers the message.
People process only one inbound message at a time: an audience will either listen to the presenter or read the slides, never both.

A slide application's default master is a report format, and a text-filled default slide takes about twenty-five seconds to read — forty such slides spend over sixteen minutes of the talk with the audience reading instead of listening.
Planning the structure with the time frame in mind is what guarantees staying inside the slot and prevents racing through the remaining slides at the end.
There is no right number of slides — the count follows the presenter's pacing — so slide count must not be used as a proxy for talk length.
Hollywood analysts keep scenes under three minutes for fear of losing interest, and because the presentation medium is more static than cinema, no slide should stay up for more than two minutes.
Putting one idea per slide produces more slides than a traditional deck, and that is acceptable rather than a fault.
Reduce slide density until the audience can process each slide in under three seconds: keep only elements that help recall, cut large phrases to single words, and move the rest into the notes.
Notes can hold unlimited detail: running presenter view turns the presenter's own machine into a teleprompter while the audience sees clear, sparse slides.

A request for a five-slide overview to be read rather than delivered is a request for a document, not a presentation, and a document should be as comprehensive per page as it needs to be — sparse slides are for presenting.
condition: when the artifact will be read on its own rather than delivered live

statement: Persuasive presentations should balance analytical and emotional appeal appropriately rather than maximize emotion; the emphasis on emotional appeal exists because it is underused, not because it outranks analysis.

Topic type sets the natural weighting — subjects like gun control, racism or abortion invite emotional argument while science, engineering, finance and academia invite analytical ones — but an analytically weighted presentation must still not be void of emotion.

For an audience in a stereotypically analytical profession only a tiny percentage of the appeal should be emotional, but emotion must not be removed entirely — at minimum open and close with why, since the reason people entered such a field usually has an emotional component.
condition: when the audience works in a stereotypically analytical field such as economics, science, engineering or research

statement: Kairos — speaking in the right moment in the right way — requires understanding the situation, cross-checking it, and modifying the presentation's emotional and analytical balance to fit.
Over-amplified emotion makes an audience feel manipulated; emotional appeal is only effective when it furthers the argument, and imbalance in either direction damages the presenter's credibility.

A broad audience responds viscerally, is receptive to emotion and needs a story-weighted structure, whereas an analytical audience responds cerebrally, is suspicious of emotion and needs a report-weighted structure — so the rhetorical triangle is dynamic, not a fixed equal balance.

Highly analytical audiences read heavy heartstring-tugging as manipulation and wasted time, yet material showing how lives will be changed does motivate them provided it is not presented melodramatically.
exception: unless it is delivered melodramatically, in which case it backfires

statement: Emotionally driven audiences want to know the details were carefully considered but do not want twenty slides of them; a few proof points suffice.
Host a screening before delivery to test the messages, filtering out meandering structure, obstructed messages and confusing language, and come to it expecting to rework a share of the material.

A presentation's quality will not exceed the quality of the planning process that precedes it, following Conway's Law that a design mirrors the communication structure of the organization that produced it.

Assemble screeners who match the target audience profile — industry analysts, employees, trusted customers or a focus group — and deliberately include naysayers who will scrutinize, criticize and challenge the perspective.

When the organization's own review environment is sugar-sweet or dysfunctional — late-engaging leadership, fear-driven paralysis, message invention without strategy, no seat for experts, flattery-driven consensus, or self-focus over customer insight — go outside the organization for honest feedback.
condition: when the internal review culture matches one of the named dysfunctional patterns

statement: Give each screener a printout of the slides and notes, run the whole presentation once and then revisit each section, budgeting roughly three times the presentation's length for the review.

Solicit feedback nondefensively, let screeners challenge every assumption, and refuse the 'yeah, but' or 'if they really knew' excuses — the presenter's receptivity to feedback is what determines the material's receptivity for others.
When the deciding panel spans disciplines, the idea must be conveyed so it resonates with a specialist in any field, not only the presenter's own.
condition: when the audience is a cross-disciplinary review or funding panel

statement: Covert rehearsed his fifteen-minute Pioneer Award presentation twenty times with scientists from varied backgrounds, collecting and incorporating feedback each round, and only at the nineteenth and twentieth did reviewers stop asking for changes.

In a cerebral scientific setting even a thin veneer of emotional appeal goes a long way: adding why the project would change research, alongside how it works, made the pitch inspirational as well as instructive.
Acting on rehearsal feedback requires a humble stance, because it means adding material while cutting pieces the presenter has grown fond of.
Scientific presentations commonly clutter slides with too much data; a clean minimalist slide design is the balanced alternative.
Metering just the right amount of new information before every climax is what lets a presenter grab attention and carry it along.

Explanations, analogies and metaphors must be pitched consistently at the audience's level of understanding and drawn from items already familiar to them, which is how complex theory held young children's attention for an hour.

Isolating a complex whole into layers, explaining the theory behind each, demonstrating them separately and only then presenting the complete piece leaves the audience able to perceive nuances they would otherwise miss.
An effortless, casual-sounding delivery is the product of dogged preparation: Bernstein worked for days on each script, rehearsed it repeatedly, and left as many as ten revisions on file.
Each metaphor and allegory should be vetted for appropriateness to the specific audience before it is used.
Rehearsal can extend to anticipating multiple audience reactions and writing alternate sections for each, and to notating where and how the presenter will stand on stage.
Review the recording after each delivery and identify specific improvements, so the same mistakes are not committed repeatedly and each presentation is better than the last.
condition: when the presentation was recorded

statement: Practice does not reach perfection — there is always room to improve — so the loop is rehearse, re-rehearse, solicit feedback, review the recording, and begin refining again.
An idea confined to one person's mind is not alive; it becomes alive only as it is adopted person by person until it reaches a tipping point and a groundswell of support.

Framing a vision so every listener holds a share of the responsibility changes how they describe their own role — the NASA janitor who answered that he was putting the first man on the moon rather than that he cleaned floors.

Systemic adoption of an idea takes many deliveries of the presentation rather than one: Gore had given his climate presentation hundreds of times, going back to the 1970s, before An Inconvenient Truth reached a wide audience.

Communication milestones along an idea's life cycle are catalysts in their own right — each is an opportunity to adjust strategy, collaborate and realign the team — and the discussions held while assembling a presentation sometimes carry as much value as the presentation.
If a business is a decision factory, the presentations that inform those decisions determine the decisions' quality.

Presentations are a powerfully persuasive tool that must be used to build up rather than to deceive; the Enron executives faced criminal counts arising directly from their earnings-call and employee presentations, including wire fraud because the presentations were transmitted across state lines.

A slick presentation can carry a fraud past an audience that senses something is wrong: Enron managers and analysts stared at each other in confusion at the LJM partnership pitch, thinking it sounded too good to be true, and went along anyway.
A warning buried in a dense deck and softened by conciliatory margin notes fails to function as a warning; stating the risk plainly and unmissably is what a presenter owes an audit audience.
condition: when the presentation's purpose is to warn decision-makers of a risk

statement: Communication designed to abandon reason and truth turns a presentation into a propaganda device, and when it collapses the credibility of everyone involved is obliterated.
The communicator's job is to make others see the idea, because ideas gain traction on being seen — an executive, manager, engineer and marketer each see their piece before it exists.

A consulting firm the client judged smarter lost a multimillion-dollar bid because dense, smart-sounding slides obscured its findings while the rival communicated usably — all the smarts in the world are useless if they are not understood.

Getting stakeholders to understand an idea while a competitor's stays obscure is itself the competitive advantage, because a clearly presented smart idea becomes the spark that mobilizes human and material resources.
A recorded presentation transcends the moment it was given and can reach millions who were not present, so a message that is clear and worth repeating will be repeated.
condition: when the presentation is recorded and distributed

statement: King's 'I Have a Dream' moves between what is and what could be rapidly, a pace matched to the heightened energy of that gathering rather than a universal tempo.
condition: when the occasion carries heightened collective energy

statement: King's delivery devices were dramatic pauses, repeated word sequences for emphasis with 'I Have a Dream' recurring like a hymn's refrain, and metaphor and visual language that build images in the mind.

King established common ground by quoting material the audience already held — familiar hymns, Scripture, Shakespeare — and by drawing lines from the Declaration of Independence, the Emancipation Proclamation, the Constitution and the Gettysburg Address.

In King's sixteen-minute speech the audience applauded twenty-seven times, roughly once every thirty-five seconds, and his varied pacing produced three distinct crescendos building to a closing description of the new bliss.
There is always one person in the audience to whom the communicator is really speaking, so the work is justified even when it visibly reaches only that one.
Embodying an emotion moves an audience more than describing it: Graham did not dance about grief but sought to be its embodiment, and a grieving spectator who could not cry was freed to do so.
Some feelings cannot be put into words, and a communicator may legitimately aim for material to be felt rather than understood.

Original material comes from sustained accumulation, not inspiration: recording thoughts, observations, impressions and quotations over time and reading widely across unrelated fields until the notebooks reveal a pattern that can be written out as a detailed script.

Fear of presenting is surmountable by repeated attempts rather than by talent: Graham was so nervous she fled to a locked dressing room, yet after trying again and again became the most effective cultural ambassador the State Department had sent to Asia and lectured until she was ninety.
Transparency moves the presenter's instinct for self-promotion out of the way so the audience can see past the presenter to the idea.
There are three keys to being transparent: be honest, be unique, and do not compromise.

Presenting as a flawless know-it-all is not honest; sharing how the presenter has failed and how they overcame it, including moments of pain or pleasure, is what endears them to an audience that already knows nobody is perfect.

The presenter's unique accumulation of trials and triumphs is what brings new insight to a topic, so differences should be surfaced rather than concealed in order to fit in — even when the presenter is the only one who sees what they see.
If the presenter genuinely believes the message, they should speak confidently and not back down, accepting that ridicule or rejection is sometimes the price of naming what others will not.
An idea that is not communicated well loses its value and adds nothing, so the care invested in communicating an idea should be proportional to the value placed on the idea itself.
Presenting did not come naturally to the communicators profiled in this book: each invested many hours and agonized over the words, structure and delivery of their ideas.
Amid so much disingenuous noise, an idea presented with sincerity and passion is what stands out and resonates.

Structure enables listeners to anticipate what comes next, which is why the three-part sonata form works: the exposition introduces and repeats the theme so listeners can recognize it later, the development alters it to create tension and surprise, and the recapitulation restates it after modification.
The audience must thoroughly grasp the initial theme before it is modified, because that grasp is what makes the later gap between what is and what could be identifiable.

Music layers three contrasts — tonal (movement away from and back to a home key), dynamic (loud against soft, sometimes sudden and sometimes gradual), and textural (unison against melody-plus-accompaniment, and varying note density) — and contrast in varying layers is what makes a sonata interesting, exactly as in a presentation.
Sonatas follow standard rules yet never sound contrived or formulaic because great composers work flexibly within the form — the same relationship a presentation should have to the presentation form.
The presenter is the public persona of one individual, but the best presentations result from the collaborative effort of an empowered team behind the scenes.

Hitchcock built each film through two successive frameworks — a written one developed with a screenwriter through argument and discussion, then a visual one of sketches and storyboards with a production designer — so ideas were written and drawn before they were filmed.

Hitchcock envisioned each film in such detail before shooting — sets modelled, camera moves and shot distances planned — that he never consulted the script during production because he knew the whole film by heart.

Collaborators typically take one of the leader's suggestions and expand it into the collective process, so a leader should use the team's strengths, stay open to modifying the vision, and honour the people who are not on stage.
Know the rules before breaking them: Cummings trained in traditional forms and did not break a rule until he fully understood it, which is why his rule-breaking created meaning rather than noise.

An idea far enough outside convention will initially be rejected — Cummings was turned down by fourteen publishers and unrecognized until fifty-six — but persistence moves an idea from rejected to considered to adopted.
Sometimes an idea must stand out enough to shock in order to be noticed, and standing out against convention carries the cost of being reviled at times.
Rule 1 of the book's codified method: resonance causes change.
Rule 2: incorporating story into presentations has an exponential effect on outcomes.
Rule 3: if a presenter knows the audience's resonant frequency and tunes to it, the audience will move.
condition: the presenter must first know the audience's resonant frequency

statement: Rule 4: every audience will persist in a state of rest unless compelled to change.
Rule 5: use the big idea to filter out all frequencies other than the resonant frequency.
Rule 6: structure is greater than the sum of its parts.
Rule 7: memorable moments are repeated and retransmitted, so they cover longer distances than the presentation itself.
Rule 8: audience interest is directly proportionate to the presenter's preparation.
Rule 9: the presenter's imagination can create a reality.

The book's noise-in-communication model is the Shannon-Weaver model from Shannon's 1948 mathematical theory of communication, slightly modified and retrofitted to presentations rather than derived independently.
The claim that an audience cannot listen and read slides simultaneously is sourced to Mayer's Multimedia Learning, giving it experimental rather than anecdotal backing.
The book flags its own NASA janitor anecdote as an urban legend of sorts, so it illustrates the point about shared vision rather than evidencing it.

The applause-and-contrast finding is sourced to Heritage and Greatbatch's study of rhetoric and response at British party political conferences, published in the American Journal of Sociology in 1986.
Presentation literacy is positioned as a competitive advantage whether the goal is closing a deal, advancing a social cause, or engaging staff.

The book carries an explicit scope disclaimer that its advice and strategies may not be suitable for every situation and that a professional should be consulted where appropriate, so its guidance is not warranted as universally applicable.
The problem with most presentations is that the speaker has no compelling story to tell before they open the slide software, which locates the failure upstream of slide design.
Being purposeful about how and where the presentation takes the audience is something most presenters fail even to consider, let alone construct.
Success follows from intentionality: telling the story on purpose and setting out deliberately to cause the change one claims to want.
The book's stated purpose is presenting visual stories that transform audiences — the transformation of the audience, not the delivery of the deck, is the declared unit of success.

An audience will either listen to the presenter or read the slides, but not both, because listening and reading are conflicting activities and people focus on one stream of verbal communication at a time.
People can attend to verbal and visual communication simultaneously, so a slide works best as a visual aid that reinforces the speaker's spoken message rather than as text to be read.
A slide carrying more than 75 words has become a document rather than a visual aid; either move the content into the notes or reclassify the artifact as a document.

When the artifact is genuinely a document, hold a meeting instead of a presentation, circulate the document beforehand or let the audience read it at the start, then spend the remaining time discussing content and building action plans.
condition: the deck is a document rather than a visual aid

statement: Slides of roughly 50 words each function as a teleprompter for the presenter; this default professional style usually follows from too little rehearsal, leads presenters to turn their backs on the audience, and makes the audience read ahead and perceive the presenter as slow.
On-slide text acts as a crutch for an under-rehearsed presenter.
Slides should support the presenter's communication rather than constitute the communication itself.

Before delivering, assess the deck you built and decide explicitly whether you created a document or a presentation, then either convert it into slides or accept it as a document the audience can read and circulate.
If the only goal is to convey a file of facts and figures, cancel the meeting and send a report instead of presenting.
condition: the aim is transferring facts and figures rather than winning adoption of a point of view

statement: Presentations too often carry the presenter's agenda instead of building a connection with the audience.
Brand is what a company stands for in the hearts and minds of its customers rather than its name, logo, or tagline, and success requires an emotional connection with the consumer.

In many instances a presentation is the last engagement and last impression a customer has of a company before a purchase decision, which makes it a brand touchpoint that should be held to the same standard as paid marketing.

Presentation development rests on three interdependent legs — message, visual story, and delivery — and each requires comparable attention; presenters commonly develop the message leg and neglect the other two.

Crudely constructed presentation graphics — poorly rendered perspectives, inconsistent light sources, jarring animations — force the audience to resolve visual dissonance, leaving them subtly agitated and less receptive to the message, and visuals lacking clarity can produce a subliminal loss of trust in the presenter.
Anticipate what the audience needs and adapt delivery to the channel: content built for in-person delivery must be modified before it resonates with a web-based or mass-media audience.
condition: the same content will be consumed through a different channel than the one it was designed for

statement: Audience members care primarily about what the presenter can do for them, not about the presenter's own success in delivering.
Stories are how people understand and relate to the world, and people naturally associate a story with fitting imagery.
Making bad slides is easy and damages a career, so invest both in the slides themselves and in your own visual-communication skills.

Presentation software is the first application broadly adopted by professionals that requires thinking visually, and most people never make the jump from the verbal expression taught in school to effective visual expression.
Constraining a presentation to say more with fewer words is worthwhile because the medium forces the presenter to order their thoughts into a consumable sequence.
Presentations are high-stakes internal and external communications that influence stock value, sales revenue, promotions, and behaviour change, so they warrant proportionate preparation time.
The time required to develop a presentation is directly proportional to how high the stakes are.

Reusing an old keynote with minimal modification is acceptable for low-stakes occasions, but a big deal to close or a critical vision to present warrants starting from scratch with a creative process that takes in audience needs and colleague feedback.
condition: the engagement is high-stakes

statement: As a working estimate, an hour-long 30-slide presentation takes 36 to 90 hours in total: 6-20 hours research and input gathering, 1 hour building an audience-needs map, 2 hours generating ideas on sticky notes, 1 hour organizing them, 1 hour of colleague critique on audience impact, 2 hours sketching structure or a storyboard, 20-60 hours building slides, and 3 hours rehearsing.
Schedule preparation time and review cycles on the calendar as soon as a speaking engagement is known, rather than compressing the work into the night before.
The creative process for a presentation is messy and takes more iterations than expected, and exploration, informal input, and review cycles produce a stronger result.

Interrogate the audience before building anything, using seven questions: what are they like, why are they here, what keeps them up at night, how can you solve their problem, what do you want them to do, how might they resist, and how can you best reach them.
Build audience personas before building slides, because painting a picture of a real human with real needs makes the connection more effective.
Place an audience-persona slide at the front of the deck as working context for the author, and do not project it during delivery.
Create as many audience personas as the diversity of the audience warrants rather than a single profile.
condition: the audience spans distinct segments

statement: Thinking about the audience first supplies a benchmark against which the message can be checked.
Every presentation must answer 'so what?' with a clear call to action, because an audience cannot act on a message until it is told what the message is worth to them.
Anticipate what would keep the audience from adopting the message and carrying out the call to action, and address that resistance in the presentation.
Match the delivery channel to how the audience prefers to receive information, including room setup and what material is available after the presentation.
Presenting is about creating meaning and being present, not about aesthetics, and the target is that each audience member feels they are in an individual conversation with the presenter.

Presenters who count on stage presence alone underestimate the story, which comes from a time-intensive collaborative process of settling the message, becoming intimate with content and staging, and repeated rehearsal.
Brainstorm the context first — setting, audience membership, the messages they need to hear, and the call to action — and only then develop the storyline and message.

Keep the presentation's meta-structure (a blocking document) displayed and continuously updated during development meetings, because focusing too early on perfecting a single idea forfeits the chance to explore potentially better ideas.
Presentation software was never intended as a brainstorming or drawing tool; the applications are containers for ideas and assets, not the means to generate them.
Start ideation with pen, pencil, and paper away from the desk and the computer, and change environment when creative work is needed.

The primary objective of the ideation phase is a large quantity of ideas rather than finished pictures; ideas may be words, diagrams, or scenes, literal or metaphorical, provided they express the underlying thought.
Do not adopt the first idea that comes to mind; keep sketching through several more, because stronger solutions frequently surface only after four or five ideas have percolated to the top.
Keep generating ideas even when they wander into apparently unrelated territory.
After generating a large volume of ideas, classify, challenge, and filter them down to a small core set that meets the objective of the vision being communicated.
Capture one idea per sticky note written with a Sharpie; if an idea needs more space than a sticky note or more detail than a Sharpie can give, the idea is too complex.
Sticky notes let ideas be captured, sorted, and re-arranged, which makes it easy to re-order content until the structure and flow feel right.
No single ideation method is prescribed — linear storyboarding of detailed ideas is an equally valid alternative to sticky notes — provided the method generates many ideas quickly.
Simplicity is the essence of clear communication.
A slide's form should embody its message: if the message is simplicity, the slides themselves should feel simple.
When technical detail on a slide distracts from the main message, split the content across more than one slide instead of compressing it.
condition: secondary detail competes with the slide's single main message

statement: Reorganize slide content conceptually rather than merely cleaning up the existing slides; thinking outside the slide can reveal that the underlying structure differs from what the old deck asserted.
Keep on the slide only what is actually addressed verbally, and use a series of slides to build the impact rather than loading one slide with supporting information.
Sketching is iterative: take rough ideas, fine-tune, re-organize, and sketch again until a story is visible.

Draw a stick figure body-first — body, then head placed relative to the body, then facial expression with an angled nose for direction, then legs with small ovals for feet, then arms — because the body carries the gesture and the legs convey more energy than the arms.
Sketch quality does not matter, and the first sketch is usually the most obvious one; further thought yields additional and potentially better ideas.

Test-drive sketches with a colleague or two before going on the road: ask them to judge whether the sketches capture the intent rather than only listening to the words, and to ask clarifying questions or sketch their own version when confused.

An audience should process a chart one point at a time rather than all at once, so complex charts benefit from being drawn or revealed progressively while the presenter speaks to surface the hidden point.
For a cross-cultural audience use culturally neutral images rather than bullet-loaded slides, because images translate and words do not.
condition: the audience spans languages or cultures
