statement: Keep graphics extremely simple for cross-cultural audiences because not all cultures process information left to right, and animate content to appear gradually so the intended processing order is guided.
condition: the audience spans languages or cultures

statement: A detailed script hinders the presenter from connecting with the audience; slides should give the presenter structure without cramping their style or putting words in their mouth.
Keep sketching loose and quick — doodles — and pull reference images and vignettes from stock libraries, magazines, and video while sketching.
Sketch inside the slide's layout format so the elements are checked to work spatially before any digital build.
Sketching acts as proof-of-concept: ideas that are too complex, time-consuming, or costly reveal themselves as candidates for elimination at the sketch stage.
When sketches alone fail to convey the intended vision to others, collect images that represent the feeling of the final artwork to communicate the intent.
condition: collaborators cannot read the sketches

statement: Discarding all generated ideas but one is the intended destructive part of the creative process, which is why a large quantity was generated first.

Choose the execution that works best for the idea — multiple scenes across several slides, a manipulated image, a custom illustration, or a short video — rather than the one that is easiest to execute.

Enlist a designer when you lack the skill to execute the chosen concept digitally, and plan far enough ahead that one is available, because effective communication matters more than executing it yourself.
condition: the presenter lacks the digital execution skill

statement: A diagram is the appropriate device for explaining how the parts of a whole interact, because shapes symbolizing relationships are near-unavoidable in professional communication.

Diagrams fall into six common types split between abstract concepts — flow, structure, cluster, radiate — which combine shapes to show relationships, and realistic concepts — pictorial and displayed data — which are more literal; the taxonomy is a sampling, not exhaustive.

Choose the flow diagram by the shape of the process: linear for a definite start and end, circular for a continuous process with no end point, divergent or convergent when elements collide or split off, and multidirectional for complex combined relationships such as flow charts.

Choose the structure diagram by what is being structured: a matrix to compare at least two data sets (one may be a yes/no checklist), a tree for clear hierarchy, and layers for elements that stack or build, which can carry both hierarchy and sequence.

Choose the cluster diagram by the relationship being asserted: overlapping for shared sets, interest, or responsibility; closure — a Gestalt effect where shapes combine into another shape — for 'the sum is greater than the parts'; enclosed to mark which elements belong to a higher order and which stand alone; and linked when a line, shape, or connector unifies related groups.

Choose the radiate diagram by the origin structure: from a point for a directional burst with a clear origin, with a core for a parent-child relationship held together by a central element, and without a core when elements connect only through proximity or mutual attraction to a central area.

Choose the pictorial diagram by communicative job: process for how something works sequentially, reveal for hidden inner workings exposed by slicing or peeling, direction for how to get from a start to a destination, location for where something sits within a geography or system while keeping context, and influence for the resulting impact of interacting elements.

Displayed data is itself a kind of diagram, chosen by the intended reading: comparison to juxtapose sets and show difference, trend when one parameter is time and change over time is the point, and distribution to correlate singular instances into a larger pattern.
Successful information design can incorporate multiple parameters to tell a richer cause-and-effect story rather than oversimplifying the complexities of statistics.
Communicate a complex concept by connecting more than one diagram type into a system diagram, and build that diagram up over time because the audience processes one idea at a time.
condition: the concept involves elaborate or invisible relationships

statement: Spending additional time refining a diagram's concept — for example coalescing separate ideas around a central character or motif — imbues the individual concepts with context, sequence, and association, producing a coherent family of graphics instead of merely adequate ones.
Clarity is the one principle that overrides all others when displaying data on a slide.
Projected data is at an inherent disadvantage to print because the audience cannot pull the slide close to examine it, so every data slide must carry a clear message on its own.
A data slide is not about the data but about the meaning of the data.

When it matters that the audience examine the data and reach their own conclusions, distribute the data as a printout instead of projecting it, because slides are usually a poor medium for complex data.
condition: the audience must draw its own conclusions from the data

statement: Show data in a presentation only when it helps illustrate your conclusions, and render it so it can be absorbed easily even from the back of the room, because a cluttered or overwhelming data slide can derail even a compelling speaker.
Treat whatever data you do show with absolute integrity, and be prepared to provide access to the complete data set on request and to answer questions about your conclusions.

Analytical, scientific, and engineering-minded audiences read data skeptically, so data that has been boiled down or clarified too far can read to them as manipulated marketing data; avoid decorating data because ornamentation detracts from credibility.
condition: the audience is analytically or scientifically trained

statement: Articulate the conclusion you want the audience to adopt — usually a point about causality, the conditions that produced the result or the conditions the result will create — before building the data slide, because that conclusion determines the graph type and whether and how to apply emphasis.
The same data set supports several different conclusions, so choose deliberately what the audience should focus on so they process the intended point quickly.
When a slide carries only one key message, or the message is simply a number, dropping the chart entirely can increase the slide's impact.
condition: the slide carries a single key message or a single number

statement: When several consecutive slides carry charts, align the chart axes from slide to slide so the content does not jump.
condition: charts appear on consecutive slides

statement: Use a pie chart only for large differences in proportion — parts making up a whole, or one set's percentages against another's — start the first data set at the 12 o'clock position, cap it at eight sections, and make the percentages total 100%.
Use a bar chart when precise relationships matter: bars are visually more precise than a pie, accommodate larger data sets, and can be stacked to carry an additional data set.

Compose a data chart in three layers — a background of tick marks, scales, legends, and grid lines in neutral colours for context and scale; the data itself with enough contrast to be distinguished at a distance without straining; and a foreground emphasis layer that highlights the key message or conclusion.
The purpose of a slide is to communicate conclusions and insights rather than to show all the data; the slide can reference handouts for the dense data.

Simplicity matters more on a data slide than elsewhere because the data itself can already confuse the viewer, so strip chart decoration — extra lines, ticks, gradients, borders, fills, and 3D effects that Tufte calls chartjunk.
Remove depth and 3D effects from charts because depth serves no purpose and can visually skew the data, while a flat chart reads as more visually precise.

Check chart colours for unintended meaning: shades of red conventionally annotate negative information, especially in financial reporting, so a red or maroon brand colour should be redirected to non-data elements rather than used to plot results.
Avoid tilting pie charts because tilt gives undue prominence to the foreground data, and keep the same colour for the same entity across paired charts.
Too many bold colours obscure a chart's focal point; changing the chart's proportions, such as lengthening it horizontally, can emphasize the intended comparison instead.
Presenters commonly put their emphasis on what the information is rather than on how it is best communicated, and molding the information into an effective form is what separates good from great.

When a cause depends on empathy to move people to act, use raw and real photographs and dig through as many images as needed to find ones that elicit an emotional response, because stock imagery lacks content while real photos carry credibility and import that staged images do not.
condition: the goal is emotional motivation to act

statement: Illustrate statistics with icons that let the audience see the numbers, because retention of data increases when the numbers are made visible.

Bullet points are only one option for displaying text, not a requirement: isolating each statistic as a large statement on its own slide paces the information and gives it more impact than competing content on a crowded slide.

Design-oriented firms have been found to outperform their more traditional peers financially, but dressing up a presentation will not by itself raise a company's value — dressing anything up runs counter to good design.
Design at its core is problem solving and experience, not only aesthetics: designers work to let users resolve their problem in the most convenient, simple, and elegant way.

To succeed as a presenter, think like a designer: make every decision intentional, let reason and logic underpin the placement of visual elements, and let meaning determine the order and hierarchy of ideas.
Design decisions represent the presenter and feed the audience's perception of who they are, so they function as a personal or organizational brand.
Define a brand's character with verbs describing what the organization does rather than adjectives describing what it is.

A presenter's transformation can be attributed largely to investing heavily in internalizing the subject matter, rehearsing the delivery, and seeking and accepting expert guidance, rather than to innate stage talent.
A presentation can tap emotion and incite grass-roots change, which makes the medium capable of shifting mass perception.

Effective slide design rests on mastering three things: arrangement (contrast, hierarchy, unity, space, proximity, flow), visual elements (background, colour, text, images), and movement (timing, pace, distance, direction, eye flow).
A slide behaves like a broadcast signal: its arrangement, visual elements, and movement either deliver information clearly or act as noise that clouds the message and makes the viewer tune out.
In the vast majority of cases a slide fails because of its fundamental construction, not its style, so familiarity with the mechanics of a well-designed slide is the presenter's most important tool.
There is a limit to how much new information a person can process, so visuals meant to play a supporting role impose excessive cognitive strain when they add non-essential material.
How elements are arranged has arguably the greatest impact on whether a slide's message is visually clear; arrangement tells a story and can itself provoke tension, confusion, and agitation.

Each arrangement tool buys a specific audience outcome: contrast lets them find the main point quickly, flow tells them the processing order, hierarchy shows the relationships between elements, unity signals that the information belongs together, proximity conveys meaning from location, and whitespace gives visual breathing room.

Putting everything on one slide at equal value is laziness on the presenter's part and overcrowding does not add clarity; decide the priority of the information, giving some elements dominance and practising restraint with others.
Viewers immediately perceive the difference between the attributes of two or more elements, which focuses their attention; larger text reads as the most important element regardless of where it sits.
Apply contrast by the smallest effective difference: use just-noticeable differences that are definitive, effective, and minimal, and only when necessary.

Any stylistic difference between two elements suggests importance, urgency, or value to the viewer consciously or subconsciously, so unintentional contrast confuses the message at best and contradicts it at worst; base every stylistic choice on a well-defined purpose.
Western readers are conditioned to start at the top left and scan back and forth in a Z-shaped path — the conditioned carriage return — before assigning meaning to what they have seen.
When a graphic must flow counter to natural eye movement, either build it over time with discrete elements appearing in the intended order or mark the starting point with a clear symbol or arrow.
condition: the required flow is counterintuitive to natural eye movement

statement: Organize every slide to guide the audience's eyes through the content in an obvious way; the principle applies to diagrams and images as much as to text.
When using images of people, ensure they are looking at the slide's content rather than away from it or fleeing it.
The audience should be able to tell at a glance whether a data chart is to be read horizontally or vertically.

Control flow with concrete limits: avoid more than three layers of information on a single plane, create one main point and at most two sub-points, develop flow within the slide intentionally, and choose images and diagrams whose directional flow leads to the focal point or toward the next slide.

An audience processes hierarchy almost as quickly as contrast, and hierarchy is a parent-child structure in which the visual structure must mirror the structure of the information it represents — making bullet points heavier than their title disrupts the logical flow and is hard to make sense of.

Changing the relative size and proximity of objects changes the story the diagram tells about their relative importance — equal elements, dominant parent, or dominant child are three different messages — so set size and proximity deliberately.

If the presenter does not supply the intended message explicitly, the audience will construct meaning from its own interpretation, so verify that the graphical hierarchy represents the intended message accurately.
Unity can be achieved through structure (a grid), look (graphical style), and theme (the big idea), and the grid chosen should reflect the presenter's or the company's identity.

A grid of rectangular regions, each a container for one element, anchors elements so they do not appear haphazard, lets the audience detect placement patterns and anticipate where content will appear, and stops elements from jumping across similar consecutive layouts — for instance keeping graph axes in a constant location while the data changes.
Grids streamline design decisions in organizations where thousands of employees build slides independently, and similar grid-following slides can be reused.

Build a grid by sketching it, pencilling in where images, text, and objects go, deliberately leaving plenty of tiles open as clear space, drawing the grid lines on the master slide, removing them when design is complete, and saving the grid for reuse in a new file or on a slide at the back of the deck.

Varying element shapes and sizes within a regular underlying grid produces a sense of structure and solidity, and leaving the top and bottom channels of the grid empty creates a cinematic feel while reserving space for titles.
Breaking the grid can effectively focus attention on specific elements, but it must remain the exception because overuse diminishes its impact.
exception: overuse — repeated grid-breaking loses the effect

statement: When more than one element or person appears in a scene, their placement relative to each other tells a secondary story that can communicate antagonism or protagonism, chaos or order, decline or growth, so place associated elements intentionally to preempt unintended interpretations.

Placement of human subjects carries conventional meaning: a subject at the left or right edge is often read as weak relative to one nearer the centre, a subject at the bottom as submissive or vulnerable and one at the top as dominant, isolated subjects carry more visual weight than grouped ones, subjects on opposite sides read as distant or antagonistic while central subjects read as closely related, generous surrounding space suggests freedom, and clustered subjects out of balance emphasize action.

Whitespace — the unused areas of a slide, which need not be white — is as much an element of the slide as titles, bullets, and diagrams, and its use or misuse largely determines the slide's effectiveness.

Any slide that has to sacrifice whitespace to make room for content is packed too tightly, and when a slide is expected to hold more information than it comfortably can, the slide is the wrong tool for the job.

Reduce an overloaded slide by asking what can be taken away without changing the meaning and where the content can be split across more than one slide, because a slide's value comes from how clearly it communicates, not from how much information it holds.
Clear space on a slide is acceptable; clutter is a failure of design.
Splitting dense content across several slides helps but does not by itself solve density: display the elements sequentially so the audience is guided through the information.
Design is not decoration or ornamentation but making communication as easy and clear for the viewer as possible.

Choose element styles once and stay consistent, because consistent elements become visual triggers of the brand; a single deliberate inconsistency after a long consistent run creates a memorable emphasis, whereas breaking the rules constantly forfeits that emphasis entirely.

Treat the background as a container or surface whose opacity, texture, and light source are deliberate choices, abandon the default templates and their preordained ornamentation, and select a background that serves the information rather than competing with it.

A logo is not required on every slide since the audience generally knows who the presenter works for; identify the presenter or company on the first and last bumper slides, and if a logo on every slide is mandated, place it in the lower right where the right rag of text can wrap around it.
condition: an organization mandates a per-slide logo

statement: A background is a setting, not a work of art: keep it open, spacious, simple, and intentionally clean, because slide real estate is valuable and ornamented templates can consume a third or more of the usable live area.

Derive a background from the timeless visual elements already in the company's marketing material — grid system, line structures, bounding boxes, colour palette — rather than from the application's default masters.

Choose either a 2D or a 3D space for a deck and use only one: flat bold colour minimizes depth and therefore complexity, while adding shadows, lighting, or depth commits the whole file to a three-dimensional environment.

Once a deck is committed to a three-dimensional space, obey the laws of environmental consistency — one vanishing point, one light source, and a consistent effect on all elements, held throughout the entire file — to reduce visual vertigo.
condition: the slide introduces any glisten, shadow, highlight, or depth

statement: Treat each slide as an environment: elements that do not map to the established vanishing point and lighting present an unnatural scene that leaves the audience unsettled and subliminally frustrated.
An environment is established whether or not the presenter intends one — the moment a graphic is drawn, its style determines the environment — so the choice should be made consciously.

To build a consistent 3D scene, use one line of a grid of thirds as the horizon, draw lines converging to a point on that horizon as the vanishing point, and match every placed object's angles to that horizon and vanishing point rather than mixing angles within one scene; an isometric grid is the alternative with no horizon or vanishing point.
Choose the light source deliberately, because it dictates how light falls on the background and therefore how shadows and highlights are cast on every object placed on it.

The background is a surface, stage, or backdrop rather than the focus, so everything in it must be subordinate to the real content; avoid photographs in the background because the audience will spend effort trying to work out what the obscured image is.

Colour sets the tone and establishes what the audience expects of the journey, so choose colours that represent the presenter, the company, and the stance being taken, and try to meet the expectation the palette creates.

Screen a candidate palette against three questions — does it appeal to this audience, does it differentiate from competitors while avoiding colours that carry negative meaning in this industry (red for a financial institution but acceptable for a blood bank), and does it reflect who the presenter is.

Understanding the colour wheel, on which the presentation applications' colour pickers are based, supports choosing a harmonious palette: three evenly spaced primaries blend into the full wheel, tints add white toward the centre and shades add black toward the outside; any point at any saturation is selectable provided it contrasts and projects well.

Pick a colour scheme by the contrast and tension it produces: monochromatic needs black, white, and greys plus a broad range of tints and shades to gain contrast; analogous colours touching on the wheel give a narrow harmonious, predominantly warm or cool feel; complementary colours from opposite ends give the most contrast and should be limited to two and arranged so they do not clash; split complementary keeps high contrast with less tension; triadic gives vivid interest and tolerates substituting a tint or shade for one pure hue; tetradic pairs two complements for strong contrast with harmony but needs one dominant colour because equal amounts of four hues will not harmonize.
Determine the background colour before selecting the rest of the palette.

Two factors decide whether a dark or light background is appropriate: the formality of the event and the size of the venue; because the eye needs contrast, pure black and pure white give the greatest contrast opportunity while mid-range coloured backgrounds diminish contrast enough to render parts of the palette unusable.

A dark background reads formal, does not influence ambient lighting, offers fewer shadows but lets objects glow, suits large venues, and does not work well for handouts; a light background reads informal and bright, illuminates the room, works well for handouts, suits smaller conference rooms, and forgoes dramatic lighting and spotlight effects.

Verify the palette contrasts against the background and against the other chosen colours and holds up under a projection test, because colours that look right on a computer screen can appear different or diluted when projected; use your own projector or arrive early enough to adjust the venue's.
Tweak colours manually while projecting, because projectors vary and subtle on-screen colour differences get lost.

Derive an industry palette by eyedropping colours from a series of images that support the subject matter, and choose which elements of those images to draw from — for instance basing an automotive palette on metals and gold with grey primaries so brighter colours pop, rather than on vehicle paint colours.
Assemble a palette from three to five core colours plus a neutral and a highlight colour, starting from the logo colours or industry-appropriate colours and experimenting with tint and shade.

Use neutral colours for background elements, visual hierarchy, and divisions of space, and for secondary data in charts and diagrams so that the emphasized data stands out; neutrals can be shades of the logo colour or tints and shades of the background colour, provided the added surface is not distracting.
Reserve highlight colours for accentuating text and creating emphasis in charts and infographics.
Select explicit light and dark tones of the colour set, because they define the depth of range for gradients — the dark tone becomes the shading and the light tone the highlight.

Do not give every colour equal value: keep additional colours in a secondary supporting role to the core palette to avoid visually overwhelming the audience, and add black sparingly to raise contrast where a point needs emphasis.
About one in twelve people has some form of colour vision deficiency, so vary brightness as well as hue and choose distinguishable shapes to carry the visual story.

Check slides for contrast before presenting by converting the file to greyscale and printing it on a black-and-white printer: anything indistinguishable from the background or from other components there may also be indistinguishable to someone with a colour vision deficiency.
Keep the colour palette open while searching for images so the images work with it, and when shooting original photography have the models wear wardrobe that complements the scheme.

Presentations are a glance medium more closely related to billboards than to other media, so ask whether the slide's message can be processed within about three seconds, letting the audience grasp the meaning and return their attention to the presenter.
Content should be typeset correctly as well as quickly processable, because type is a long-standing part of the culture and most people inherently recognize when it is balanced and well used.

Every font carries a personality, so study height, weight, ascenders and descenders, the counters formed in the negative space, and x-height in order to pick a typeface that reflects the brand's personality — and use true typographic apostrophes rather than foot marks.

Serif faces are intended for sequences of words that run beyond a single line, since their feet visually connect letters and keep the eye on the line in dense copy while varying stroke weights speed letter identification; sans serif letterforms are bigger and bolder and are conventionally used in short bursts such as headlines, subtitles, and captions.

Legibility studies comparing serif and sans serif are inconclusive; the argument that slides should be set in sans serif rests on the analogy to billboards and one informal observation of which billboards were legible at a distance.

Combine no more than two fonts in a presentation — one for headlines and subheads, one for blocks of text — with a third justified only rarely for special emphasis; prefer colour or italics for emphasis, and using a single font throughout is perfectly acceptable.

There is no official word-count rule for a slide: include enough words to serve as a mnemonic that the presenter is comfortable delivering, but keep the count very low, because a wordy slide is read faster than the presenter can explain it and makes the presenter irrelevant to their own presentation.
The default presentation-application template is a slideument — a document rather than a visual aid — and its structure encourages two-line titles and multiple levels of sub-points.
Avoid two-line titles in a presentation because of the distance the eye must travel across the slide, and consider a titles-only deck.
Build text sequentially rather than revealing it all at once, because visible bullets tell the audience what points are coming and leave them bored or agitated waiting for the presenter to catch up.
When repeating an agenda slide for context, grey out the previously covered text using a lighter or darker shade of the background colour so the audience can jump visually to the current point.
condition: an agenda slide recurs through the deck

statement: Do not animate text unless the animation adds value, meaning, or emotion to the content.

Typeset large standalone words and word-plus-image slides properly, because typographic laziness distracts visually attuned audience members in the same way grammar and punctuation errors distract others.
condition: the slide uses large words alone or combined with an image

statement: Type alone can carry a message: often a single word or phrase is all a slide needs.

Apply typographic detail to display text: use ligatures where letterforms join (commonly fl, fi, ft, ff, ffl, ffi), turn on auto-kerning and manually kern the capitals A, R, T, V, W, and Y, and adjust letterspacing or tracking to control a word's density.

Distinguish paragraph spacing from line spacing when setting a block of text — each bullet counts as a new paragraph while a wrapped second line does not, a soft return produces line spacing and a hard return paragraph spacing — and if sub-bullets are used, space them so each is visually associated with its primary bullet rather than with the next one.
Inspect the rag of left-aligned text for a distracting shape and for widows, and fix both by adjusting the text block's width, inserting manual soft-return line breaks, or both.
If bullets are used at all, use them sparingly, and ignore prescriptive counting rules such as 4x4, 5x5, or seven words per slide in favour of composing the bullet slide with design sense.

A bulleted text slide presents headlines only and the presenter supplies the body text, so write each bullet as succinctly as a newspaper headline, keep every line in parallel structure with the same tense and part of speech and the same sentence-or-fragment form, and avoid sub-bullets wherever possible.

Follow one capitalization convention consistently — conventionally title case for titles and initial caps elsewhere, or the company's brand guidelines — use all caps sparingly and only for emphasis because caps read as shouting, and keep punctuation and bullet conventions uniform across the deck.

Validate minimum font size empirically rather than by rule: place a marker as many feet from the screen as the screen's diagonal is in inches and check what is still legible, view the deck in slide sorter at 66 percent, click through every slide from the back row of the actual venue, or divide the oldest audience member's age by two.
For keynote slides do not go below 28 point; consistently dropping under 24 point and reaching third-level bullets means a document has been created rather than a slide.

At large venues, a walk-in or curtain-warmer animation of quotes, trivia, factoids, imagery, or video fitted to the event theme — optionally timed to music with voice-over — is simple to produce yet can carry as much impact as a produced video, and the same assets serve as interstitials that fill the screen during breaks or demo switches.
condition: a large venue with an audience filling the room, or gaps between sessions

statement: Maintaining an organizational library of reusable, pre-approved image parts benefits the whole organization: key design decisions are already made, employees stop scrambling for industry-appropriate imagery, and effort shifts from creating elements to building effective content.

Choose a family of photographs that works as a cohesive system, as if one photographer had shot them all with similar lighting and colour tones, rather than grabbing the first result from an image search.

Favour realism over staged or metaphorical approximation in photography, because stock situations such as hands shaking in front of a globe or nondescript people smiling over a laptop do not occur in real life and so fail to connect with the audience.

Select images of people that reflect the audience's culture or ethnicity, are context-appropriate, are not cropped at the neck, represent the industry, customer experience, and real-life situations, and account for the current era.

Compose photographs on a grid of thirds and place key features at the crosshairs, called power points, because an off-centre focal point reads as balanced, carries energy, holds more interest than a centred element, and leaves open space on the slide for text; recompose an existing shot when needed and enable the camera's built-in grid.

When the photograph that would tell the story does not exist in stock libraries, shoot a custom one: decide what picture tells the story before searching for existing images, light the subjects carefully, avoid awkward shadows, and let extra planning remove the need for later digital manipulation.
condition: no existing stock image conveys the intended message

statement: Own the images used in a deck and never take them from the Web, because if the presentation becomes popular online the rights holder can demand usage fees that are expensive.

Lines are the foundation of an illustration and each width, type, and texture carries a temperament — straight lines with sharp corners read direct and analytical while curved lines read playful and casual — so choose lines that support the rest of the design, optionally assign line styles to distinct purposes as a system, and stay consistent throughout.
The thinnest lines are hard to project and may not appear at all in a large venue.
condition: projection in a large venue

statement: Textured lines cannot be produced in presentation software: use another application, or draw them by hand and scan them in.

A hand-drawn overlay can be produced by printing the photo, tracing over it on tracing paper, hand-drawing or painting new elements, scanning the sketch, making its background transparent, and layering it on the photo — and the overlay can then be animated.
Build an icon library relevant to the industry either by buying pre-illustrated icons or by hiring an illustrator for a custom set.

Drawing an icon library in isometric style — no vanishing point, so opposite sides stay parallel — lets anyone assemble the graphics because every icon appears to sit on the same surface and can be connected with horizontal or diagonal lines, giving large arrangement flexibility.

An organization pioneering an industry can establish dominance by investing in an art library and giving it away to the whole industry, competitors included, so that its own representations become the industry standard.
condition: the organization is pioneering a new industry or category

statement: Complex infographics that show how a system works should be built and animated so the audience grasps the interconnectedness of the parts over time.
Bring in a professional illustrator when the illustrations become too complex to execute.
condition: illustration complexity exceeds in-house skill

statement: Hand off to an illustrator by telling them the story to be told rather than what to draw, so they can propose a solution from a fresh perspective that the audience can digest easily.
Give an illustrator time for research, ideation, and revision cycles; when time-strapped but holding a clear vision of the final product, supply a sketch to save time and money.
Treat the illustrator as the expert and trust their input, because untrained and subjective opinions can derail the outcome of the project.
Consolidate all stakeholders' feedback into clear, objective, non-conflicting direction before giving it to an illustrator.

Diagrams that differ in scale, surface, lighting, and texture each carry their own personality and look absurd together in one file, so standardize on a single texture, light source, or pattern unless the concept genuinely requires more.
exception: unless the concept being communicated needs more than one

statement: Never use clip art.
When buying illustrations online, select ones that look as though a single illustrator created them all.

Derive a deck's visual system from the story's setting rather than from an industry default: a home-centred health message was distinguished from a sterile clinical look by using domestic textures such as wood grain, fabric, and leather, hand-drawn illustrations for a tactile feel, and photos framed the way a family displays them.
A subtle gradient placed behind a chart increases its contrast against the background.

Video slides depend more on the creativity of the idea than on production quality: a clip of a few seconds to half a minute, produced only well enough to make the point and without elaborate staging, can carry powerful unexpected impact and convey complex points economically.

Humans are hard-wired by the fight-or-flight instinct to look at whatever moves, so animation added without purpose inevitably pulls the audience's attention away from the presenter and toward the movement.

Every change on a slide, however subtle, creates distraction and every animation affects the audience's ability to grasp insight, so animation should be used only where it helps the audience process information.
Animation is a key communication strategy rather than last-minute icing, so the time-based elements of a presentation must be designed intentionally.

Animation should look natural and alive with movement that seems familiar and makes sense, should convey the interrelatedness or sequence of the information, and should let the audience process the information in the order the animation presents it.

Identify in advance the specific places where animation will help make the point and invest planning, thinking, and time there — treating each element as an actor in a scene — rather than animating everywhere.

Because viewers read and process visual information the instant it appears, a slide with several visuals while the speaker expounds on one creates confusion as the audience listens and reads ahead simultaneously; hide elements until they are referred to so the discussed item stays the focus and the audience listens more and reads less.
Slow Ken Burns-style animation can create a feeling of nostalgia or the passage of time, while fast-moving quick cuts can create excitement, energy, or surprise.

Animation's legitimate purposes fall into five groups: change in relationship (proximity, hierarchy, flow, comparison, separation or inclusion, influence, attraction or repulsion), direction (enter or exit, zoom, new viewpoint, pan, cover or uncover, construct or deconstruct), change in object (morph, modify, vary, scale, simplify or elaborate), sequence (scene transition, time lapse, growth or decay, process, pattern emergence), and emphasis (controlling eye movement, contrast, moving forward or back, highlighting).

Screen direction carries built-in audience reactions: the eye moves comfortably left to right because it mimics reading and less comfortably in reverse, so protagonists conventionally enter from the left and antagonists from the right; downward motion reads as natural under gravity while upward motion reads as illogical; descending diagonals read as easy and the right-to-left ascent is the most difficult of all screen directions because it opposes both reading direction and gravity.

Approach presentation development more like a screenwriter than a speechwriter — being fluent in what the audience sees on screen, not only in the content — because the same material can be either documented or dramatized.

Animation choices determine both how quickly the audience can process information and how far their eyes must travel, so plan the pacing, the path an object travels, and where the object sits in space; gratuitous motion such as text dropping and bouncing into place is bothersome and carries no meaning, and sometimes combining more than one animation effect tells the story better.

Make motion obey physics to look natural: a descending object should drift in the direction of its entry angle, ground contact should deform its shape, and its exit arc should be shorter because energy was lost on impact — which requires combining several animation effects.

Objects entering or exiting from a distance need a path-based animation combined with a scaling effect, and establishing a horizon and vanishing point on the slide creates the illusion of a third dimension so objects shrink or grow as they move between background and foreground.

Content can pan from scene to scene rather than only from slide to slide: when one slide lacks the real estate, split the content across slides and connect them with a push transition so the audience perceives one continuous space and treats the information as connected — for instance a complex timeline split into a pushed sequence that reads as one long timeline.
condition: the content exceeds what one slide can legibly hold

statement: Displaying complex content all at once instead of over time makes it illegible and drives the audience to read ahead.

Overzealous animation can induce motion sickness and lose part of the audience outright — in one briefing two of twenty executives sat through most of the presentation with their eyes closed, a tenth of the room.

The presence of an animation feature in the application is not a reason to use it; specific animations can be banned outright when they are counter-cultural to a brand's personality, and many custom animation features are best treated as if they did not exist.

Animation is being used wrongly when it is unnatural or counterintuitive, when its pace is frenetic, annoying, or chronic, when it adds no value or serves no purpose, when the movement distracts from the presenter, when a feature is used just because it exists, when so many animations confuse the purpose, when the style is inappropriate to the content, or when a sudden animation startles the audience.

When more than one person builds presentations for an organization, a well-built template system is mandatory: templates raise productivity, constrain exploration, protect the brand investment, and reduce the design skill each author needs.
condition: more than one person authors presentations in the organization

statement: Centralize presentation design decisions with a few individuals, then distribute and justify those decisions through written template guidelines, which preserves the brand's visual attributes and streamlines development even when a deck is assembled at the last minute.

Employees are ambassadors of the brand whose daily interactions keep it visible, so equipping them with the right presentation tools both tells a cohesive visual story and streamlines their development process.

Build a template from the timeless components of the brand or industry — the visual attributes that rarely if ever change — rather than from an inspiring new campaign or marketing whim, because a large company's template transition takes a Herculean effort that temporarily tanks productivity.
Audit all the material the company produces to separate purely decorative elements from the truly essential visual brand elements, and put only the essential elements in the template.
A template is a basic shell for words and images, not a stand-alone work of art.

Decide what belongs in the template versus on the slide empirically: collect files from many departments, audit them, determine the communication patterns, and build a template that meets each group's communication needs.

An effective template accustoms viewers to where content will appear and signals that content is structured and aligned; content must not bounce from slide to slide, and titles and bullet copy should occupy the same locations unless a deliberate design purpose says otherwise.
exception: unless a variation is intentionally designed to serve a purpose

statement: Publish the reasoning behind the template's placement decisions and divisions of space, because once corporate power-users understand the logic they recognize the underlying structure and have a rationale to use the template — and are more likely to express the brand consistently and accurately.

Consult the IT department before developing a template: ask about the migration plan for the presentation application and build against the newest release if a major upgrade is near, and confirm storage capacity, because presentation files multiply and a 1MB image-heavy template can accumulate to terabytes in a single department within a month.
Supply both a light and a dark template variant so the identity holds up whether the deck is projected to a large formal audience or printed and distributed ad hoc.

Design the branded walk-in and transition screens first and explore several options rather than settling on the first obvious one, because the walk-in visual is the audience's first impression of the presenter.
Once the look is chosen, use it as the building block for the rest of the template so its distinguishing motif carries through the other layouts.
Template guidelines may run from about five slides to a hundred and fifty, and should include a visual representation of the design decision chosen for every form of content the organization uses.

Build the template around how the organization actually communicates — several diagram pages for a diagram-heavy organization, many chart types for a financial institution, image-usage layouts for a photography-rich consumer product, Gantt charts, timelines, and roadmaps for an engineering-driven one — and provide multiples of a layout where needed.

A template's layout inventory divides into segue slides (branded walk-in, title, transition, and a Q&A branded walk-out), content slides (text, text with graphic, quote, charts and tables), and components (grid, colour palette, component style, images overview).
Internet-based presentation applications let collaborators in different locations work on the same file at the same time, with the finished file viewable online or downloadable to present offline.

Presenters should characterize their relationship to their slides as codependent, interdependent, or independent, because dense slides are addictive: default template settings encourage enough text to turn the slide into a document, the slide then serves as a teleprompter, and reading it aloud requires no rehearsal and replaces connection with the audience.

Slides were intended as a visual aid and mnemonic device to help the audience retain and recall material — the stage in a play or the actor's costume, providing context and setting rather than being the star of the show.
Constraining and restricting yourself and your media is the way to break a codependent relationship with slides — restrictions act as liberators — and it takes hard work and commitment.
The biggest issue facing presenters is not taking the time to rehearse; actors are effective because they spend hours memorizing scripts and more hours practising delivery.
The hundreds of visual triggers a presenter puts on slides while formulating the content are a private safety net that means nothing to the audience.

Reduce text by rehearsing the slides, highlighting one keyword per bullet, rehearsing again from only the highlighted word, then deleting every word except the keywords — and replacing the keyword with an image where possible.

Record the delivery by reading the script or presenting the slides aloud, then listen to the recording during a commute or before sleep, because many people are auditory learners and absorbing the content this way makes reducing on-slide clutter feel safe.

Repeat the content aloud several times and then from memory, using flash cards, mind maps, or a written summary to tell yourself the story and work past stumbling blocks, before deleting as much text and junk from the slides as the remaining key points allow.

Removing clutter is a process demanding courage, practice, time, and trial and error, and a presenter may show more nervous energy at first, but it shifts the presentation toward connection with the audience and away from the slides.

Use the application's setting that projects the image on the big screen while showing notes view on the presenter's own screen, so the computer becomes the teleprompter or comfort monitor instead of the projected screen.

Memorize a talk with the Roman Room method: build the speech as a mental building whose rooms and features are each associated with an idea, so the story is the architecture and any route through it still covers the whole story; when visual aids are used, fix them in one specific order the way a tour guide walks a building.

Attention spans are short and shaped by thirty-minute sitcoms, ten-minute videos, and fifteen-second commercials, so content that is necessary but not emotionally stimulating gains impact by being packed into a smaller time slot.

Constraining a presentation's length forces the presenter to be concise and to remove anything superfluous to the message; the world's most influential speakers deliver powerful content in eighteen minutes or less.

The Pecha Kucha format — exactly 20 slides each advancing automatically after 20 seconds, six minutes and forty seconds in total — forces the presenter to edit their own work ruthlessly and ends a weak talk quickly.

For internal company meetings, constrain the presentation and reserve part of the meeting for conversation, collaboration, and Q&A; capping the number of slides and moving rapid-fire lets more insight be shared in one sitting.
condition: internal company meetings

statement: A presenter who crams in more content than the slot allows brings the resulting auctioneer pace and the avoidance of questions and discussion on themselves.

Evaluate and reject the habits formed from relying on presentation software — consider what would happen to the talk in a power outage — because being able to present without slides forces ownership of the content.
For a small audience, non-projected visual aids — flip charts, props, handouts, flip books, physical devices — work and their tactile quality increases the presenter's humanness.
condition: a small audience

statement: In a large venue, blank the screen with the B key for black or the W key for white to force attention onto the presenter, and if the keyboard is out of reach, place an all-black slide in the deck as a visual pause.

A pause creates drama and meaning and reinforces the point; going to black gives the audience time to contemplate, and turning the projector off during a critical passage makes the audience feel they are interacting solely with the presenter, which can build credibility and trust.

The projected screen dwarfs the presenter — roughly eight times a person's size in an average business venue and nearly forty times in a large 16:9 keynote venue — and that visual dominance shifts the audience's focus from the presenter to the images.
Fear of public speaking ranks higher than fear of dying.

Treating slides as an extension of one's persona — competing on how sexy or jazzy the deck looks — is a trap: the presenter's top concern should be how well they communicate, not how good they look, because slides that look great do not necessarily convey useful meaning.
Polished slides cannot compensate for the absence of a strategy; prettying up thin content leaves presenters exposed in front of an audience.

The 10/20/30 rule — ten slides, no more than twenty minutes, and no font smaller than thirty points — is proposed for presentations where the audience must reach consensus, on the reasoning that a person cannot comprehend more than ten concepts in a meeting and that needing more than ten slides to explain a business suggests there is no business.
condition: the audience needs to reach consensus, such as a venture pitch

statement: A venture pitch should cover ten topics: problem, solution, business model, underlying magic or technology, marketing and sales, competition, team, projections and milestones, status and timeline, and a summary with a call to action.
condition: pitching to investors

statement: Plan to deliver the pitch in twenty minutes of an hour slot, because setup consumes time and attendees arrive late and leave early, leaving roughly forty minutes for discussion.

Presenters use small type for two reasons — not knowing the material well enough, and believing more text is more convincing — and forcing a minimum of thirty points improves the presentation because it compels the presenter to find the most salient points and explain them well.
As soon as the audience works out that the presenter is reading the slide text, they read ahead, leaving presenter and audience out of sync.

A single prescriptive slide-count rule does not fit every situation: investors being asked for millions want written content they can study and circulate, and details and facts matter to them as much as message clarity.

When following a minimal slide rule, put the script and supporting text in the notes area and design the notes master well — printed two-up, the notes view yields a handout almost as sophisticated as a brochure while keeping all the content available.
condition: a low-slide-count deck must still leave the audience with complete content

statement: The Lessig method — a very large number of slides carrying one big idea each, delivered at a fast pace — works but is not easy and requires practice.

There is no correct slide count: one slide every two minutes is the common default, yet some presenters need four slides a minute and others linger four minutes on one, so use as many slides as the message requires and keep to one point per slide because anything more demands more than most audiences will give.

Presentations authored for online repositories and embedding must be built more like a brochure — complete thoughts and phrases on a slide or across a series, with simple images — because there is no presenter and usually no audio to supply the missing narration.
condition: the deck will be consumed online without a live presenter

statement: A presentation authored once for online distribution can be seen by millions of viewers, which is a reason to invest proportionate time in it.
Match the medium to the room: projection is best for a big room with a big audience, while projecting slides for only a couple of people in a small room comes across as impersonal.
Flip charts suit small collaborative settings because audiences enjoy watching someone draw, and flip books work when only one or two people are seated at the table.
condition: small, collaborative, or table-side settings

statement: When the information on the slides is complex or dense, always distribute a handout — preferably at the end so paper is not rustling during the talk — and include an appendix with the dense data so the audience can verify the facts.
condition: the slide content is complex or dense

statement: Content distributed on a handheld device needs accompanying audio and slides built specifically for that format, because large amounts of text and data do not survive the scaling — on-screen 24-point type can reduce to an unreadable 4 points on a phone.
condition: delivery on a small handheld device

statement: Videotaping a presentation or converting slides to video reaches a broad web audience, but the content must stay short because most video sites cap length at around ten minutes.
condition: distribution as web video

statement: Uploading or collaboratively building a presentation on the web serves as a cheap web-conferencing tool and lets bloggers embed the deck in their posts.

A web-cast viewer sits close to the screen and can move closer for detail, so more text is acceptable than in projection; where multitasking and distraction are high, break the content into bite-size bursts to keep interest.
condition: delivery by web cast

statement: An in-person projected presentation can create energy and a moving shared experience that the other media cannot translate, but the screen behind the presenter is huge and the slides visually dominate.
A prop must translate from the stage or under video magnification; a real, tangible item — a rare object, a costume, a revealed surprise — is a powerful way to drive a point home.
condition: the prop remains legible at stage distance or on a video feed

statement: Ensure the content is readable at each screen size on which it will be consumed, and change the visual aid to suit the audience rather than assuming slides are the only solution.

Drawing or writing while speaking prevents the audience from reading ahead and keeps them captive to the story; a few key words or a sketch boiled down succinctly acts as a mnemonic the audience recalls later, and repeating the same sketch across successive sessions reinforces the point.
A flip chart can serve an audience of thousands provided a video feed magnifies it onto a large screen so everyone can see it.
condition: a video feed magnifies the chart for the room

statement: When the screens are not carrying content, projecting calm ambient imagery keeps the audience focused on the message rather than on a dead screen.

A memorable presentation does not need many slides: strong storytelling, large gestures, and a single memorable physical prop can surpass the need for media, with the few slides used only to supply context.
Two different presentation methods for the same message are not ranked against each other when the outcome is the same, so the method is instrumental to the outcome rather than a value in itself.
Presentations are a human medium and the presenter's own experience, passion, and way of expressing are what set the talk apart, because that expression cannot come from anyone else.

The presentation format pushes presenters toward automaton delivery — using slides as a metronome for prescribed information, often with their back to the audience — and the applications do not inherently help the presenter come across as a real person, so that has to be worked at deliberately.

The healthiest relationship with slides is interdependence, and the relationship has a third party — the audience — so the media should let the audience see what the presenter is saying rather than showcase the presenter or their dependencies.
Judge success by the audience's response: whether they appear enlightened, moved to act, or willing to change their behaviour.

Review the content through the eyes of the audience, take them on a journey by showing something they have never seen, and combine strong stories with convincing information delivered in a genuinely human way.
Treat the audience as king: they came to find out what the presenter can do for them, so give them a reason for spending their time, content that resonates, and clarity about what they are to do.

Getting people to feel they have a stake in an idea is the hard part of spreading it, and communicating with strong visual grammar that engages all the senses is how an audience comes to adopt an idea as its own.

Epiphanies and profoundly moving experiences come from moments of clarity, so guide the audience through ideas in a way that helps rather than hinders comprehension and appeal to their visual as well as verbal senses.
Practise design rather than decoration: instead of making pretty talking points, display information in a way that makes complex information clear, which is what turns audiences into evangelists.
Display information in the way that best serves comprehension rather than in the way the presenter needs as a visual crutch, because it is the content carriers who connect with people.
